finding_triage.finding: Two outcome-claim landmines in the card's own copy: the PPN 018 sentence ('the number a company publishes gates its eligibility for £5m+ contracts') is an inference the PPN text does not support, and 27.2% is presented as a measured non-compliance rate when it is Filing date minus End date.
finding_triage.why: Engine-never-arbiter is violated by the marketing, not by the core value — the engine is pure arithmetic over the customer's own rows against published formulas behind a Companies House auth-code gate the product structurally cannot pass — so both sentences are struck and the mechanism framing survives.

reposition.one_liner: Filing Period turns a UK qualifying company's own AP ledger export — plus, where the law requires one, a client-retention extract — into the statutory payment practices report field-for-field in the order the GOV.UK publish service asks for it, with an invoice-level derivation workbook naming which date field, which exclusion rule and which speed band produced every figure; priced per filing, computed as arithmetic against DBT's published formulas, with the director reviewing, approving and publishing.
reposition.price: £149 per entity-report (standard) / £249 per entity-report where the SI 2025/75 construction retention block applies; £999/yr multi-entity pass covering up to 10 entities (20 filings) plus the SI 2025/1152 directors'-report payment block. THE ANCHOR IS THE REGULATOR'S OWN NUMBER: DBT's Final Stage Impact Assessment (Feb 2024, DBT024(F)-23-BG) puts 'prepare reports twice yearly' at £630/£700/£770 low/central/high per non-construction business — roughly £350 per report — with collate/approve/submit at £377 and a total ongoing burden of £1,195 central (£1,702 construction). £149 is ~43% of the government's own per-report preparation estimate; two filings a year is £298, ~25% of the total burden, leaving the director-approval and submission portion the product does not do clearly outside the price. Construction at £249 sits against a £1,051 prepare estimate. The £999 group pass prices at ~£50/filing against IA footnote 20's observed £3,000–£15,000/yr self-reported reporting spend (n<5, the only observed transaction range in the category). THE MONTHLY LADDER IS DEAD AND MUST BE DELETED: £99/month = £1,188/yr is 99.4% of the entire annual burden, and 63.1% of 2026 filings landed in January and July alone, so a subscription bills ten months a year for zero use. Per-filing is the only shape the corpus supports.
reposition.wedge: DBT PUBLISH SERVICE (free first-party): concede the entire eligibility-and-deadline half — /decide/ and /deadlines are free, good, and in the buyer's path, and a reminder product is why the prior ballot died. Flank on the half DBT publishes a spec for and prepares nothing of: its own words today are 'Once you've prepared all your report data, you must publish your report online.' No calculator, no template, no CSV upload, no API, verified 2026-08-20 (/api, /report/upload and /account/sign-in all 404). Residual pain to price: receipt-date convention (guidance: explicitly not the software posting date), reg 6 qualifying-contract tests, the four exclusions, value sums mandatory for FYs from 1 Jan 2025, the two retention ratios, and the derivation record. Design so keying convenience is never more than a third of the value, because a DBT CSV import would delete that third and nothing else. SAGE X3 (KUK, page dated 28 Jul 2026 — actively maintained): sharpest flank in the file. Its documented Excluded calculations list opens with 'Invoice, open item, or payment amounts' — value statistics are impossible in X3 by design, not by omission — and it ends 'you need to manually enter the data on the UK government website.' Every X3 filer must compute the mandatory value block somewhere else. DYNAMICS 365 F&O (ms.date 2026-05-12, ER v67.18): the weakest flank, so target it last. It already ships per-vendor/per-payment detail tabs and a receipt-date parameter, pre-empting the workbook and lineage story for its users. Position as the consumer of its export, not its replacement: ingest Payments_made/Payments_due and complete the value sums, the retention block, the directors'-report block and the assembled artifact — the three things its own doc declines, ending 'use the report data to prepare the final report about payment practices for publication.' BUSINESS CENTRAL (the mid-market ERP that actually serves this buyer, ms.date 2024-06-21): ships a generic global report producing average agreed payment period, average actual payment term and % within agreed period — the Swedish shape, not one field of the UK 0-30/31-60/61+ bands, and not updated for the 2024 or 2025 amendments. It produces zero usable UK output. XERO / QUICKBOOKS / SAGE 50/200 / NETSUITE (NetSuite UK Localization verified: payment formats and tax framework only, no payment-practices report): total absence of any helper. THIS IS THE BEACHHEAD — BC and the no-report packages first, X3 second, D365 last. FORVIS MAZARS + ACCESS GROUP 'bespoke reporting package': quote-only, unpriced, human-paced, and the Mazars page is stale enough to still cite 'BEIS' (abolished Feb 2023) and to call the duty 'annual' when it is twice-yearly. Flank on price transparency, same-day turnaround inside a 30-day window, and a machine-readable derivation record; and sell TO them as a self-serve multi-entity white-label back end rather than only against them. FREE REGISTER BENCHMARKING (gov.uk check service, Capitalise credit reports): concede outright. Benchmarking is a lead-generation surface and must never appear as a priced feature or a moat claim.
reposition.distribution: (1) PROGRAMMATIC SEO OFF THE OGL v3 REGISTER — the largest free surface, one nightly GET of check-payment-practices.service.gov.uk/export/csv/ (102MB, 52 cols, 114,624 reports, 10,235 named companies, live to yesterday). Page classes: one per company for all 10,235 ('<Company> payment practices report', '<Company> average time to pay', showing their own published history, days between period end and filing for each report, and sector percentile); ~700 SIC-sector distribution pages ('payment practices benchmark — <sector>'); period/deadline pages ('payment practices reporting deadline for period ending <date>'). Query patterns targeted: '<company> payment practices', '<company> average time to pay', 'payment practices report <sector> average', 'how to calculate payment practices value statistics', 'construction retention reporting SI 2025/75', 'directors report payment data SI 2025/1152'. (2) FREE-TOOL WEDGE — upload an AP CSV, get the count-based statistics (average days, the three bands, % not paid to terms) free, because that is precisely what D365 and Sage X3 already give away so it costs nothing competitively; pay for the value sums, the retention block, the directors'-report block, the assembled submission pack and the derivation workbook. Trial-by-doing with no human in the loop. (3) ENFORCEMENT-EVENT TRIGGER — the highest-intent list in the corpus, and the one that survives the 'you only reach people already doing the job' objection. DBT has written to 500+ firms and over half returned to compliance (Lord Leong, 15 Oct 2025); a company that returns to compliance publishes catch-up reports, and 992 of 2026's late filings are >90 days late with 860 reports >180 days late. A daily register diff names every late and catch-up filer, with company number, within 24 hours of publication — companies that have just been forced through the job manually and must repeat it in six months. (4) CALENDAR TRIGGER, PER ENTITY, FROM THE REGISTER — each company's period end + 30 days is computable from its own filing history, so outbound is dated, entity-specific and carries their own last-published figures; concentrated into the two real windows (January and July carry 63.1% of filings), not a year-round drip. (5) NON-FILER ENUMERATION VIA COMPANIES HOUSE ACCOUNTS DATA PRODUCT (free, live, daily ~100MB iXBRL zips) — tag turnover / balance sheet / employees, intersect against the register, produce the 'appears in scope, never filed' set that the register-driven plan is blind to. Ship it as a second-wave SEO surface ('does <company> have to report payment practices?'), not as the acquisition thesis, because that cohort has nine years of revealed preference for doing nothing. (6) SPEC-EVENT CONTENT — when the Commercial Payments Bill passes and its secondary legislation specifies interest-paid/interest-owed reporting and the persistent-late-payer board commentary, that is a new spec, a new field set and a fresh page class; a maintained generator is the natural landing page for every 'what do I have to report now' search. NO SALES CALLS, NO PARTNERSHIP MOTION, NO DEMOS ANYWHERE IN THIS PLAN.
reposition.why_winnable: The job is arithmetic over the customer's own rows against a formula the regulator publishes — one jurisdiction, one regulator, one HTTP GET, no scraper fleet, no per-customer human work, and the product literally cannot file or sign because the publish journey is gated behind a Companies House authentication code, so engine-never-arbiter is structural rather than promised. Nobody is in the market: ten independent search angles across four validation lenses found no SaaS, no published price, no directory listing and a GitHub search returning zero. Two ERP vendors fund recurring UK localisation and both stop at the identical line — no value sums, no retention, no artifact — and a top-10 accountancy firm staffs a service line for it, which is what a real recurring job looks like. The spec churns constantly (thresholds Apr 2025, value stats Jan 2025, retention Apr 2025, directors' report Jan 2026, a Bill in Lords Report stage now), and churn is exactly what an unattended maintained generator monetises and an ERP release train does not. THE HONEST DOUBT, STATED PLAINLY: willingness to pay is unproven at any number and the register shows a competent population with near-100% field completion, so there is no visible distress to rescue — the sale is time, cost and a defensible derivation record, not fear. The pitch cannot lean on criminal liability, which is legally exact and commercially inert after nine unprosecuted years. The gross ceiling is roughly £1.9m/yr at £149 across ~13,000 filings at 100% share of a flat-to-shrinking base with a known threshold-uplift step from 2027, so a realistic 10–25% penetration is a £200–500k/yr business — real for a zero-marginal-cost company, not a venture outcome. And the first build must be the free calculator with a live checkout behind the paid half, because the one thing that must be tested before anything else is whether a finance manager will actually pay £149 in a filing window.

residual_risks: WILLINGNESS TO PAY IS THE WHOLE BET AND IS UNTESTED. Not one price, invoice, quote or listing exists for this artifact anywhere; the nearest evidence is IA footnote 20's n<5, 5x-wide £3,000–£15,000/yr range. The £149 figure is derived from the regulator's cost model, not from anyone's observed purchase. Gate: a live checkout on the free calculator must convert before any further build.

DBT SHIPS A CSV IMPORT. The service was rebuilt Jun–Dec 2024 specifically because the original was 'hard to maintain and update', the codebase is now extensible, and the Bill forces another change cycle. No upload route or API today (verified: /api, /report/upload, /account/sign-in all 404), but an import would delete the keying-convenience third of the value. Mitigation is to keep keying convenience under a third of the value; watch the DBT digital blog and the publish service weekly.

SAGE OR MICROSOFT CLOSES THE VALUE-SUMS GAP IN ONE LOCALISATION RELEASE. Both are actively maintaining (X3 page 28 Jul 2026, D365 12 May 2026). If either adds the sum totals per band and the sum not paid within terms, the residual product is pack assembly, lineage and the directors'-report block. D365 shops are already partly pre-empted (per-vendor/per-payment tabs, receipt-date parameter) and should be the last segment targeted, not the first.

THE RETENTION DIFFERENTIATOR HAS A LEGISLATED DEATH DATE. The Commercial Payments Bill voids new and pre-existing construction retention clauses after a two-year transition. The £249 construction tier and the SI 2025/75 block have a horizon around 2028–29; the offsetting new interest-paid/interest-owed fields are not yet specified in secondary legislation, so the replacement revenue is promised, not scheduled.

SPEC AMBIGUITY THE PRODUCT MUST RESOLVE AND DISCLOSE, NOT SILENTLY DECIDE. SI 2025/75 Sch 2 para 10(1) requires a percentage 'of the difference between' sums A and B while para 10(2) gives the formula sum A / sum B x 100 (same conflict in para 11); DBT guidance resolves to the ratio. Similarly, SI 2025/1152 reg 1(4) applies the whole of Sch 7 Part 9 from FYs beginning 1 Jan 2026 while DBT guidance phrases it as elements 4 and 5 only. Every such divergence must be shown on the face of the pack with both readings named — this is reg 9 territory and the exact place an unattended engine could accidentally arbitrate.

GARBAGE IN ON THE RECEIPT DATE. SI 2024/444 para 14 makes a payment 'made' when received by the supplier, not when the AP run clears, and guidance says invoice receipt is not the software posting date — yet D365 defaults Receive document date to invoice date. The average-days statistic is wrong no matter how good the arithmetic if the field is wrong. The substitute field used must be named on the pack and in the workbook every time, never quietly substituted.

THE INPUT IS NOT ALWAYS ONE CSV. Retention sum B is receivables-side (company vs its clients) and absent from any purchase ledger for the ~13% of filers with qualifying construction contracts; the SI 2025/1152 block is group-consolidated and full-year. The uploader and the marketing must both stop claiming one-CSV universality, which narrows the frictionless case to the plain-vanilla non-construction single entity.

SEASONAL CASH AND SEASONAL CHURN. With 63.1% of filings in January and July, revenue arrives in two bursts and there is no monthly relationship to retain a customer between them; the persisted settings and lineage archive are the only retention mechanism and they are unproven as such.

TAM IS SMALL, FLAT, AND STEPS DOWN. ~6,340 distinct filers in 2026 vs 7,538 in 2019, only ~297–450 genuinely new filers a year, and ~6,000 companies economy-wide reclassify as medium under the April 2025 uplift with drop-out landing from 2027 (two-balance-sheet test). Model the ceiling at ~£1.9m/yr gross before committing build time.

TWO CARD STATISTICS ARE DEAD AND MUST NOT SURVIVE INTO MARKETING. The '696 blank value fields' signal (all nil returns) and the '3,762 group structures' claim (3,492 filed exactly two, ordinary cadence) are refuted by the corpus itself. The 27.2% figure must be restated as 'filed more than 30 days after period end' (30.2% of companies filed at least one such report), never as a measured non-compliance rate, and the PPN 018 register-gating sentence must be struck entirely — the PPN text does not reference the register.

REGISTER COUNTS DO NOT RECONCILE WITH DBT'S OWN STATISTIC. Local parse gives 13,308 reports filed in 2025 against DBT's published 11,178 valid reports, and at least one exact duplicate row exists. Any register-derived number used in a public benchmark page must carry a stated derivation and definition, or the SEO surface itself becomes an accuracy liability.

THE PUBLISH JOURNEY MAY ALREADY PREFILL NARRATIVE ANSWERS. It sits behind a Companies House auth-code gate that could not be tested. If DBT prefills last period's tick-box and narrative answers, a meaningful slice of the 'persisted answers' value evaporates on day one and cannot be discovered without a real filer's credentials.

THE REGIME HAS A LEGISLATED HORIZON. SI 2024/444 moves the sunset to 6 April 2031 with a review at 6 April 2029 — comfortable, but finite, and the review is a real decision point that a company built entirely on this one mandate must watch.

survivors.name: Article 14 (CRA exploit clock)

finding_triage.finding: ENGINE-NEVER-ARBITER AT THE CORE: 'your clock is already running' asserts a legal determination (Guidance C(2026) 5252 para 213 'reasonable degree of certainty after an initial assessment'; Art 3(42) + recital 68 'manufacturer establishes'). Raised independently by all four lenses.
finding_triage.why: The violation lives in the headline promise, not the mechanism — the engine can state only feed facts ('CISA added CVE-X at 17:00:32Z'), artifact facts ('your v2.3.1 SBOM contains purl Z'), and regulation citations, with the customer pressing 'Acknowledge awareness' to start a timer they own; two of the four validators independently prescribed exactly this fix, which is the definition of fixable-by-mechanism-framing and therefore fails the Class A 'unfixable' test.

finding_triage.finding: THE EUR 15M ANCHOR IS VOID FOR THE TARGET SEGMENT: Art 64(10)(a) exempts micro and small enterprises (<50 staff, Rec. 2003/361/EC) from administrative fines for missing the Art 14(2)(a)/14(4)(a) 24-hour deadline.
finding_triage.why: A price-anchor constraint, and a narrow one — the exemption covers only the 24h early-warning deadline, leaving the 72h notification, both final reports, Art 13/Annex I, non-monetary corrective measures under market surveillance, and the entire 50–249-staff band of the stated ICP fully exposed; the standard treats price floors and anchors as constraints to be repriced.

finding_triage.finding: NO LEGAL DUTY TO MONITOR — THE PRODUCT MANUFACTURES ITS OWN CUSTOMER'S LIABILITY (Commission FAQ 5.1: monitoring 'is not required'); subscribing converts a non-obligation into a running clock plus a discoverable record that the customer knew.
finding_triage.why: This is the report's strongest finding and it kills surveillance-as-a-product, but not answerability-as-a-product — awareness arrives through the inbound channels the FAQ enumerates precisely because they happen (customers, researchers, CERTs, the SCA tooling this segment already runs), and the pain being sold is 'which of the versions I placed on the EU market contain this, and who did I ship them to' on a 24-hour fuse, which the product does not create and cannot be answered without a per-release archive.

finding_triage.finding: A PRICE-MATCHED COMPETITOR HAS ALREADY SHIPPED THE IDENTICAL PRODUCT AND THE IDENTICAL WEDGE: CVD Portal, live, Free/€99/€299/€1,499, 'Article 14 notification workflow (24h/72h/14d)', SRP-ready package, SBOM registry, plus a free no-signup classification tool.
finding_triage.why: Under the corrected standard this is the single most valuable finding in the report and it points the opposite way from how it was scored — a live incumbent selling this exact job at a published price is proof the market pays and sets the clearing price to beat or flank, and the validator concedes customers, funding and churn are all unverified (it posted to HN five weeks ago).

finding_triage.finding: THE FILING LOOP CANNOT BE CLOSED, EVER: ENISA SRP FAQ Q15 — 'no Application Programming Interfaces will be provided at this stage'; submission is EU Login web UI with CSIRT validation of registered representatives.
finding_triage.why: This is a level constraint on every vendor in the category rather than a differential disadvantage (the competitor advertises the same copy-paste deliverable and says so on its own homepage), and it is the WH-347/Ratepin precedent exactly — the absence of any automated path raises, not lowers, the value of a validated, paste-ready, field-complete artifact.

finding_triage.finding: THE CARD'S OBLIGATION MODEL IS INCOMPLETE: omits the one-month final report for severe incidents (Art 14(4)(c)), the CSIRT intermediate-report power (14(6)), the parallel user-notification duty (14(8)), and the four-step main-establishment routing cascade for non-EU manufacturers (14(7)).
finding_triage.why: A build-spec defect that the validator has already corrected free of charge; each omission becomes either a deterministic branch with a citation or a customer-asserted input (14(7) routing must be customer-asserted regardless, since 'main establishment' is a legal characterisation).

finding_triage.finding: NO DEMAND SIGNAL AT T-MINUS-23-DAYS: 2026 CRA stories on Hacker News score 6 and 5 points with zero comments while the 2022–23 outrage posts scored 215/183/151/137/126; live discussion is political, not operational.
finding_triage.why: This measures the wrong channel rather than absent demand — EU embedded, IoT, firmware and on-prem vendors are not HN's population, the card's own risk note already flagged HN as politically hostile to the CRA, and the distribution plan must not depend on it.

finding_triage.finding: MATCH CEILING PLUS NEAR-ZERO EVENT RATE: only 278/1,671 (16.6%) of KEV resolves to any package identifier; ~0.88 KEV additions/day worldwide implies roughly one purl-matchable addition every six days globally and 0–2 hits per customer per year.
finding_triage.why: Fatal to an alerting product's retention but not to an archive product whose value is availability-on-demand rather than event frequency — and partly over-read, since 83.4% of KEV is proprietary vendor software (Microsoft, Cisco, Ivanti, Fortinet) an SME does not ship as a component, making whole-KEV the wrong denominator; it is a hard constraint that dictates the packaging, which is what constraints do.

finding_triage.finding: SILENT-GREEN MATCHING FAILURE, DEMONSTRATED LIVE: Debian/all.zip yields 0 KEV matches while Debian:12/all.zip yields 175; Ubuntu records are keyed UBUNTU-CVE-… with aliases:null so alias-joins silently return zero.
finding_triage.why: An engineering-quality bar with a known fix — per-release bucket enumeration, CVE-from-ID parsing, and a golden-set regression suite (Log4Shell, CVE-2021-3156) gating every deploy — not a fact about the market or the corpus.

finding_triage.finding: THE DELIVERABLE IS THINNER THAN THE PITCH: per ENISA FAQ Q16 only ~six fields are obligatory at the 24h stage and CVE/EUVD ID is merely Optional; the judgement-heavy fields (severity, impact, malicious-actor detail, remediation) all sit at 72h/final and are exactly what an engine must not invent.
finding_triage.why: A packaging constraint that correctly relocates the value away from the 24h form and onto the shipped-version answer, the dated evidence chain, and the 72h/14-day/one-month packet — and it hands over the exact field schema for free, so the build target is small, public and testable.

finding_triage.finding: COMPETITIVE GROUND ALREADY TAKEN AND NO DATA ARBITRAGE: sbomify ships a 'CRA Compliance Wizard' in its $159/mo Business tier and owns the SBOM-archive position; ENISA's EUVD exploited list is a 99.6% mirror of CISA KEV (1,671 of 1,678 shared).
finding_triage.why: A bundling-gap finding that fails the standard's adequacy test — sbomify's own CRA page (fetched) claims no KEV monitoring, no clock and no ENISA drafts, and its Dependency-Track partner still has no KEV at all — while 'no data arbitrage' is true of every competitor equally and simply confirms the moat must be the customer's own unbackfillable shipped-version history rather than the feed.

finding_triage.finding: THE FREE OSS SUBSTITUTE IS ONE MERGED PR FROM CLOSING THE GAP: Dependency-Track (Apache-2.0, free) already has EPSS/NVD/GHSA/OSV, and KEV ingestion is an open, maintainer-acknowledged request (#2267, discussion #5461) whose requester explicitly cited CRA reporting.
finding_triage.why: Textbook free-substitute-with-worse-UX — an issue open since 2022-12-10 with 'there is a plan' after four years is evidence of low maintainer priority, not imminence, and even if it ships it closes only the detection half, leaving per-release immutable history, the dated evidence chain, the SRP-shaped artifact and the fact that DT must be self-hosted by someone.

finding_triage.finding: PRICING IS BROKEN: $99 entry prices below the segment reference ($159 sbomify) against a $0 credible substitute and destroys the anchor; $799 sits above every published self-serve price; and 'shipped versions under watch' is a value metric nobody in the segment uses and is anti-correlated with value.
finding_triage.why: This is free pricing advice, not a kill — adopted wholesale below, with entry moved to €149 (at the reference, not under it) and the meter moved to products with digital elements placed on the market, which is the CRA's own legal unit.

finding_triage.finding: NO DEMAND-SIDE EVIDENCE EXISTS: no customer, review, procurement thread or case study for any Article 14 clock product at any price; every CRA-specific vendor (craevidence, CMA Testing, ONEKEY, Black Duck) is sales-led with no published number.
finding_triage.why: An unproven, not a disproven — the standard permits a contested market to be tested by launching, and this is the one finding I weight heaviest and price the bet against, not the one that disqualifies it.

finding_triage.finding: THE PLANNED FREE-SCOPE-CHECKER WEDGE IS ALREADY OCCUPIED: cra-facts.com gives away a Scope & Class Checker, Obligations Checker and SBOM tool and explicitly refuses to sell software; CVD Portal runs a free no-signup classifier.
finding_triage.why: This kills that specific wedge — and it should, since a scope checker is also the artifact closest to legal advice — but not the company; the free tier moves to the per-release ledger, which nobody gives away and which no competitor can retroactively backfill.

finding_triage.finding: TAM IS NARROWER THAN WRITTEN: Commission FAQ 1.2 puts standalone SaaS and cloud solutions outside the definition of products with digital elements, removing much of the '10–200 person software vendors' ICP.
finding_triage.why: The standard states plainly that small-but-real TAM is a constraint rather than a kill, and this one sharpens the ICP into a better-defined and more genuinely forced buyer — embedded, IoT, firmware, on-prem, desktop and SDK vendors placing physical or installable products on the EU market.

finding_triage.finding: SCHEDULE DEPENDENCY ON AN UNFINISHED GOVERNMENT SYSTEM: the SRP is not live 22 days out, its public URL is unpublished, the testing period is only 'expected', the only field spec is FAQ prose, and an Art 14(10) format implementing act is discretionary ('may').
finding_triage.why: Affects every vendor in the category identically and is mitigable in code — form definitions must be data-driven and the ENISA/Commission pages diffed weekly, which is itself a publishable distribution asset rather than a cost.

reposition.one_liner: Ship Record keeps an immutable, hash-anchored SBOM of every version you have placed on the EU market, and when a component inside one of them appears in CISA KEV or ENISA's EUVD it hands you a dated evidence packet and a pre-filled ENISA SRP form skeleton — it never decides whether Article 14 applies and never starts a clock: you press Acknowledge awareness, and the timer is yours.
reposition.price: Free 'Shipped-Version Ledger' (1 product, unlimited releases, archive + attestation, no watch) -> EUR 149/mo Record (1-3 products, unlimited versions and components: KEV/EUVD/OSV adjacency watch, dated evidence packets, customer-started clock, 24h SRP form skeleton, VEX suppression list) -> EUR 399/mo Answer (up to 10 products: 72h / 14-day / one-month packet skeletons with judgement fields blank-and-required, Art 14(7) routing worksheet, Art 14(8) affected-user list, customer-facing SBOM/VEX distribution portal, procurement-questionnaire export) -> EUR 899/mo Fleet (unlimited products, authorised-representative and importer/distributor sub-accounts for non-EU manufacturers). Anchors, all fetched 2026-08-19: entry is set deliberately AT the two observed reference prices and not below them — CVD Portal Reporting at EUR 99/mo (the exact-job competitor) and sbomify Business at USD 159/mo billed annually (the adjacent reference the whole segment prices against); EUR 399 sits at the top of the observed self-serve band (Aikido Basic USD 300, Aikido Pro USD 600, Acuna GRC ~CHF 449/mo) and well under CVD Portal Enterprise at EUR 1,499/mo; EUR 899 stays below both CVD Portal Enterprise and Interlynk's AWS Marketplace equivalent of USD 1,500/mo. The card's USD 99 entry is abandoned because it prices under the reference against a EUR 0 tier, and the meter changes from 'shipped versions' (metered by nobody, and anti-correlated with value since trunk-based teams burn versions while carrying one product's exposure) to 'products with digital elements placed on the market' — the CRA's own legal unit, since Art 14 obligations attach per product.
reposition.wedge: CVD Portal (EUR 0/99/299/1,499, live, same job): flank on the archive and on counter-positioning. Their registry is a current-state SBOM store plus a workflow; ours is an immutable per-release ledger tied to CI artifact hashes, and no vendor — including us — can retroactively backfill what a customer shipped in 2024-2026, so the switching cost is created by the customer's own release cadence. Second flank is one they cannot copy without abandoning their headline: their pitch is the clock workflow, ours is 'we never start your clock' — for a CTO who has read Commission FAQ 5.1 (no duty to monitor), 'the acknowledgement is yours, and the record shows exactly what you were shown and when' is the legally safer purchase. Third flank: our free tier keeps the ledger; theirs gates the registry. sbomify (USD 159/mo, 'CRA Compliance Wizard', Dependency-Track integration): flank on exploit signal and evidence chain — sbomify's own CRA page markets the 24-hour framing but claims no KEV monitoring, no clock and no ENISA drafts, and Dependency-Track still has no KEV after four years, so the gap is dated KEV/EUVD adjacency plus a citable evidence packet plus the SRP-shaped artifact; also flank on caps, since Business stops at 5 products / 200 components and we cap components never. craevidence.com (all tiers 'Custom', sales-led, does daily KEV monitoring): flank on self-serve alone — they gate with 'a member of our team will be in touch within one business day'; a CTO at 23:00 holding a customer email asking 'are you affected by CVE-X' can be live on us in ten minutes with a card, and a zero-human company can publish a price they structurally cannot. CMA Testing (launched 2026-06-25, 'AI compliance assistant automatically generates ENISA-compliant early warning, detailed and final reports'): flank by refusing to do it — we assemble the skeleton deterministically, inject only verified feed and artifact facts, and leave every judgement field blank and required with its Art 14(2)(b) citation; 'nothing in your filing was written by a model' is simultaneously the A2/A3-clean design and the pitch to the customer's counsel. Black Duck / Snyk / Socket / Mend / Sonatype (bundling risk): flank on unit and price — Snyk meters USD 25/dev/mo, Socket floors at USD 125 and USD 1,000/mo, Black Duck is contact-sales, and none meters per product placed on the market, so a six-person firmware vendor with three products pays per-seat enterprise shapes for a feature that is SCA alerting, not shipped-version history; bundling is not near-universal in embedded/IoT and the bundled feature is not the job. OWASP Dependency-Track (USD 0): flank on what it structurally lacks — no KEV (issue #2267 open since 2022-12-10), no per-release immutable history (it models current projects, not a ledger of what you shipped), no dated evidence chain, and someone has to host and run it. cra-facts.com and OpenCRA (free checkers and templates): do not fight them — concede the scope-checker wedge entirely (it is also the artifact closest to legal advice) and give away the ledger instead, which nobody gives away.
reposition.distribution: Four programmatic SEO surfaces, each generated from a public entity list on a cron, with no opinions and no conclusions on any page — only feed facts, artifact facts and regulation citations. (1) One page per exploited CVE, keyed to two public lists that update themselves: CISA KEV (1,671 entries today, ~0.88 additions/day) and ENISA EUVD exploited (1,678, keyless JSON) — query patterns 'CVE-XXXX-YYYYY CRA Article 14', 'is CVE-XXXX-YYYYY reportable under the Cyber Resilience Act', 'CVE-XXXX-YYYYY ENISA reporting'; each page carries KEV dateAdded, EUVD exploitedSince, EPSS, affected purls resolved through OSV, and the Art 14 decision tree with citations. (2) One page per affected package, 'pkg:<ecosystem>/<name> CRA Article 14', fanned out from the 278 purl-resolvable KEV CVEs across their OSV version ranges — the long tail the developer actually types. (3) Twenty-seven pages, one per Member State, '<Member State> CSIRT CRA Article 14 reporting', built from the public NIS2/CSIRT designation list — the Art 14(7) routing question every non-EU manufacturer has and nobody has SEO'd. (4) Fifty-two pages mapping each of the 26 published ENISA SRP fields to CycloneDX 1.7 and SPDX 3.0.1. Free-tool wedge (not a quiz): an MIT-licensed GitHub Action and CLI that generates and hash-anchors a per-release SBOM into a free hosted archive for one product — listed on the GitHub Marketplace, which is a real self-serve channel a zero-human company can occupy, and present under github.com/topics/cyber-resilience-act. Enforcement-event triggers, two crons: a KEV/EUVD addition auto-publishes its CVE page within the hour and pushes to a public, free 'KEV -> EU CRA adjacency' JSON+RSS feed that nobody publishes today (EUVD mirrors KEV but never frames it for Art 14) — being the canonical free feed is the top of funnel; and a weekly diff of the ENISA SRP FAQ, Commission guidance C(2026) 5252 and any Art 14(10) implementing act, auto-published as a dated public changelog, which earns links precisely because the only field spec in existence is FAQ prose that will move. Marketplaces: GitHub Marketplace, AWS Marketplace SaaS (Interlynk's listing proves this channel converts in this category), Azure Marketplace — all self-serve, all zero-human once listed. Timing: the free ledger must be indexed before 11 September 2026 so the first-day-of-obligation searches land on an already-crawled site. No partnerships, no sales calls, no HN dependence.
reposition.why_winnable: The corpus is free, keyless and hourly-pollable and every competitor reads the identical feed — CISA KEV and ENISA EUVD are a 99.6% mirror of each other — so nobody in this category has a data moat, and the only compounding asset available is the customer's own accumulated shipped-version history, which is created automatically by their CI, cannot be backfilled by anyone for a competitor's new signup, and grows more valuable with every release. That is the ideal asset for a zero-human company: it accrues without labour. The second structural advantage is that craevidence, CMA Testing, ONEKEY and Black Duck are all sales-led with no published price, so simply publishing a number and shipping a Stripe checkout is a flank a company with no salespeople gets for free. The third is that the distribution plan is 3,400+ pages generated from two self-updating public lists plus a 27-row government registry — work a machine does better than a person. The honest doubt, stated plainly: there is not one line of demand-side evidence in the entire validation — no customer, no review, no procurement thread — so every price observed is supply-side belief, and the headline alert fires perhaps once a year per customer, which means retention rests entirely on whether the ledger and the customer-facing distribution portal get opened weekly during release cycles and procurement questionnaires. If they don't, this churns hard regardless of the regulation. I would fund it as a fast, cheap, deadline-timed test with a hard 90-day kill on zero paid conversions — not as a conviction position.

residual_risks: Zero demand-side evidence exists anywhere in the validation: no customer, review, case study or procurement thread for any Article 14 clock product at any price. Every observed price is supply-side belief. The first 60 days after launch must produce paid self-serve conversions or the thesis is falsified — this is the risk I weight above all others.

The headline alert fires 0-2 times per customer per year (16.6% KEV purl-resolution ceiling against ~0.88 KEV additions/day worldwide). Retention therefore depends entirely on the ledger and the customer-facing distribution portal being weekly-use artifacts during release and questionnaire cycles, not on the alert. If they are not, churn kills it whatever the regulation says.

CVD Portal shipped the same job first at EUR 99/mo with a free tier and a free classification funnel. Its customers, funding and churn are unverified; if it is well-resourced the flank narrows to counter-positioning ('we never start your clock') plus the unbackfillable archive, which is thinner than a price or coverage advantage.

Dependency-Track KEV ingestion (issue #2267) could ship at any time and commoditise the detection half for free and self-hosted. The archive, evidence chain and SRP artifact survive, but the pitch narrows and the free-substitute comparison gets harder.

ENISA's SRP is not live 22 days from the obligation date, its public URL is unpublished, its only field spec is FAQ prose, and an Art 14(10) implementing act specifying format is discretionary. Form skeletons must be data-driven and the schema diffed weekly, or the artifact silently goes stale.

The awareness trap survives the reposition for some buyers: counsel who has read Commission FAQ 5.1 may advise a client not to instrument awareness at all. Selling answerability rather than surveillance mitigates this but does not eliminate it, and it will show up as a depressed conversion rate rather than as an objection anyone voices.

TAM is embedded, IoT, firmware, on-prem, desktop and SDK vendors only — standalone SaaS is out of scope per Commission FAQ 1.2. That segment is smaller and historically more sales-led and hardware-shaped than a self-serve GitHub-App motion assumes, so the free-CLI wedge may under-convert against a buyer who does not live in GitHub.

Silent-green matching failure is a demonstrated live trap, not a hypothetical: OSV bucket naming (Debian vs Debian:12) and Ubuntu records with aliases:null both return a confident zero. Without a golden-set regression suite gating every deploy, the product lies confidently to a customer relying on it — the worst possible failure mode here.

Art 64(10)(a) voids the fine anchor for sub-50-staff buyers on the 24-hour deadline specifically, so the EUR 15M number must never appear in copy aimed at that band; conversion there has to be carried by procurement pressure and answerability alone, which is a softer and slower sell.
Twenty-two days to 11 September 2026. Missing the date forfeits both the only timing advantage and the SEO index lead time, and there is no second deadline until 11 December 2027.

Engine-never-arbiter discipline is permanently load-bearing: scope, Art 14(7) routing, product-level exploitability, and every 72h narrative field must stay customer-asserted forever. That permanently caps the automation story against competitors like CMA Testing who are willing to have a model write the substance of a regulatory filing, and some buyers will read the more automated product as the better one.

survivors.name: ExclusionAuto (OIG/SAM exclusion re-screening)

finding_triage.finding: THE MANDATE DOES NOT EXIST AS PITCHED — OIG's 2013 SAB says verbatim that providers are 'not required by statute or regulation to check the LEIE'; the monthly duty in 42 CFR 455.436 binds State Medicaid agencies.
finding_triage.why: The pitched copy is false and must be rewritten, but the job is demonstrably compelled and paid for anyway — 42 CFR 1003.200(b)(4)'s 'knows or should know' standard, a $25,595-per-item penalty with a treble assessment, named OIG settlements (Lowry $292k, Northridge $227k), and state-contract push-downs like MassHealth Bulletin 196 — so this is a positioning defect, not the Class A 'zero enforcement AND zero intrinsic pain' case.

finding_triage.finding: DEMAND HAS NO LEGAL FLOOR — compulsion is contractual and state-by-state, making willingness-to-pay soft and price-sensitive.
finding_triage.why: Soft compulsion is a price constraint, and the market has already revealed the price band it clears at ($25 one-time to $299/mo bundles across eight live vendors); a soft mandate lowers the ceiling, it does not remove the buyer.

finding_triage.finding: PRICED ABOVE THE INCUMBENT IT CLAIMS TO UNDERCUT — $49/mo proposed vs ExclusionScreening's published $30/$40.
finding_triage.why: This is a refutation of one arbitrary number on the card, not of the market; it is exactly the clearing-price signal the corrected standard says to re-anchor against.

finding_triage.finding: THE STATED MOAT IS REFUTED — LEIE+SAM is not differentiation; $40/mo already buys LEIE + SAM + 46 state lists.
finding_triage.why: A false moat claim kills the pitch, not the company — it forces the wedge onto a different axis (artifact, archive, workflow), which is precisely what a reposition is for.

finding_triage.finding: THE WEDGE IS ALREADY OCCUPIED — HealthProviders DB sells flat-fee, self-serve, uncapped continuous monitoring at $89/mo covering more lists, page modified the day of validation.
finding_triage.why: A live incumbent selling the same job at a real price is proof the market pays and sets the anchor to beat or flank; under the Ratepin standard this is a validation, and it is a single unfunded-looking solo operator, not an entrenched platform.

finding_triage.finding: PRICE LOSES AT THE SMALL END — $25/100 metered and $30/mo beat $49 for a 100-name roster, and that is most of the TAM.
finding_triage.why: Correct, and it is a segmentation instruction: abandon sub-100 rosters to the free tier and the metered incumbents, and sell only into the 150–2,500-name band where the caps and quote walls bite.

finding_triage.finding: BUNDLING PRESSURE — Accountable includes federal exclusion screening free in every subscription; Compliancy Group bundles it at $249+$10-12/employee; Viventium ships it inside healthcare payroll for 9,000+ providers.
finding_triage.why: Bundling kills only if near-universal in the segment AND adequate; these are three vendors in a fragmented market, and the bundled feature is federal-monthly screening with no point-in-time archive and no counterparty packet — inadequate for the staffing flow, and per-head pricing inverts brutally at 200+ workers ($2,249/mo).

finding_triage.finding: WILLINGNESS-TO-PAY IS CAPPED BY A FREE GOVERNMENT SUBSTITUTE — OIG's own searchable DB (free) plus the free 15.5MB CSV.
finding_triage.why: This is the textbook pricing-and-positioning constraint: OIG's tool caps at 5 names at a time, has no roster memory, no monthly recurrence, no dated evidence archive, and no counterparty artifact — abundant residual pain to price, and it is not in the 300-name agency's existing path.

finding_triage.finding: THE PRODUCT CANNOT COMPLETE THE JOB IT SELLS — no SSN/EIN in the downloadable file, so OIG requires final verification through its Online Searchable Database; every candidate match is handed back.
finding_triage.why: This is a scope fact, not a corpus death: it defines the honest deliverable (a dated record of a published search plus raw candidate rows) and hands OIG the identity determination, which is the correct place for it — the residual hand-back volume is a support-cost risk to measure, not a disqualifier.

finding_triage.finding: ENGINE-NEVER-ARBITER FORBIDS THE ARTIFACT THE MARKET IS ACTUALLY PAYING FOR — a clean 'compliant' attestation.
finding_triage.why: The Class A test is that the CORE value only sells if it asserts a legal outcome, unfixable by mechanism-framing; here OIG's own guidance defines the valuable artifact as documentation of the name search performed ('such as a print screen'), which is a pure mechanism claim, and a live competitor already words it that defensively at $89/mo — so mechanism-framing fixes it.

finding_triage.finding: ENGINE-NEVER-ARBITER STRAIN — the card's numeric 'match score' is a number the customer acts on.
finding_triage.why: A design defect with a known fix: publish a binary, reproducible rule (normalized name equality + DOB equality), show every raw candidate row and field-level agreement, emit no score and no clearance language.

finding_triage.finding: SAM.GOV IS NOT A FREE, KEY-FREE, AUTONOMOUS FEED — the card's endpoint returns 404 and does not exist; GSA requires an identity-proofed account, an API key, and throttles non-role users to 10 requests/day.
finding_triage.why: Explicitly the Class B 'licensing obtainable with one-time setup' case — one registration, one key, and a single daily pull fits inside even the 10/day floor; the card's endpoint error is a fact correction, and LEIE alone (key-free, live) carries the product if SAM ever goes dark.

finding_triage.finding: A4 vs MARKET FIT IN DIRECT CONFLICT — 44+ state lists, five sampled states produced five ingestion patterns (rotating filenames, ASP.NET postback, WebSphere portal, unverifiable), and ProviderTrust's own map lists 'States with Email Requests Only'.
finding_triage.why: Email-only states are a genuine A6 breaker for those states, which makes state coverage a scope decision, not a kill: ship the machine-retrievable subset, print exactly which lists and which file dates are covered, and never claim 46 — conceding coverage is survivable only because the wedge is moved off coverage entirely.

finding_triage.finding: 'DETERMINISTIC MATCHING' IS FALSE AND DRAGS IN EMPLOYEE PII — real NPI on only ~10.3% of individual rows; DOB (98.9%) is the actual disambiguator, so the product must ingest HR PII.
finding_triage.why: A corrected mechanism plus a real compliance burden (breach-notification scope, likely BAA requests), both of which are priceable and designable — DOB-optional with an honestly labelled degraded mode, click-through BAA — not a fact that voids the corpus or the market.

finding_triage.finding: MATCHING QUALITY DEGRADES WHERE THE MONEY IS — SAM has no DOB or EIN, CA's 23,894-row list has no NPI, NY collapses name and AKA into one free-text field.
finding_triage.why: It sets an accuracy ceiling that must be printed per source on the artifact; it makes the product a record rather than a determination, which is where the arbiter rules already put it.

finding_triage.finding: FALSE NEGATIVES ARE STRUCTURAL AND UNMEASURABLE — no alias/AKA column, names recorded as of the exclusion date; Exclugo sells 'Alias Exclusion Monitoring' as a separate SKU.
finding_triage.why: A permanent blind spot that must be disclosed on every artifact, and disclosing it is consistent with selling a mechanism record; it also confirms a monetised adjacent gap rather than proving the core is worthless.

finding_triage.finding: FRESHNESS MISREPRESENTATION RISK — OIG labels the current file '07-2026' while it is stamped 2026-08-10 and contains only prior-month actions, leaving a ~40-day blind window.
finding_triage.why: Fixable and in fact differentiating: key staleness detection on Last-Modified plus supplement-file existence, and print 'exclusions through end of prior month' on the face of every record.

finding_triage.finding: PROBABLE FCRA EXPOSURE — a third party furnishing exclusion-match reports used in employment decisions may be a consumer reporting agency, dragging in dispute-handling duties incompatible with an unattended product.
finding_triage.why: Explicitly flagged as unverified in the report and not on the Class A list, but it is the single most dangerous open item: it must be answered against primary FTC/CFPB text before build, and mitigated by contracting the product as a billing-eligibility/compliance database-search record with the customer as sole decision-maker.

finding_triage.finding: NO FIRST-PARTY BUYER TESTIMONY EXISTS — no RFP, no procurement solicitation, no named buyer stating roster size or current spend; all segment evidence is vendor marketing.
finding_triage.why: Weak demand-side evidence is a diligence gap, not a fabrication: eight vendors with observable pricing pages and two named OIG settlements are real market signal that survives removing every vendor blog claim.

finding_triage.finding: THE '46 STATE LISTS' FIGURE CAME FROM COMPETITOR MARKETING, NOT A PRIMARY ENUMERATION.
finding_triage.why: A sourcing error in the card that must be corrected before it appears in any copy; removing it changes the build scope but leaves the LEIE corpus, the penalty regime, and the observed price band untouched.

reposition.one_liner: A monthly exclusion-screening record-keeper for healthcare staffing agencies and home-health operators: we run your roster against the dated federal exclusion files under a published binary rule, hand back every candidate row raw with a direct OIG verification link, archive every file version from the day you start, and generate the per-client proof-of-screening packet your hospital customers contractually demand — we document what the files said on a date; we never say anyone is clear.
reposition.price: Free: 25 names, LEIE-only, monthly, no archive, no signup — sized to make OIG's own free tool ('up to 5 individuals or entities at a time', oig.hhs.gov quick-tips) the thing it beats. Paid, self-serve card checkout, no demo: $59/mo up to 150 roster names; $149/mo up to 500; $349/mo up to 2,500. Anchors, all fetched 2026-08-19: HealthProviders DB Continuous Exclusion Monitoring $89/mo flat, self-serve, no stated cap (the real floor to beat on value, not price) and $25 per 100 providers one-time; ExclusionScreening.com $30/mo and $40/mo, both hard-capped at 'Up to 100 screens per month' with 'Contact Us for Custom Pricing' above and every CTA demo-gated; Compliancy Group Growth $249-299/mo PLUS $10-12 per employee/mo — $2,249-2,699/mo for a 200-worker agency — and Accountable Plus $299/mo, which together mark the ceiling. The $59 tier deliberately undercuts $89 while starting where ExclusionScreening's wall is; the $149 tier sits ~93% below the per-head bundlers at 200 workers. $49 flat is abandoned: it loses to $25/$30 at the small end and buys nothing at the large end.
reposition.wedge: vs ExclusionScreening ($30/$40, 100-name roster cap, demo-gated): flank on the cap and the checkout — card-in purchase at 150-2,500 names, the exact band where their page says 'Contact Us'. Concede state-list count out loud; do not fight there. vs HealthProviders DB ($89/mo, self-serve, uncapped, more lists — the only true head-to-head): flank on artifact and time, not coverage. (a) Point-in-time archive: OIG states it 'only archives monthly supplement files for the previous 12 months', so an archive of every UPDATED.csv and every YYMMexcl/YYMMrein file kept from launch lets a customer re-run any past month's roster against that month's actual file — a competitor cannot back-build it. (b) The two-sided packet from SAB footnote 21: a hospital 'may reduce or eliminate its CMP liability if [it] can demonstrate that it reasonably relied on the staffing agency... agreed by contract... and the hospital exercised due diligence' — so the agency must produce proof and the hospital must collect and audit it. No vendor in the report sells that document flow. vs ProviderTrust, Verisys, Streamline Verify, MedTrainer, 1stHCC (all quote-walled; /pricing returns 404 or a lead form): flank on published price and zero-touch purchase — a 300-name agency should not wait 24-48 hours for a quote. vs Compliancy Group / Accountable / Viventium (bundled): flank on the per-head inversion and on artifact depth — their included screening is federal-monthly with no point-in-time archive and no counterparty packet; concede the sub-50-name buyer who already pays them, and do not target them. vs the free OIG tools: match and exceed the free tier (25 names vs 5), link to exclusions.oig.hhs.gov on every candidate row so the free substitute becomes a feature of ours, and price only the residual pain OIG leaves untouched — batch size, monthly recurrence, dated retention, month-over-month change detection, and the packet an external counterparty demands.
reposition.distribution: All zero-human, no partnerships, no outbound, no calls. (1) Free-tool wedge: a no-signup 25-name batch screen returning raw candidate rows plus per-row OIG verification links — strictly better than OIG's 5-at-a-time cap, and the top of every funnel. (2) Programmatic SEO on public entity lists: 51 state reference pages ('[State] Medicaid exclusion list — current file, publication date, format, and whether the state pushes screening down to providers'), regenerated monthly with live file dates and honest 'no list published' / 'email request only' entries, correcting the unverified '46' figure with our own enumeration. (3) Monthly new-exclusion digest pages built from YYMMexcl.csv and YYMMrein.csv, sliced by state, provider type and exclusion authority — targeting 'new OIG exclusions [month year]', 'OIG exclusions [state] [year]', 'LEIE reinstatements [month]'; these compound permanently because OIG itself deletes supplements after 12 months. (4) Entity-level pages for the 3,446 excluded businesses in the LEIE (official public record, dated, verification-caveated, reinstatement-corrected from the rein files), targeting vendor-screening queries — business entities only, never individual-name pages. (5) Enforcement-event trigger: poll OIG's CMP-and-affirmative-exclusions listing and auto-publish a dated brief within hours of each new 'Employing an Excluded Individual' settlement; supply is real and recurring (Center at Lowry $292,000, Center at Northridge $227,000, listing runs through July 2026). (6) Penalty-number reference pages ('$25,595 per item or service — 42 CFR 1003.210(a)(4), 2026 adjustment, Fed. Reg. 2026-01688'), which is the figure compliance officers actually search. (7) Developer backlink surface: a free public JSON endpoint of the month-over-month LEIE diff and a file-date/staleness feed, embeddable and citable. (8) Two-sided pull: every counterparty packet is a permalink the agency sends to its hospital client, so the recipient lands on our verification page and becomes the next lead with zero outbound.
reposition.why_winnable: The core corpus is key-free, machine-readable, on a stable published cadence, and required no negotiation to obtain (LEIE UPDATED.csv, HTTP 200, 15.5MB, monthly), so fulfilment is genuinely unattended; SAM is a one-time key registration, not per-customer human work, and LEIE alone carries the product if it lapses. The arbiter constraint and the market demand point the same direction here rather than fighting: OIG itself tells providers to 'maintain documentation of the initial name search performed', so a dated, reproducible record of a published rule IS the sellable artifact, not a compromise from one. The SAB footnote-21 flow is the only demand in this space with a hard external forcing function — a hospital contractually auditing its staffing agency — and no vendor found is selling it. The archive compounds monthly and cannot be back-built by anyone who starts later. The honest doubt is real and I would size the first check accordingly: this is a crowded, price-compressed market with a competent $89 self-serve incumbent, there is not one line of first-party buyer testimony anywhere in the validation, the false-positive hand-back volume against a turnover-heavy roster of common surnames is unmeasured and a flat fee does not fund it, and the FCRA question is unanswered. This is a workflow-and-archive bet, not a price or coverage bet; if the false-positive rate per 100 roster names is high, it fails on support load long before it fails on competition, and that number must be measured against a synthetic roster before any build commitment.

residual_risks: FCRA / consumer-reporting-agency classification is unresolved. If furnishing exclusion-match reports used in employment decisions makes the vendor a CRA, disclosure, authorization, adverse-action and dispute-handling duties inject unbounded human work and break A6. Must be answered against primary FTC/CFPB text as a pre-build gate; mitigate by contracting the product as a billing-eligibility/compliance database-search record with the customer as sole decision-maker, and by never rendering an employment recommendation.

False-positive hand-back volume is unmeasured and is the number-one churn and support risk. 9.24% of LEIE individuals share an exact first+last name with another record (MARY JOHNSON x12); on a 300-name turnover-heavy roster the monthly candidate-row volume could exceed the manual work the product removes. Measure FP rate per 100 roster names on a synthetic roster before committing.

DOB ingestion makes this an HR-PII processor — state breach-notification scope and near-certain BAA requests. A negotiated BAA is a human loop that punctures A1/A6; mitigate with a click-through BAA and a DOB-optional, honestly-labelled degraded name-only mode.

HealthProviders DB at $89/mo could cut price or bolt on an audit packet. It appears to be a single-author operation (Tom Kohl byline, no team page), so the $89 anchor is of unknown durability and could move in either direction.

Shipping fewer than the full set of state Medicaid lists is a permanent, visible feature deficit against a $40/mo incumbent. The entire reposition depends on the counterparty packet and point-in-time archive being worth more to the target segment than list count — unproven by any buyer source.

Some state lists are obtainable only by emailing a state agency (ProviderTrust's own map legend). Those states can never be covered autonomously and must be printed as uncovered; if a target buyer's state is one of them, that buyer is not winnable.

Alias and maiden-name false negatives are structural — no AKA column, names recorded as of the exclusion date — and the product must print that blind spot on every artifact, which weakens the pitch. Exclugo sells alias monitoring as a separate SKU, so the gap is real and monetised elsewhere.

The ~40-day freshness blind window (files carry only prior-month actions; the current file was labelled '07-2026' while stamped 2026-08-10) must appear on the face of every record, further limiting what the buyer believes they bought.

SAM.gov access depends on an identity-proofed GSA registration and a role for the 1,000/day tier; a policy change or key revocation takes the SAM leg dark. A LEIE-only fallback must be designed in from day one rather than retrofitted.

Programmatic-SEO pages naming excluded parties carry reputational, defamation and de-indexing risk. Restrict to business entities and aggregate/state/monthly pages, state only what the dated government file says, and run a reinstatement-driven correction pipeline keyed to the YYMMrein.csv files.

Any surviving copy asserting a federal monthly screening mandate is factually false against OIG's own bulletin and is itself a liability. The rewrite to the 'knows or should know' standard plus state contract terms is mandatory, not optional, and must be enforced at the template level so no generated page can reintroduce it.
The state-list count must be independently enumerated before it is published anywhere; the '46' figure in the ballot card came from a competitor's marketing page and has no primary source.

survivors.name: CarrierWatch (FMCSA carrier monitoring)

finding_triage.finding: The card's named L&I Socrata datasets (qh9u-swkp, 9mw4-x3tu, 6eyk-hxee) are frozen since 2026-05-14 with zero rows after May, while reporting rowsUpdatedAt of today — so the card's own staleness detector would have shipped green over dead data for three months.
finding_triage.why: The corpus did not die, it moved: the Motus successors (yu5v-wbh6, c5y8-a4uz, wb4f-neki, inys-ebih) plus az4n-8mr2 are live, daily, free and on the same unblocked portal with the same access method — the card named wrong dataset IDs, which is a build-spec error the validation itself already corrected, and the fail-open trap becomes a hard design rule (validate row-level max(date), never rowsUpdatedAt) rather than a kill.

finding_triage.finding: Motus covers only ~103k distinct USDOTs (12.8-23% of legacy active-authority carriers), so the product would be blind on ~6 of 7 carriers in an established broker's approved network while showing them green.
finding_triage.why: Refuted on re-verification: my own SoQL queries show Motus AuthHist carries events back to 1936 and runs 17,216 (Jun) / 16,710 (Jul) / 9,808 (Aug 1-19) events per month against legacy's 19,514 (Apr) and 20,324 (Mar) — throughput parity — with 1,022 events on carriers numbered under DOT 100,000 and 9,396 under DOT 1,000,000; the 14% figure counted carriers with an event in 97 days, not coverage of the event stream, so it is a sampling artifact, not a coverage gap.

finding_triage.finding: Current baseline authority/insurance status for an arbitrary carrier is not derivable from any bulk file today — only changes are visible.
finding_triage.why: A genuine build constraint with two identified solutions (QCMobile behind a free webkey, or SAFER Company Snapshot), both requiring one-time setup rather than per-customer human work, and it is survivable because the reposition sells a dated capture of the record rather than an assertion of current status.

finding_triage.finding: The UCR leg of the headline promise has no machine-readable source: fux9-ij6p is a 2018 href stub with zero columns pointing at Indiana's payment system, HTTP 403 on any SODA query.
finding_triage.why: One of three promised signals dies, but the two that actually carry post-Montgomery negligent-selection exposure (authority status and insurance filings) are live and daily — this is a scope reduction that removes UCR from the promise, not a premise collapse.

finding_triage.finding: QCMobile is not keyless — it returns HTTP 404 'Must provide Webkey', falsifying the card's stated basis for a 2-4 week MVP.
finding_triage.why: The key is free and self-registered, so this is a licensing/setup cost obtainable with one-time setup — explicitly Class B — invalidating a timeline estimate rather than the business.

finding_triage.finding: Engine-never-arbiter breach: 'looks like a chameleon re-registration' is an unattended product publishing a fraud accusation about a named business, in a category with live defamation judgments (Greenline ~$458K, Penguin ~$612K).
finding_triage.why: The chameleon score is not the core value — continuity monitoring and the per-tender evidence record are, and both are pure mechanism — so this is curable by amputation rather than reframing; and my check that az4n-8mr2 holds only 501 prior_revoke_flag='Y' rows out of 4,487,571 destroys the 'FMCSA publishes the link itself' defense, confirming the tier should be cut outright rather than reworded.

finding_triage.finding: 'The moment a carrier lapses... you know before you tender the load' is an outcome/completeness guarantee an unattended product cannot sign.
finding_triage.why: This is marketing copy attached to a mechanism that is itself signable — 'here is the FMCSA record for DOT X, retrieved at timestamp T from dataset D, and here is the row that changed since date E' — so it is a promise rewrite, not a structural defect.

finding_triage.finding: Name collision: DAT sells a product literally named CarrierWatch at $149/mo, and Truckstop has a CarrierWatch product line, both to the identical buyer.
finding_triage.why: A naming decision made before anything ships; non-negotiable but zero-cost to fix, and it is evidence the category is validated rather than evidence the company cannot exist.

finding_triage.finding: Bundling kill pattern #3: Truckstop Carrier Hub Basic is $99/mo with unlimited carriers monitored, and DAT ships CarrierWatch inside broker load-board plans from $159/mo — inside software the small broker must already have.
finding_triage.why: Bundling kills only when near-universal AND adequate, and the conjunction fails on universality: Carrier Hub is a separate paid SKU layered on top of the load board and DAT sells CarrierWatch standalone at $149, so monitoring is a paid upsell rather than an included feature — though it is adequate enough that the reposition must concede commodity monitoring instead of fighting for it.

finding_triage.finding: Price-floor inversion: the card's $39-149/mo band has free tiers underneath and $99/mo unlimited beside it, so there is no gap at any point on the curve.
finding_triage.why: Price floors are named Class B, and the claim is partly wrong on its own evidence — the observed floor for a paid monitoring SKU is $99/mo with the artifact tier at $515/mo, leaving a real $19-49 band that is empty for the evidence artifact even though it is correctly described as hopeless for commodity monitoring.

finding_triage.finding: The card's central willingness-to-pay evidence is vaporware: VerifyCarrier's $49/$99/$249 monitoring tiers are all marked 'Launching Soon' and not purchasable.
finding_triage.why: Class A requires that NO real market signal remain once the bad evidence is removed, and deleting VerifyCarrier entirely leaves DAT $149, Truckstop $99/$200/$369, CarrierOK $149/$349/$499, Carrier Assure $149, SaferWatch $250 MSRP, RMIS $340 and MyCarrierPortal $515 — the signal is denser after the removal, not absent.

finding_triage.finding: The strongest reshape — defensible documentation for negligent-selection defence — is already a shipped incumbent feature: Descartes MyCarrierPortal AuditLog.
finding_triage.why: This is the Ratepin standard's central case: a live incumbent selling the reshaped job at $515/mo unlimited-user is proof the job is paid for and sets the price to flank, and AuditLog documents the broker's own review workflow (self-generated evidence) rather than an independent third-party capture of the federal record.

finding_triage.finding: Free first-party and third-party substitutes exist: FMCSA SAFER Company Snapshot, and usdotwatch.com free with daily sync over 4,487,796 registrations plus a chameleon section.
finding_triage.why: Both are pull-based point-in-time lookups that retain nothing — not equal-or-better UX for the actual job (standing watch plus a dated, preserved, citable record), not in the buyer's path at the moment of tender, and leaving the entire residual pain of 'prove two years from now what the record said on the day you tendered' unpriced; it is nonetheless the most serious Class B item because usdotwatch also occupies the obvious SEO surface.

finding_triage.finding: CarrierOwl, a genuine micro-SaaS in this niche, abandoned watchlist monitoring subscriptions for $29 one-off human-reviewed reports.
finding_triage.why: A real negative signal about commodity monitoring specifically — which is why the reposition must abandon it too — and simultaneously a positive one, since it establishes that a $29 per-artifact price clears in this exact buyer segment.

finding_triage.finding: Platform migration risk: 91 FR 23144 confirms FMCSA is sunsetting the ICC Licensing & Insurance system and MCMIS registration components in favour of Motus during the build window.
finding_triage.why: The migration has already happened and the successor is live and verified at legacy throughput, so this is a realized and navigated risk rather than a prospective one — the company simply builds on Motus, which the card should have done.

finding_triage.finding: No latency edge exists: 49 CFR 387.313(d) gives 30 days' cancellation notice, so every competitor sees the same insurance event at the same moment.
finding_triage.why: Correct and irrelevant to the reposition, and in fact enabling — the 30-day telegraph is exactly what makes an unattended nightly cron sufficient and what makes a forward-looking record possible (1,680 carriers currently sit inside a served-but-not-yet-effective suspension window).

finding_triage.finding: A3 fail-open hazard baked into the source: two datasets share the name 'ActPendInsur - All With History', one refreshed today and one frozen since 2023-12-06.
finding_triage.why: An engineering hazard fixed by pinning dataset IDs and validating row-level max(date) on every run, which is the same discipline the frozen-legacy finding already forces.

reposition.one_liner: TenderProof captures, timestamps and preserves exactly what the FMCSA federal record said about a carrier at the moment you tendered a load — an immutable, hash-sealed, source-cited PDF and API record you can still produce two years later when a negligent-selection plaintiff asks what you knew on the day.
reposition.price: $19 one-off single-tender record; $29/mo Solo (50 records/mo); $79/mo Desk (500 records, standing watch, webhook); $199/mo Brokerage (unlimited records, API/MCP, bulk export, 7-year retention). Anchors, all first-party fetched 2026-08-19: CarrierOwl's $29 per-report price proves a per-artifact point clears in this exact segment; Truckstop Carrier Hub Basic at $99/mo unlimited is the commodity-monitoring floor we deliberately price under and refuse to fight; Descartes MyCarrierPortal at $515/mo unlimited-users is the artifact tier (AuditLog) we undercut ~17x; Carrier Atlas's independent survey of $2-10/carrier/mo and $50-500/seat/mo brackets the band. The $19-79 range is the only part of the observed curve with no paid product in it.
reposition.wedge: Truckstop Carrier Hub ($99/mo, unlimited carriers, bundled with the load board): concede monitoring entirely — it is adequate and cheaper than we could profitably match. Flank on the artifact it does not produce: a per-tender immutable capture bound to a specific load, hash-chained, with the source dataset ID and retrieval timestamp on the face of it — and load-board-agnostic, so it covers tenders made outside Truckstop's workflow. DAT CarrierWatch ($149/mo): alerts forward, retains no defensible retrospective record tied to a tender; flank on artifact plus 5x price. Descartes MyCarrierPortal AuditLog ($515/mo): documents the broker's own review decisions, which is self-generated and therefore the weakest evidence class; flank on independent third-party capture of the federal record, self-serve with no demo, at 1/17th the price. CarrierOK ($149/user, $349/5 users, $499/10 users): priced per seat and per profile; flank on per-tender pricing with no seats. Carrier Assure (free tier, $149 Premium): its free tier sells a carrier *score* — an opinion we structurally cannot and will not offer; flank by never scoring and always citing. Highway (demo-gated, reported $1,500-2,500/mo): enterprise sales-led; flank on self-serve signup. VerifyCarrier (monitoring unlaunched, API $19-99 live): not a fight we enter — and its live API is a usable fallback baseline source if QCMobile rate-limits. usdotwatch.com and FMCSA SAFER (both free): pull-based, ephemeral, retain nothing; a broker cannot produce in 2028 a proof of what SAFER displayed on 2026-07-03. Flank on retention, immutability, timestamp and citation — the exact residual pain the free tools leave on the table. CarrierOwl ($29/report, human-reviewed, one business day): flank on instant and unattended, generated at tender time rather than written up the next day.
reposition.distribution: (1) Free tool wedge — the Tender Record: enter a DOT number, get one hash-sealed, timestamped PDF of the federal record with dataset IDs and retrieval time, free forever at 3/month. It is inherently forwardable (into shipper threads, E&O underwriters, defense counsel) and every footer carries the URL, so the artifact is itself the channel. (2) Enforcement-event trigger, and the strongest engine here: Motus RevokeSuspend currently holds 1,680 carriers with a suspension order served but not yet effective on a fixed 30-day clock (49 CFR 387.313(d)). Publish a free public page regenerated daily — 'FMCSA suspension orders taking effect in the next 30 days' — pure record recitation, no characterization, no scoring. It refreshes itself from a federal file, is linkable, and nobody publishes it. (3) Programmatic SEO on the *legal* surface, not carrier profiles: usdotwatch already owns 4.49M carrier pages, so do not fight there. Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II is 98 days old and its query surface is thin — generate state-level pages against the query patterns 'freight broker negligent hiring [state]', 'negligent selection evidence broker [state]', 'FAAAA preemption after Montgomery', 'what proves a broker vetted a carrier', hydrated from the public 50-state list plus the 4,487,571-row az4n-8mr2 census aggregated by state, never per-carrier. (4) Machine channel: ship a REST API and an MCP server and list on public API/MCP directories — Cipher & Row's $299/mo Essential tier already proves brokers in this segment buy an MCP server. No partnerships, no sales calls, no BD in any of the four.
reposition.why_winnable: The mechanism is fully deterministic — fetch federal rows from pinned Motus dataset IDs, verify row-level recency, timestamp, hash, render, store — with no LLM anywhere in the decision path and no legal conclusion ever asserted; the product states what the record said and when, never whether the broker exercised reasonable care. The demand event is real, dated and unsubstituted: Montgomery (9-0, 5/14/26) attached broker liability to what the federal record said on the day of tender, which is a retrospective evidentiary need that no alerting product satisfies. The honest doubt is threefold and I would not fund this without pricing it in. First, the pain is latent — a broker feels negligent-selection exposure only when sued, which is rare per broker per year, and insurance-shaped products churn; the retention bet is that the evidentiary chain accrues and cannot be ported, but that bet pays over 18 months while the first 6 look like churn. Second, Truckstop or Descartes can add 'capture the record at tender' as a checkbox in a quarter, and the only real defense is price and the load-board-agnostic position, not technology. Third, the free incumbent usdotwatch.com already owns the obvious distribution surface with the same corpus, which forces the harder legal-SEO and enforcement-event channels rather than the easy one.

residual_risks: Baseline status gap: for a carrier with no Motus event since 2026-05-14, current authority/insurance status is not derivable from bulk files at all — the record capture depends on QCMobile (free webkey) or SAFER HTML, and QCMobile's rate limits at watchlist scale are unverified and untestable without registering a key. If QCMobile throttles, per-tender capture degrades to 'change events only' and the artifact weakens materially.

Motus backfill is unknown: pre-2026 history in Motus AuthHist is thin (hundreds/month through the 2010s versus legacy tens of thousands), so the successor holds a complete live event stream but only a partial historical backfill. FMCSA has published no coverage statement and fmcsa.dot.gov is Akamai-403 to automated fetch, so whether the legacy population is ever backfilled cannot be monitored from primary sources.

Latent-pain churn is the central commercial risk: a broker who is never sued perceives zero value in month 7, and the evidentiary-chain lock-in that justifies retention takes roughly 18 months to become switching-costly. Early cohort churn will look indistinguishable from failure.

Distribution surface is contested by a free product with the identical corpus: usdotwatch.com is free, daily-synced, and already indexes 4,487,796 registrations, foreclosing carrier-profile SEO and forcing reliance on the thinner legal-query and enforcement-event channels.

Fast-follow risk from adjacent incumbents: Descartes AuditLog and Truckstop Carrier Hub can each add per-tender record capture as a feature, and both already own the buyer relationship and the workflow; the defense is price and load-board neutrality only.

Chameleon/fraud signals must be cut entirely, not softened — az4n-8mr2 carries only 501 prior_revoke_flag='Y' rows out of 4,487,571, so any collision detection would have to be computed rather than recited, which is precisely the defamation-exposed path the category's judgments (Greenline ~$458K, Penguin ~$612K, both secondary-sourced) warn against. This removes the card's only claimed differentiator from the onboarding tier.

Silent-staleness is an ongoing operational hazard, not a one-time fix: two datasets share the name 'ActPendInsur - All With History' (one live, one frozen since 2023-12-06) and the frozen legacy files still report rowsUpdatedAt of today, so every run must pin dataset IDs and assert row-level max(date) or the product emits confident records over dead data.
Name must change before anything ships — DAT sells a product literally named CarrierWatch at $149/mo and Truckstop has a CarrierWatch line, both to this exact buyer.
TIA's $700M-$1B fraud-loss estimate and the FMCSA complaint-volume growth figures remain unverified against any primary source across all four validation lenses and are unusable in marketing copy.

Motus itself may shrink the job for free: the Federal Register notice puts individual identity and business verification at the forefront of registration, and if FMCSA exposes verification outcomes in the public bulk files, part of the screening value becomes a free government field.

survivors.name: MarkDocket (trademark docketing + watch)

finding_triage.finding: Free first-party substitute #1: USPTO emails courtesy §8/§9/§71 reminders on day one of each statutory window, containing the anniversary deadline, grace deadline and per-class fee.
finding_triage.why: It is one push, once, to the address of record — an address set 5-10 years earlier that is frequently the filing attorney's or a dead domain — and USPTO both disclaims it ('not obligated... failure to receive a reminder does not excuse you') and separately instructs owners to check TSDR themselves every three to four months, which is the agency conceding its own free channel is not sufficient; that residual (persistence, address freshness, escalation ladder) is priceable exactly as Free File leaves residual for TurboTax.

finding_triage.finding: Free first-party substitute #2: tsdr.uspto.gov/maintenanceview/ computes and publishes the §8 earliest/latest/grace dates free and unauthenticated (verified live, 2,155 bytes).
finding_triage.why: It is a per-registration PULL surface with no alert, no portfolio, and no persistence — and the same lens verified it returns HTTP 503 for pending applications (sn79286868), so USPTO computes nothing at all for the entire pre-registration half; a free number you must remember to go look up is a positioning constraint, not equal-or-better UX in the buyer's path.

finding_triage.finding: Free first-party substitute #3: MyUSPTO configurable status-change alerts and Trademark Center's bundled free docketing feature.
finding_triage.why: The report itself files both in Unproven — the only source describing MyUSPTO docketing of arbitrary third-party serials is a nine-year-old 2017 blog post, USPTO's own current page scopes Trademark Center docketing to 'applications filed through Trademark Center', and whether it sends deadline (vs status) alerts is unverified because the features page is an SPA shell; an unverified bundle cannot be a near-universal adequate bundle.

finding_triage.finding: Live incumbent DeadlineDocket ships MarkDocket's literal build (TSDR prosecution-history import → auto-generated OA/SOU/§8/§9 deadlines) at $89/mo, $890/yr, unlimited marks, self-serve, 14-day trial, no free tier, ©2026.
