finding_triage.why: Under the corrected standard this is the single strongest VALIDATION in the report — a self-serve incumbent surviving with no free tier proves the job clears at real money — and 'unlimited marks' does not erase the wedge, it confirms it: $890/yr is priced for a portfolio of fifty, and a three-mark owner facing $890/yr is by definition an unserved price band.

finding_triage.finding: The watch tier's pricing thesis is arithmetically inverted: $9-15/mo/mark = $108-180/yr against Markify's live $39/yr US Federal Full with weekly reports across all classes — 2.8x-4.6x MORE expensive, not undercutting.
finding_triage.why: This is a miner arithmetic error, not a market fact — Markify's $39/yr was fetched correctly and is now the named clearing-price anchor the reposition must sit at or under, which is precisely the 'price floor' the corrected standard classes as a constraint to be repriced against.

finding_triage.finding: Free watch substitutes below Markify: Trademarkia's free weekly confusingly-similar alerts (monetised by a $379 C&D upsell) and PageCrawl.io's Free Forever tier.
finding_triage.why: These are lead magnets and page-diff monitors, not standalone businesses — Trademarkia's free watch only reaches people already inside its filing funnel, and PageCrawl watches pages you name rather than ingesting a filing feed, so it structurally cannot surface a new application by a stranger; the correct response is to stop selling watch standalone, not to abandon the product.

finding_triage.finding: Bundling: Alt Legal sells watch as a +$30-95/mo rider on docketing it already bills, LegalZoom ($249/yr) and Trademark Engine bundle monitoring onto registrations they filed, and USPTO bundles docketing into its own free filing tool.
finding_triage.why: Not near-universal in the named segment — Alt Legal's rider reaches only firms already paying $720-3540/yr, and the LegalZoom/Trademarkia bundles reach only their own filing customers, leaving every owner who filed pro se, filed through an attorney who no longer represents them, or acquired marks by assignment outside all three bundles.

finding_triage.finding: 37 CFR 2.62(a) makes the office action itself the authority ('Each Office action shall set forth the deadline for response'; defaults apply only 'Unless the applicant is notified otherwise'), so the card's 'computed by fixed rule from TSDR prosecution history' is a derived guess.
finding_triage.why: The premise is not false against the primary text — §8/§9/§71 windows genuinely ARE statutory arithmetic (15 U.S.C. 1058/1059/1141k) and the SOU window genuinely is six months from the NOA — and for the one branch that is declared rather than computed, the report names its own fix (quote the deadline the document states, with the document attached), which is a mechanism-framing correction, not a dead mandate.

finding_triage.finding: Wrong-date surface larger than the card models: §66(a) gets six months with NO extension, §1058 can anchor on the §12(c) publication date, §1141k anchors on certificate-of-extension issuance, SOU extension-request limbo under 2.89(c), 2.196 weekend/DC-holiday rollover, 2.66 petitions to revive.
finding_triage.why: Every one of these is a build-complexity constraint with a verified deterministic input — the corpus lens confirmed the §66(a) basis flags are machine-readable free from TSDR statusview ('Filed 66A: Yes / Currently 66A: Yes'), and 2.196 needs a static federal holiday table maintained once, which is one-time setup, not per-customer human work.

finding_triage.finding: Engine-never-arbiter: 'Every statutory trademark deadline on your marks, computed' is a deterministic outcome claim with terminal, non-revivable liability sold to buyers with no counsel.
finding_triage.why: Fixable by mechanism-framing, and both lens 01 and lens 02 independently construct the fixed form ('USPTO's office action dated X states a response deadline of Y — here is the document'; 'TSDR shows event NOA mailed 2026-03-04; USPTO's own §1(d) rule sets a six-month window from that mailing; here is the raw row') — the Class A bar requires the core value be UNFIXABLE by reframing, and the value here is monitoring, persistence, aggregation and a dated archive around a number the agency publishes but does not reliably push, none of which requires asserting a legal outcome.

finding_triage.finding: The watch tier arbitrates in effect — a ranked similarity score reads as a likelihood-of-confusion verdict, text-only matching sells silence as safety, and the base rate is brutal (7,650 oppositions + 19,130 EOTs against 824,000+ classes filed in FY2025, so ≥99% of alerts are noise).
finding_triage.why: The card's own A3 text already ranks rather than opines, and the false-negative problem is discharged by publishing the scope limit as a hard product statement ('US federal word marks only; we do not see design marks, phonetic-only equivalents or foreign equivalents; no alert is not a clearance'), while the <1% base rate is a threshold-tuning and alert-frequency constraint that argues for annual bundled pricing rather than per-alert monthly.

finding_triage.finding: A4 DATA PATH BROKEN: bulkdata.uspto.gov has no DNS A record (BDSS retired 2025-04-11), api.uspto.gov/api/v1/datasets/products/TRTDXFAP returns HTTP 401, and data.uspto.gov's dataset page is an SPA shell — the collision feed is unobtainable as specified.
finding_triage.why: Directly refuted inside the same report by the only lens that actually tried to fetch a file: lens 02 downloaded apc260818.zip (53,213,551 bytes, Last-Modified 2026-08-19 08:02:12 GMT) containing a 1,058,760,367-byte XML with 64,762 case-files and 1,062,793 event statements, established daily ~08:00 UTC cadence, and confirmed a 2025-08-13 file still served for backfill — the CARD's URL is dead, the CORPUS is alive at data.uspto.gov/ui/datasets/products/files/TRTDXFAP/, with two verified free unauthenticated per-mark fallbacks (tsdr.uspto.gov/statusview/, /maintenanceview/) and a free one-time-registerable API key as a third path.

finding_triage.finding: The card's own A4 evidence was a false positive the miner did not notice — data.uspto.gov returns a byte-identical 20,666-byte SPA shell for the real dataset, for /apis/api-rate-limits, and for the invented path /bulkdata/datasets/THIS-DATASET-DOES-NOT-EXIST-12345.
finding_triage.why: A genuine and damning verification failure that voids that specific citation, but the Class A bar is that NO real market signal remains once the bad evidence is removed — and what remains is four independently fetched live paying markets (DeadlineDocket $890/yr, Alt Legal $720-3540/yr, Markify $39/yr, LegalZoom $249/yr) plus a corpus another lens then verified by downloading it.

finding_triage.finding: No observed paying cohort between $0 and $60/mo, and zero demand-side evidence was gathered for whether a 1-10 mark owner pays anything once told USPTO already emails the maintenance deadline.
finding_triage.why: Small-but-real TAM and an untested price point are constraints, not kills — but this is the honest core doubt, and unlike every other finding it is not refuted anywhere in the report, so it must be carried into the reposition as the primary underwriting risk rather than argued away.

reposition.one_liner: MarkDocket watches USPTO's own record for the marks you name and pushes you what USPTO published — its computed maintenance dates from TSDR's maintenance view, the response deadline printed on your office action with the document attached, and the statutory window each prosecution event opens — re-sent on an escalating schedule to an address you actually maintain, with a dated snapshot of the source record at every alert.
reposition.price: $79/year flat, up to 10 marks, docketing and US-federal word-mark watch bundled — no monthly tier, because a 1-10 mark owner's deadlines arrive once every few years and monthly billing is why nobody has cleared this band. Anchors, all observed live 2026-08-19: DeadlineDocket $890/yr unlimited marks (we are 1/11th of the only self-serve incumbent doing this exact build, priced for the portfolio of three rather than the portfolio of fifty); Markify $39/yr US Federal Full watch (we are 2x that and the watch is thrown in, so we never fight Markify on a standalone watch price we would lose); LegalZoom $249/yr monitoring (we are under a third); and the failure cost — USPTO's own fee schedule at $325/class for §8, $325/class for §9, a $100/class grace surcharge and $125 for an office-action extension — so the subscription costs less than the surcharge on filing one class late. Second tier for the solo practitioner: $249/year up to 50 marks, ~65% under Alt Legal's $720/yr floor.
reposition.wedge: vs USPTO courtesy email (free): they send one email, once, on day one of a window that opens 5-10 years after registration, to the address of record — frequently the filing attorney's or a dead domain — and USPTO both disclaims it and tells owners to check TSDR every 3-4 months themselves; we re-send at T-180/90/30/7 and again at grace-period entry, to the address you are actively billing from. vs tsdr.uspto.gov/maintenanceview (free): it is pull, per-registration, no alert, no portfolio — we poll it and push it, and we QUOTE its numbers with attribution so the customer can verify them against the agency, which no paid competitor does; and it returns 503 for pending applications, so the entire pre-registration half (office action, NOA/SOU, extension ladder) has no free USPTO-computed equivalent at all. vs MyUSPTO / Trademark Center docketing (free, bundled): USPTO's own current page scopes it to applications filed through Trademark Center — we track any serial or registration number, filed anywhere, by anyone, including marks acquired by assignment. vs DeadlineDocket ($890/yr): price, plus we quote the office action's stated deadline from the document per 37 CFR 2.62(a) rather than computing a date the regulation lets USPTO override, plus a dated evidence snapshot of the USPTO record at each alert. vs Alt Legal ($720-3540/yr + $360-1140/yr watch rider): not the same buyer; the flank is the 20-mark solo practitioner paying the 50-matter tier. vs Markify ($39/yr): do not fight it standalone — bundle watch so it is included, and win only where we actually win, daily ingestion against a 30-day opposition window versus weekly reports; concede openly that Markify covers 190 registers and design marks and we cover US federal word marks. vs Trademarkia/PageCrawl free watch: both are funnel bait or page-diff monitors — PageCrawl watches pages you name and structurally cannot surface a new filing by a stranger; our flank is the published scope limit, stated as product copy: US federal word marks only, we do not see design marks, phonetic-only equivalents or foreign equivalents, and no alert is not a clearance.
reposition.distribution: All of it runs off the one free daily corpus verified live: data.uspto.gov/ui/datasets/products/files/TRTDXFAP/apc<yymmdd>.zip, ~64,762 case-file records and ~1,062,793 prosecution event statements per day, posted ~08:00 UTC, with a year of backfill still served. (1) Programmatic SEO over the public entity list of every US trademark — one page per serial and per registration, each showing mark, owner, status, full prosecution timeline and the maintenance dates quoted from USPTO's own maintenance view. Query patterns: '<MARK> trademark status', 'trademark serial <NUMBER>', 'registration <NUMBER> renewal date', 'when is my section 8 due', '<MARK> trademark expiration'. Justia and Trademarkia already contest this surface — we win only on the maintenance-date and deadline-window facts neither of them surfaces. (2) Event-triggered daily pages, the strongest surface, because they are the enforcement-event equivalent: the daily file carries NON-FINAL ACTION E-MAILED (~26,807/day) and NOA E-MAILED - SOU REQUIRED FROM APPLICANT (~18,958/day), so auto-publish 'Notices of Allowance issued <DATE>', 'Office actions issued <DATE>', and 'Section 8 windows opening <MONTH YEAR>' — the moment an owner's office action lands is the moment they search for what it means. (3) Free-tool wedge, the Free-File-vs-TurboTax move: a no-signup 'when is my Section 8 due?' page — paste a registration number, get USPTO's own maintenance-view dates attributed and a countdown, free forever for one mark. The paid ask is the escalation ladder, nine more marks and the watch. This is also the highest-intent landing target for (1) and (2). (4) Auto-updating public statistics pages built from the daily status codes — registrations cancelled or expired this month for failure to file — which is simultaneously a crawl magnet and the most persuasive sales argument we have, using only public register facts in aggregate. Explicitly NOT doing: cold-mailing owners of record whose addresses sit in the public file (deliverability and reputational suicide), paid search against filing services that give watch away to acquire $500 filing customers, and anything called a partnership.
reposition.why_winnable: Marginal cost per customer is genuinely near zero and the economics are structural, not aspirational: one daily 1.06 GB parse serves every customer simultaneously, and each additional watched mark is a string match plus a row lookup — which is why $79/yr has real margin where a human-in-the-loop watch service needs $249. The corpus is free, daily, a year deep, and reachable three independent ways (unauthenticated signed-CloudFront file path, free unauthenticated tsdr.uspto.gov/statusview and /maintenanceview per mark, and a free one-time-registerable TSDR API key at 60 req/min — ample when the whole customer base is 10-mark portfolios). Support load is bounded by construction because the product only ever quotes USPTO and attaches the source. Enforcement is the strongest on the ballot: miss a §8 and the registration is cancelled with no revival, at $325/class to refile plus lost priority. And pSEO over a public entity list of millions of marks with a daily event feed is exactly the distribution shape an unattended company can run. The honest doubt, and it is the one I would underwrite hardest: the report gathered ZERO demand-side evidence, and the $0-to-$60/mo gap may be empty because USPTO's free email is good enough for the median owner, not because nobody tried. This bet lives or dies on the free-tool funnel converting at 1-2%+ on cheap organic traffic. If it converts at 0.2%, this is a hobby, and I would want that number before spending on anything but the free tool and the pSEO surface.

residual_risks: No demand-side evidence exists at any price. The report never tested a buyer, and the $0-$60/mo band may be empty because USPTO's free courtesy email genuinely satisfies the median 1-10 mark owner. This is the primary underwriting risk and the reason to build the free tool first and instrument conversion before building anything else.

ODP access hardening could break the unauthenticated corpus path. The working route (browser-shaped headers on data.uspto.gov/ui/datasets/products/files/TRTDXFAP/<file>) is an incidental interface, not a documented one — there is no unauthenticated manifest, so filenames must be constructed by the apc<yymmdd>.zip convention, and the report surfaced unverified claims that ODP requires a signed-in USPTO.gov account with MFA from June 2026 and four additional profile fields from Aug 18 2026. Fallbacks (free API key, free per-mark TSDR views) exist and are Class B, but if USPTO ever ties a key to per-customer identity, A4 breaks outright.

The highest-value alert depends on a keyed dependency. Doing 37 CFR 2.62(a) correctly means quoting the office action's own stated deadline, which requires the TSDR document API at 4 PDF/min per key. Fine at 10 marks per customer; it becomes a real throughput constraint at scale, and it is the one place where the free daily XML alone is insufficient.

Trademarks411's claimed forever-free 15-mark status-and-collision alert plan was never verified (HTTP 403 Cloudflare on both WebFetch and browser-UA curl). If real, it is a second free substitute covering BOTH tiers for exactly our segment, and it must be confirmed in a browser before any spend.

The daily XML's event stream was verified for exactly one day. Whether every deadline-bearing event reliably appears the day it occurs — and whether the 3.1% of records lacking a word mark correlate with any deadline-relevant subset — is unmeasured longitudinally. A silent gap in the feed on the day an office action issues is indistinguishable from not having the product.

Watch-tier false negatives are a permanent, undischargeable exposure. Text-only matching cannot see phonetic equivalents, design marks or foreign equivalents, and a paying customer reads no-alert as safety. The scope disclaimer must be product copy on every digest, not buried in terms, and even then it is the single most likely source of an angry customer.

The pSEO surface is contested by well-resourced incumbents. Justia, Trademarkia and TrademarkElite already index the trademark register at scale. The differentiated content is narrow — the maintenance-window and prosecution-deadline facts they do not surface — and if Google treats our pages as duplicative register scraping, the entire distribution plan has no substitute.

Alt Legal's §2(d) Watch uses actual USPTO examiner citations of the customer's mark — a first-party judgment signal a similarity score cannot replicate. That is a genuine capability gap on the watch tier that price cannot close, and it caps how far upmarket the watch feature can ever be sold.

survivors.name: Denial Weather (CMS coverage/NCCI change alerts)
survivors.candidate: B5 — Denial Weather (CMS coverage / NCCI change alerts)

finding_triage.finding: CLV Intelligence (clvintelligence.com) is a live near-clone selling daily CMS/MAC/LCD/NCCI monitoring with RVU×CF dollar pricing at Solo $49 / Standard $299 / Practice $749 / Team $1,199 / Agency from $2,995 per month, and has already built the card's exact GTM (audit packs $349/$1,499, free per-code SEO pages, comparison matrix).
finding_triage.why: A live seller at a real price is proof the job clears — and CLV is not an entrenched incumbent but a co-entrant mid-alpha (50 founding seats at $199/mo, deadline 2026-09-15, no verified traction), whose published price ladder hands us the clearing price for the multi-NPI segment rather than closing it.

finding_triage.finding: PolicyChanges.app ships specialty-and-payer-filtered daily change alerts with automatic CPT/HCPCS/ICD-10 extraction at $19/mo per user, $45/mo for 3 users, with a free browse tier.
finding_triage.why: Classic price-floor constraint: it is a per-seat consumer of a change feed with no multi-NPI book view, no jurisdiction-scoped code-list join, and no forwardable client artifact — it caps per-seat pricing, not per-book pricing.

finding_triage.finding: PayerPolicy gives a specialty-filtered weekly CMS/commercial change digest away free forever and charges $99/mo for the real-time tier — exactly the card's Practice price.
finding_triage.why: A free substitute at specialty granularity leaves the residual pain the buyer actually has (which of MY 1,800 codes across MY 40 client NPIs in MY MAC jurisdictions moved), so it constrains price and forces the wedge upward, but does not deliver the exact job in the buyer's path.

finding_triage.finding: The stated moat is false: CMS publishes the changelog itself — medicare-ncci-2026q3-...-additions-deletions-revisions-ptp.zip (2,199 additions / 708 deletions / 14 modifier-indicator changes, ungated), the MUE equivalent, plus lcd_x_revision_history.csv and article_x_revision_history.csv inside the MCD export, plus a free no-key Coverage API What's-New endpoint.
finding_triage.why: The Class A test is whether the mandate/artifact/data exists as required — it does, abundantly and free; what collapsed is a differentiation claim, which is a competitive constraint (and cuts both ways: the same free changelog is our zero-cost, license-clean input).

finding_triage.finding: AMA CPT licensing is a pre-code gate — the MCD download agreement grants 'personal use only… non-commercial uses' and forbids 'making any commercial use of CPT'; NCCI full edit files sit behind /license/ama; AMA's FAQ requires a license for 'each product that contains CPT codes' with no descriptor/number carve-out; royalty amounts unverifiable (Cloudflare 403).
finding_triage.why: The corrected standard explicitly classes 'licensing costs obtainable with one-time setup (not per-customer human work)' as B, and this license is demonstrably obtainable — AAPC and Find-A-Code hold one — while the critical-path inputs (HCPCS Level II files, the NCCI additions/deletions/revisions zips, the customer's own uploaded code list) are ungated, so v1 ships without redistributing a single CPT descriptor.

finding_triage.finding: Arithmetic hole: a PTP edit fires on a code PAIR on the same beneficiary on the same date of service, so per-code volume totals carry zero co-occurrence information and cannot produce the headline dollar figure; MUE needs units-per-claim distributions, and CMS states some MUE values are 'confidential… not releasable'.
finding_triage.why: This is a correct and sharp product-design defect that kills the entry offer AS SPECIFIED, not the company — it is fixed by deleting the exposure total (which engine-never-arbiter forbids anyway) and shipping a mechanism statement over the cheap input, with an optional de-identified encounter-grouped code export for true co-occurrence.

finding_triage.finding: Engine-never-arbiter strain: 'before it starts denying claims' and '$41k of exposure against your last 90 days, effective October 1' assert a claims and financial outcome, and rest on an unverifiable payer-mix assumption since NCCI/MUE/LCD bind Medicare FFS while MA and commercial payers adopt variants.
finding_triage.why: Fixable by mechanism-framing — the validators wrote the compliant form themselves ('PTP pair added effective 2026-10-01 per the CMS additions file; your list contains both codes; here is the CMS row and its version') — so the gate binds the copy, not the core value.

finding_triage.finding: Value density kill, measured from the live files: Q3 and Q2 2026 practitioner PTP diffs produced ZERO hits against a standard PT code set and ZERO against dermatology; the entire Q3 practitioner MUE change set was 74 additions, 7 deletions and ONE revision nationally; LCD/Article revisions run ~10-15 article and 2-6 LCD per week across all 12 MAC jurisdictions and all specialties.
finding_triage.why: This is the most substantive finding and it is a targeting fact, not a market fact — enforcement is automatic and pain is primary-sourced (MGMA 48%), so the Class A 'zero enforcement AND zero pain' test does not fire; it kills the single-practice weekly tier and forces the segment to the aggregator whose code breadth makes the digest non-empty, which is the survival path the corpus lens itself identified.

finding_triage.finding: Pricing anchor contradicted by primary data: 'for a mid-size PT practice one changed MUE across a quarter is routinely five figures' is false when the whole quarter contained one MUE revision, on a radiation-oncology guidance code.
finding_triage.why: A fabricated anchor removed — but the market signal survives its removal (three live paid sellers, Part B News at $699/yr, MGMA 48%), so it fails the Class A 'no real signal remains once removed' test; it means we price off observed competitor clearing prices, not off an invented avoided-loss story.

finding_triage.finding: Per-seat superset incumbents undercut the card: AAPC Codify Basic $36/mo and Pro Fee $44/mo bundle NCCI Edits Checker with Change Version, NCD & LCD lookups, MPFS+MUEs, a CMS-1500 real-time scrubber, historical code sets and government publication notifications; Find-A-Code $45–95/mo bundles the CCI validator, jurisdiction-filtered LCDs/Articles and a code-change history tool.
finding_triage.why: Bundling kills only if the bundle is near-universal AND adequate for the exact job — these are per-seat lookup/scrub tools that require a human to go look, and neither performs a cross-NPI book-level pre-effective-date impact pass, so they set a per-seat price ceiling we must not compete inside.

finding_triage.finding: Bundled downstream: clearinghouse and PM scrubbers apply the current quarter's NCCI at submission (CollaborateMD 'Claim Scrubbing Level 2', Office Ally free clearinghouse), and in the card's lead vertical WebPT/Clinicient Insight pops up an edit-pair warning at coding time and auto-updates when new edits publish.
finding_triage.why: Near-universal and genuinely adequate for blocking a bad pair at submission — which is why the practice-level 'advance weather' pitch dies — but structurally silent on the job we are repositioning to: telling a billing company in September what October 1 does across a book of client NPIs, before any claim is coded.

finding_triage.finding: Free first-party substitutes stack up: MLN Connects weekly (current to 2026-08-20), per-document MCD Subscribe on any LCD/NCD/Article, the Local Coverage What's New Report with 7/30/60/90/120-day windows, free MAC listservs (Noridian, Palmetto), free MAC-hosted NCCI PTP lookup tools, and the free no-key Coverage API — plus regulatory advance notice is already structural (NCCI posted ~30 days ahead, final LCDs carry a mandatory 45-day notice).
finding_triage.why: Textbook pricing-and-positioning constraint: every one of these requires the buyer to already know which document to watch and to do the code-list join by hand across jurisdictions, so the residual pain — the join, the book-level rollup, and the dated artifact — is exactly what remains priceable.

finding_triage.finding: Differentiation collapse: CLV already sells the 'longitudinal diff history' as 12- and 24-month archive products ($349/$1,499), and the assembly work is a weekend, so there is no technical asymmetry.
finding_triage.why: A real and permanent competitive constraint — there is no build moat here, only a time-accumulating snapshot archive (CMS ships current-version-only) and whichever SEO surface is claimed first — which is a reason to price modestly and move fast, not a disqualifying fact.

finding_triage.finding: Upload friction: a practice that can produce a clean code+volume CSV could instead paste 25 codes into Codify's free-with-subscription CCI checker; one that cannot never reaches value.
finding_triage.why: True for a 3-provider practice and fatal to that segment; inverted for a billing company, where 'paste 25 codes' does not scale to 40 clients × 200 codes × 6 jurisdictions and the PM utilization export is a report they already run monthly.

reposition.one_liner: Drop Brief: for third-party billing companies and MSOs, a per-quarter and per-week pass that matches every client NPI's billed code list against the CMS-published NCCI additions/deletions/modifier-indicator files and that week's LCD/Article revision rows — jurisdiction by jurisdiction — and returns a dated, white-labelable brief naming each hit with its CMS source row, file version and effective date, plus an explicit signed-off negative when nothing was touched.
reposition.price: $5 per monitored client NPI per month, $99/mo floor (20 NPIs included), unlimited seats — so a 40-NPI shop pays $200/mo and a 200-NPI shop pays $1,000/mo. Entry offer: $249 one-time 'Next Drop Brief' covering up to 25 NPIs, sold in the ~30-day window between the NCCI quarterly posting (~Jun 1 / Sep 1 / Dec 1 / Mar 1) and the effective date. Anchors, all observed live on 2026-08-19: CLV Intelligence Agency 'from $2,995/mo' for 15 seats aimed at billing companies and Practice $749/mo are the only direct book-of-business clearing prices in the market — we undercut Agency 3-15x on the axis this buyer actually counts (client NPIs, not seats); CLV's Tripwire Audit Pack $349 and Premium Pack $1,499 bracket our $249 entry offer; PayerPolicy $99/mo and PolicyChanges.app $19-45/mo set the per-seat floor we deliberately do not compete inside; AAPC Codify $36-54/mo/seat and Find-A-Code $45-95/mo are the per-seat superset ceiling; DecisionHealth Part B News at $699/yr proves this buyer already writes a check for Medicare change guidance with no personalization at all.
reposition.wedge: vs CLV Intelligence (the near-clone, $49-$2,995/mo): they meter seats, we meter client NPIs — their Agency tier is 15 seats from $2,995 with no per-NPI scoping, so a 60-client billing shop pays $2,995 there and $300 here, and gets 60 separately-scoped per-NPI briefs instead of one merged feed; they are mid-alpha (50 founding seats, deadline 2026-09-15) with unverified traction, not an entrenched holder. vs PolicyChanges.app ($19/mo) and PayerPolicy (free weekly / $99/mo): both filter by specialty and payer, neither joins to an uploaded per-NPI code list or scopes to a MAC jurisdiction, and neither emits a forwardable client-branded artifact — the flank is the join and the artifact, not the feed. vs AAPC Codify ($36-54/mo/seat) and Find-A-Code ($45-95/mo): they are pull tools requiring a human to go look, one code at a time, per seat; the flank is push-across-a-book and the fact that our price does not scale with headcount. vs bundled PM/clearinghouse scrubbers (CollaborateMD, Office Ally, WebPT/Clinicient Insight pop-ups): they block a bad pair at submission on October 2 and are strictly better at that — we do not compete there; the flank is September 3, when the Q4 files post and nothing in any scrubber tells a billing company which of its 40 clients is about to start rejecting. vs the free first-party stack (MLN Connects, MCD per-document Subscribe, Local Coverage What's New, MAC listservs, the free no-key Coverage API): every one requires you to already know which document to watch and to do the code-to-jurisdiction join by hand; the flank is that the join is the whole job, and the negative attestation ('0 of 1,847 watched codes touched, checked against PTP v322r0 posted 2026-06-01, file hash …') is an artifact none of them can produce. vs the AMA license gate: v1 ships license-clean on HCPCS Level II descriptors (ungated), CMS-authored PTP Edit Rationale and revision-explanation text, bare CPT numbers echoed back from the customer's own upload, and deep links to the CMS document — a descriptor-free alert is unreadable to a lay practice owner and perfectly readable to a billing company that owns the code list, which is precisely why the segment pivot also solves the licensing constraint.
reposition.distribution: (1) Programmatic SEO on public entity lists CLV has not taken: they claimed the per-code page surface (72,000 ICD-10, 9,000 HCPCS), so we take the per-DOCUMENT surface — one page per LCD ID and Article ID from the MCD export (948 LCDs, 2,029 Articles) crossed with their 16,139 lcd_x_revision_history and 18,809 article_x_revision_history rows, plus one page per quarterly NCCI drop per MAC jurisdiction. Query patterns: 'L##### revision history', 'A##### what changed [date]', '[HCPCS L2 code] NCCI PTP pairs added effective October 1 2026', '[MAC jurisdiction] [state] coverage article revisions [month year]', 'NCCI Q4 2026 additions [code]'. These are mid-problem queries from a biller who just got a rejection — far higher intent than a code-definition lookup. (2) Free 'Drop Radar' tool, no account: paste or upload a code list, get this quarter's CMS-sourced hits instantly, with email capture for 'notify me when the next files post'. Zero-human wedge that converts on the drop calendar. (3) Enforcement-event triggers as the publishing calendar: four hard-dated NCCI/MUE postings (~Sep 1, Dec 1, Mar 1, Jun 1) effective the following quarter, the January CPT/HCPCS turnover, the quarterly HCPCS Level II updates (October 2026 file already posted 2026-08-18), the quarterly MPFS RVU releases, and the mandatory 45-day LCD notice period — each fires an automated public brief plus a re-mail to the free-tool list. Q4 2026 NCCI files post in roughly eleven days; that is the first shot. (4) NPPES: the NPI registry is a free bulk download that publicly identifies organizational providers by taxonomy, including 302F00000X billing/clearinghouse entities — used to generate per-state landing pages ('Medicare edit-drop monitoring for billing companies in Ohio') and to size the segment. No partnerships, no calls, no demos, no sales motion at any tier.
reposition.why_winnable: Winnable: the inputs are free, machine-readable, ungated on the critical path, and already diffed by CMS; the output is a deterministic join with no prose extraction (article_x_hcpc_code → article_x_contractor → contractor_jurisdiction → state_lookup); the purchase trigger is a published four-times-a-year calendar rather than a sales conversation; the buyer is technical enough to self-serve a PM utilization export; and the segment is the one place where neither the per-seat coder tools nor the per-client EHR scrubber can structurally reach, because neither has a cross-NPI view and the billing company — not the practice — is the party that eats the rework across a book. The white-labeled per-client brief is the thing they resell to their own clients as 'compliance monitoring', which is why they will pay above the $19-45 per-seat floor. Honest doubt, stated plainly: there is no technical moat — the build is a weekend, which is exactly why three companies already exist — so the only durable assets are the accumulating weekly MCD snapshot archive (CMS ships current-version-only) and whichever SEO surface is claimed first; if CLV's Agency tier converts they are in this segment already with a head start; and the measured density means the weekly subscription must be sold as a monitored-and-attested service with the quarterly drop brief carrying the revenue, or churn will eat it. This is a small, real, contested business — not a great one.

residual_risks: AMA CPT distribution license price and grant-ability are unverified (both compliance.ama-assn.org schedules Cloudflare-403). v1 is engineered to need no license — HCPCS Level II descriptors, CMS-authored rationale text, bare CPT numbers echoed from the customer's own upload, deep links to CMS — but if AMA later asserts that echoing customer-supplied CPT numbers requires a license and prices it punitively or refuses a micro-SaaS, the descriptor-free product degrades and the license application becomes a hard, unbudgeted gate. This is the single largest unknown and it should be tested by filing the application in week 1, in parallel with the build, not after.

Value density may remain thin even at book scale. The zero-hit result was measured only on the PTP diff against PT and dermatology code sets; the LCD/Article side against a specialty code list was explicitly never measured by any lens. If a 200-NPI book still yields a near-empty weekly digest, the subscription is a churn machine and only the four annual drop briefs are sellable — a materially smaller business (~$1k/quarter/customer, not $12k/year).

CLV Intelligence is the same company, earlier, with an Agency tier already aimed at this exact buyer and comparison pages pre-written against every differentiator. Its traction is unknown; if its alpha converts before we ship, we are the second entrant into a segment with no technical moat.

The de-identified encounter-grouped code export needed for true PTP co-occurrence is heavier than a utilization report and may push customers toward the mechanism-only output permanently, weakening perceived value; and even encounter-grouped data without dates cannot prove same-date-of-service co-occurrence, so the mechanism statement is the honest ceiling.

NCCI/MUE/LCD bind Medicare FFS only; MA and commercial payers adopt variants. Every brief must scope itself to Medicare FFS explicitly or it overstates relevance — which shrinks the visible value for practices whose Medicare mix is small, and cannot be corrected without payer-mix data we do not have.

Engine-never-arbiter discipline is load-bearing here in a way it was not for Ratepin: the moment a brief emits a dollar total rather than a published MPFS rate lookup plus a CMS source row, the product asserts a financial outcome it cannot own. This constraint permanently removes the most saleable headline and must be held under commercial pressure.

MCD Coverage API access terms are contradictorily reported across lenses (401 with token required vs free/no-key since 2024-02-08, with some endpoints needing an AMA/ADA/AHA licence token). The weekly ZIP download path works regardless, so this is a convenience risk, not a blocker — but the 'daily Coverage API poll' in the card remains unvalidated.

Programmatic SEO on LCD/Article revision pages is a slow-compounding channel with a 3-9 month lag, while the free Drop Radar tool and the quarterly calendar are the only fast channels. If neither converts by the Q1 2027 drop (files ~Dec 1 2026), there is no third distribution leg — cold outbound to NPPES-listed billing companies is the weakest and least defensible fallback.

survivors.name: QueueGuard (interconnection queue monitoring)

finding_triage.finding: Premise false at the file level: no public ISO queue file carries a milestone DUE date — CAISO publicqueuereport.xlsx (33 cols), CAISO Cluster 15 (20 cols), ERCOT GIS Large Gen (31 cols), SPP active CSV (27 cols), NYISO (339 rows) all enumerated live, zero forward-looking deadline fields; ERCOT's block literally titled 'GIM Project Milestone Dates' holds only attainment dates.
finding_triage.why: This is the closest call in the file and it is fatal to the countdown MECHANISM the card claimed — but it is a scope amputation, not a dead premise: the same four fetches PROVE the data that the repositioned product runs on (daily-refreshing status/IA/suspension fields, a Withdrawn tab with reasons, ERCOT's own change indicators), so what dies is one claimed feature, not the corpus or the job.

finding_triage.finding: The real deadline arrives by private written notice on a 5-business-day fuse and only AFTER the request is already deemed withdrawn (CAISO GIDAP §3.8; FERC pro forma LGIP §3.7 = written notice + 15 BD cure). A public-file monitor never sees the trigger.
finding_triage.why: It is a decisive kill for the single job 'backstop my cure window' — which the reposition deletes and explicitly concedes to the ISO letter in-product — and says nothing about the job 'tell me, scoped and pushed, what changed in the public record across my portfolio and around it.'

finding_triage.finding: Every computable deadline is anchored to a private per-customer issuance date that appears in no public file (GIDAP §11.3.1.2 180 days after issuance of the final Phase II report; 120 days after SIS/FAS results; 30 BD study-agreement return; 15 BD election).
finding_triage.why: Same amputation: the honest form quotes the tariff paragraph, shows the date the public field flipped, and states in terms that the issuance anchor is not visible and the clock cannot be computed — which is a mechanism claim with the unknown named, not a fabricated legal fact.

finding_triage.finding: The headline pain event is single-digits per year across an entire ISO: CAISO's own Withdrawn tab shows 'Failure to Cure Deficiency' 64 times in the queue's entire history (8 in 2025, 3 in 2026 YTD) against 617 voluntary withdrawals.
finding_triage.why: Small-but-real is a constraint, and this is not the zero-enforcement/zero-pain case — deemed withdrawal is live enforcement with a real forfeiture; what it kills is the insurance framing, while the monitoring job (status flips, study postings, neighbor withdrawals) is continuous, not rare.

finding_triage.finding: A free incumbent already ships the surviving MVP with broader coverage: interconnection.fyi / GridTracker, 43,887 requests across 50+ ISOs and utilities, compiled daily, full list view with no signup, free email alerts, free MCP server, $0.
finding_triage.why: Free substitute with a different shape, not equal-or-better UX for the exact job — it is browse-and-explore plus a broadcast Substack, and the report itself files 'whether interconnection.fyi's alerts can be scoped to a specific project or developer' as UNPROVEN, which is precisely the residual (scoped push, field-level before/after, webhook/API) left to price.

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 2 — Basepoint sells the pitch verbatim across all seven ISOs today ('import by queue ID', 'status changes as they happen', 'alerts when timelines shift or action items are due', 'Milestone deadlines and compliance dates').
finding_triage.why: Under the corrected standard a live incumbent selling this job is proof the market pays; Basepoint's /pricing returns 404 and the only CTA is 'Book demo', so its rep-led enterprise motion is the flank, not the tombstone.

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 3 — Enverus acquired Pearl Street Technologies (2025-03-13), folding developer interconnection tooling into the data suite these buyers already subscribe to.
finding_triage.why: Bundling kills only if near-universal in the segment, and ERCOT's own file shows the segment is 1,065 entities holding exactly one active large-gen request — those are not Enverus PRISM accounts.

finding_triage.finding: The ISO is a free first-party substitute and is legally superior: CAISO RIMS access is mandatory for generator owners and POC emails receive progress reports; PJM's Queue Point 'is able to handle the deficiency process, including automated notifications, integration with PJM calendars'.
finding_triage.why: Authoritative for the buyer's OWN projects in ONE ISO behind ONE credential set — it structurally cannot show a cross-ISO portfolio in one view, and it never shows the queue AROUND you (your cluster, your POI, the projects ahead of you whose withdrawal moves your cost allocation), which is real residual pain the portal is not built to serve.

finding_triage.finding: The ISO already ships the diff: ERCOT's GIS Report carries a 'Changes from Last Report' column group (Proj Name, MW Size, COD, SFS/NtP, FIS Request, INA-to-PLN status change).
finding_triage.why: One ISO, monthly, six indicator flags, and pull-not-push inside a 679KB spreadsheet you must download and open — a positioning constraint on one of five-plus sources, not an equal-or-better substitute for a same-day cross-ISO pushed field-level diff.

finding_triage.finding: A4 / autonomy — coverage collapse: MISO 403 Cloudflare domain-wide, PJM Data Miner 401 with every feed 404 unauthenticated, ISO-NE routes to the cookie-gated IRTT, gridstatus.io 403; 'only 2 of 7 ISOs machine-fetchable'.
finding_triage.why: The '2 of 7' figure is contradicted inside this very report — the corpus lens fetched CAISO (200), SPP (200, 1,028 projects), ERCOT (200) and NYISO (200) on the same day, so it is 4 of 7 clean and no-auth; PJM is a one-time key registration, which the standard names explicitly as a Class B licensing cost, and gridstatus (BSD-3) covers the remainder.

finding_triage.finding: Commoditization — the BSD-3-licensed gridstatus library already provides get_interconnection_queue across all seven ISOs, dissolving the acquisition layer into a free import.
finding_triage.why: That is a dependency that removes cost, not a competitor that removes revenue; engineering scarcity was never the moat for a zero-human company, and it is the practical bridge to MISO and PJM.

finding_triage.finding: Moat already held — GridTracker has daily queue snapshots since April 2024, a per-project change log, coverage to 1995, and leads data collection for LBNL's Queued Up; QueueGuard launches 28 months behind a partly-free archive.
finding_triage.why: A false moat claim is a constraint that forces an honest reposition, not a disqualifying fact — the repositioned company claims no historical data moat at all and competes on scoped push, published self-serve price and programmatic distribution.

finding_triage.finding: No self-serve buyer population — ERCOT's Interconnecting Entity field over 1,797 active large-gen rows yields 1,342 distinct entities: 1,065 with exactly one project, 255 with 2–4, 17 with 5–9, only 5 with 10+.
finding_triage.why: Small-but-real TAM is a constraint, and this finding actually corrects the ICP in the product's favour — it destroys the card's '10–100 requests' enterprise ICP but reveals ~1,300 named entities in one ISO alone, most holding one to four projects, which is a self-serve shape at a lower price rather than an absent market.

finding_triage.finding: Cadence fatal for ERCOT — the GIS Report is monthly (July data published 2026-08-03, run Aug 1), up to ~33 days of lag against a 5-business-day cure window.
finding_triage.why: It kills the cure-window backstop (already deleted) and constrains the freshness claim per source; CAISO and SPP refresh daily and NYISO weekly, so the honest product states cadence per ISO on every alert rather than promising uniform same-day.

finding_triage.finding: Price-floor collapse — the alert layer is $0 (interconnection.fyi, LoadFlow, ZEG) and the analytics layer starts at Cleanview's published $750/mo rising to $40,000–80,000/yr legacy contracts; no observed $99–399 self-serve slot, and the card's 'in line with what GridTracker charges' is unverifiable since GridTracker publishes no price.
finding_triage.why: Price floors are named Class B explicitly, and a published $750/mo entry price plus a published $995 report price are exactly the observed clearing anchors the reposition is required to price against — the card's unsupported anchor is deleted and replaced with them.

finding_triage.finding: Engine-never-arbiter — 'so a missed deadline never costs you the queue position' is an unattended outcome guarantee on postings worth millions, and any rendered countdown asserts a legal fact derived from an issuance date the product cannot see.
finding_triage.why: This is Class A for ANY version that renders a forward-looking due date — but it attaches to the promise sentence and one deleted feature, not to the core value; the repositioned product renders only observed cell changes with file name, report run date and row, quotes tariff text with the missing anchor named, and never displays a date in the future, which is mechanism-framing that actually holds.

reposition.one_liner: A same-day, source-cited change feed for the public ISO/RTO interconnection queues: you name the queue positions, clusters, points of interconnection and counties you care about, and it pushes the exact cell that changed — old value, new value, file name, report run date, row — including the projects ahead of you in your own cluster and at your own POI, and it never renders a deadline.
reposition.price: $0 Public (daily change log for every covered ISO, browsable, RSS + MCP endpoint) → $149/mo Watch (25 watched entities — queue positions, clusters, POIs or counties — daily email + webhook, field-level before/after with source row) → $399/mo Portfolio (250 watched entities, cluster/POI neighbour watch, CSV export + REST API, per-ISO cadence badges) → $995 one-off Cluster Change Dossier (full revision history for one cluster or POI, dated PDF + CSV). Every number is anchored to a price observed on 2026-08-19, not to the card's unverifiable GridTracker guess: Cleanview publishes Explorer at $750/mo for 5 users across all seven ISOs with an API — $399/mo with no seat minimum and no demo is 53% of that published floor; GridTracker publishes standalone reports at exactly $995 each (2026 Half-Year, SPP DISIS-2024-001 Phase 1, 2025 Annual), which is precisely where the one-off dossier is priced so the comparison is like-for-like; Cleanview's own comparison table cites legacy platforms at $40,000–80,000 annual contracts, making the top tier ~1% of the incumbent ceiling. The free tier is $0 on purpose because interconnection.fyi, LoadFlow and ZEG are $0 — the paid line is never access to the data, it is scoping, push, field-level diff and API.
reposition.wedge: interconnection.fyi / GridTracker (free, daily, 43,887 requests, 50+ ISOs, free MCP): do not fight on coverage or on the raw dataset — cite and link them. They are browse-and-explore plus a broadcast Substack; the validation report itself files per-project scoped alerting as UNPROVEN. Flank = alerts keyed to YOUR queue numbers, cluster, POI, county and PTO, delivered by webhook and email with a machine-readable field-level diff, not a newsletter. LoadFlow (free, all 7 ISOs + 5 utilities): weekly cadence and pull-only — flank on same-day CAISO/SPP detection and on push. Zero-Emission Grid Queue Tracker (free, weekly/monthly 'window-opening alerts'): cluster-window granularity only — flank on per-project field-level change. Basepoint (the exact feature set across all 7 ISOs): /pricing returns 404 and the only CTA is 'Book demo' — flank on self-serve exactly as Ratepin flanked its category: published price, card checkout, API on day one, no rep, aimed squarely at the 1,065 one-project and 255 two-to-four-project entities ERCOT's own file names, whom a rep-led motion cannot afford to serve. Cleanview ($750/mo, 5 users): they sell market analytics; we sell one job at 53% of their entry price with no seat floor. Enverus/Pearl Street, Nira In-Queue, GridStatus (all demo-gated): flank on price and self-serve; concede modeling entirely. ISO first-party portals — CAISO RIMS (mandatory), PJM Queue Point (automated deficiency notifications), ISO-NE IRTT, ERCOT RIOO: concede loudly and in-product, stating on every alert that the ISO's own letter and portal are authoritative for your own projects and linking to them. Flank = the two things a portal structurally cannot do — one view across ISOs without N credential sets, and the queue AROUND you, since your portal never shows the projects ahead of you in your cluster whose withdrawal moves your network-upgrade cost allocation. ERCOT's own 'Changes from Last Report' columns: concede — flank is that it is one ISO, monthly, six indicator flags, and only visible if you download and open a 679KB workbook.
reposition.distribution: 1) Programmatic SEO off the public entity lists, which are the queue files themselves — this is the whole distribution engine and it costs zero human minutes. One indexed, daily-updated page per queue position (9,781 active US-wide, 43,887 historical requests 1995–2026), per interconnecting entity (1,342 named in ERCOT's file, plus NYISO's Developer column), per POI/substation (CAISO's 'Station or Transmission Line' column), per cluster (CAISO C14/C15/C16, SPP DISIS-2024-001, MISO DPP cycles), per county, per state and per PTO/utility. Query patterns to own: '<queue position> interconnection status', '<substation name> interconnection queue', '<county> solar interconnection queue', '<cluster id> study status', '<entity name> interconnection projects', '<ISO> queue changes <month year>'. Every page carries that entity's live change log and a one-click 'watch this' that captures email. 2) Free-tool wedges: a public 'what changed in CAISO's queue today' diff page regenerated every morning off the 08:00 GMT file (this is both the free tool and the SEO crawl surface); a free 'paste your queue numbers, get a dated change-history PDF' one-shot that captures email; a free JSON/MCP endpoint for the change log, at parity with GridTracker's, which is now a real agent-era acquisition channel. 3) Enforcement- and calendar-event triggers, each a dated free page published automatically: cluster application windows opening and closing, study report postings, deemed-withdrawal batches appearing on the Withdrawn tabs, and the FERC Section 206 show-cause docket ladder (EL26-68 through EL26-72, 18 June 2026) — recurring, searchable moments that generate demand on their own schedule. 4) A daily/weekly digest list built entirely from those page captures, with the paid upgrade being scope and push, not content. No partnerships, no sales calls, no demos, no conference motion — none of it is executable by a zero-human company and none of it is in the plan.
reposition.why_winnable: The mechanics are winnable: four of seven sources fetched clean and unauthenticated on 2026-08-19 (CAISO daily, SPP daily, NYISO weekly, ERCOT monthly), PJM is a one-time key registration and MISO is bridgeable through the BSD-3 gridstatus library, the diff is deterministic, the SEO surface auto-generates from the same files, and support is bounded because every claim in the product is 'this cell, in this file, at this report run date, here is the row' — nothing is ever asserted that a customer cannot check against the source in one click. The honest doubt is the market, and it is substantial: with the countdown amputated, no evidence anywhere in this validation shows a developer paying anything at the $149–399 band for queue monitoring, the free tier is genuinely good and owned by a firm 28 months ahead on archive depth with LBNL's dataset relationship, and Basepoint is funded and covers all seven ISOs. The bet is narrow and I would size it accordingly: that scoped push plus a published self-serve price plus long-tail entity SEO converts a few hundred of the ~1,300 one-to-four-project filers that the rep-led incumbents cannot economically call. That is a $0.3–1.2M ARR business at a realistic ceiling, not more — I would fund it as the thinnest viable candidate on this ballot, not as a conviction bet.

residual_risks: Willingness-to-pay is unproven at any price for the repositioned job. The report searched and found no interview, forum post, or pricing page showing a developer paying for queue monitoring at the self-serve band; the only observed prices ($750/mo Cleanview, $995/report GridTracker, $40–80k/yr legacy) are enterprise or one-off. First 60 days must be a live pricing test, not a build.

GridTracker/interconnection.fyi can add per-project scoped alerts in a week at zero marginal cost. They already hold the 28-month daily snapshot archive, a free MCP server whose sample query is literally 'Which projects changed status this week?', and the LBNL Queued Up relationship. The entire wedge is a feature gap they can close on a whim.

MISO and PJM coverage is borrowed, not owned. MISO is Cloudflare-blocked domain-wide and PJM requires a registered Data Miner key; both depend on gridstatus staying maintained and staying unblocked. A MISO block that also catches gridstatus removes the largest queue and with it the credibility of any cross-ISO claim.

ERCOT's monthly cadence (~33-day lag) means the 'same-day change feed' promise is false for one of the flagship sources. Cadence must be stamped per-ISO on every alert and on the marketing page, or the product's central claim is dishonest — and that honesty visibly weakens the pitch.

Onboarding cannot be automated in CAISO. Its public file carries no developer or company name field at all (the Withdrawn header reads 'Project Name - Confidential'), so portfolio auto-mapping is impossible there and the customer must hand-enter queue numbers — a real conversion drag for a no-touch signup.

Engine-never-arbiter is a permanent operating discipline, not a one-time framing choice. The moment any surface — product, email, landing copy, support macro — renders a forward-looking due date or says 'your posting is due', the company is over the line. This needs a hard invariant that no future date is ever displayed, enforced in code and in the copy generator.

Regulatory movement cuts both ways. FERC Order 2023 compliance and the EL26-68 through EL26-72 show-cause dockets could force ISOs to publish richer per-project milestone data (which would help enormously) or could push ISOs to publish their own scoped change feeds and notification services (which would end the product). The company has no influence over which.

TAM is genuinely small and the ICP had to be inverted. The buyer is now the one-to-four-project filer, not the 10–100-position portfolio the card imagined — a lower price against a larger but less sophisticated and more churn-prone population, with no evidence that population currently pays for anything in this category.

Four of seven ISO schemas were never read directly (PJM, MISO, ISO-NE, and CAISO's own two schemas are mutually incompatible — 33 columns vs 20). Schema drift across seven churning corpora is ongoing maintenance the diff engine must survive without a human, and CAISO already proves one ISO can run two incompatible files at once.

survivors.name: SponsorScope (H-1B/PERM sponsorship data)

finding_triage.finding: The card's sole willingness-to-pay citation — the $199 Gumroad 'Sponsorship Premium' — is a job-board advertising slot on opentoworkremote.com, sales_count null, 0 ratings.
finding_triage.why: The citation is genuinely dead and the recruiter-seat price band dies with it, but real market signal survives its removal: MyVisaJobs has run a paid premium tier on this exact corpus since 2004, GoinGlobal/Interstride license it institutionally, Ellis funds $3,000–$15,000 legal services with it, and h1bapi.com sells it at $9–$79/mo — so the market pays, just not at the card's price to the card's buyer.

finding_triage.finding: h1bapi.com already ships the exact proposed API — 9,172,091 records, FY2008–FY2026, OpenAPI 3.1.0, MCP — at Free/$9/$29/$79 per month, 5–16× below the hypothesized $49–$149/seat.
finding_triage.why: This is the textbook Class B case under the corrected standard: a live incumbent selling the job at a real price proves the market pays and sets the clearing price ($79/mo ceiling) that any reposition must beat or flank — and it is flankable, because h1bapi is explicitly a *salary* API with no PERM, no worksites join, and no change events.

finding_triage.finding: USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub is a free first-party substitute covering FY2009–FY2026 Q3 with petition approval/denial counts — the outcome data DOL cannot supply.
finding_triage.why: A free government tool kills only when it is equal-or-better UX for the exact job with no residual pain; the Hub is annual, aggregate, employer-keyed by last-four-of-tax-ID, has no job title, no wage, no worksite, no PERM and no alerting — coarser grain on a different question, with abundant residual pain to price.

finding_triage.finding: h1bdata.info gives away a scriptable, no-login, row-level dump — 28,035 rows for one employer, current to 06/08/2026 — undercutting the UI tier and the API tier at once.
finding_triage.why: A free substitute with worse UX for a different job: it is a static search box over LCA salary rows with no PERM, no worksites workbook, and no way to be told when anything changes — it constrains lookup pricing to $0, which the reposition concedes outright.

finding_triage.finding: h1btrack.com is 'Free Always', updated 2026-08-19, and carries broader scope than B7 proposes — 2.2M filings, USCIS approval/denial join, E-Verify, cap-exempt lists, lottery-odds calculator.
finding_triage.why: The single hardest constraint in the report and the one I will not soften: it is broader at $0 — but it is still a lookup with no PERM longitudinal view and no standing watch, and its USCIS join depends on a source that Akamai-blocks automation, so its freshness rests on a channel we would not build on.

finding_triage.finding: Four-plus free Chrome extensions (H1BGrader v2.0.0 updated 2026-08-17, Interstride, FrogHire, Ultimate H-1B Sponsor Checker) overlay sponsor status directly inside LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor, Dice and Google Jobs.
finding_triage.why: Free-in-the-workflow, but they answer a different question at a different moment — 'does this employer sponsor at all, on the posting I am looking at now' — not 'has this employer's filing posture changed since I last looked', which no extension does.

finding_triage.finding: The recruiter/staffing buyer premise is unsupported after targeted hunting across four lenses: every monetized actor sells candidate-side (MyVisaJobs, H1BGrader, FrogHire), to universities (GoinGlobal, Interstride), or as legal lead-gen (Ellis).
finding_triage.why: Class A requires zero enforcement AND zero intrinsic pain — but the pain here is enormous on the side where money already moves (visa-dependent professionals, priced by a 22-year-old incumbent), so this is a buyer-repositioning requirement, not market death; the named buyer changes, the market does not disappear.

finding_triage.finding: Ellis (immigration law firm) and Elevate Staffing give the sponsor database away as customer-acquisition cost for $3,000–$15,000 legal services and platform demos — competitors structurally able to keep the data free forever.
finding_triage.why: This is a price floor imposed by adjacent business models, explicitly Class B; it forecloses selling the lookup at any price, which is why the reposition gives the lookup away and sells only the change monitor.

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 3 — Bullhorn ships an H-1B staffing stack (Gustav two-way integration, Fuse Verified H-1B, Terefic), Ceipal ships an LCA/immigration module, Elevate ships H-1B/OPT/CPT compliance tracking.
finding_triage.why: Bundling kills only when near-universal in the segment and genuinely adequate; every one of these handles the firm's *own* filings, PAF compliance, or candidate/sub-vendor verification — none does third-party employer filing-history change detection, so the bundle is inadequate for the job, and they are marketplace add-ons rather than universal.

finding_triage.finding: The programmatic-SEO channel — the card's only stated distribution — is 100% occupied: 18/18 page-1 slots across two live SERP tests, 12+ distinct competitors, MyVisaJobs authoritative since 2004.
finding_triage.why: A distribution constraint that kills the card's channel outright but not the company; the head terms are conceded and the reposition must earn a surface that structurally cannot exist for incumbents — change-event and worksite-joined pages, which no free tool can generate because none joins the separate 45MB worksites workbook or diffs quarters.

finding_triage.finding: Engine-never-arbiter bites structurally: the compliant output ('employer X filed N certified LCAs, case numbers attached') is what six free tools already render, while the output worth paying for ('this employer will sponsor') is a forbidden outcome assertion.
finding_triage.why: Class A requires the violation be unfixable by mechanism-framing, and it is fixable — a change event is pure mechanism ('certified LCA count went 41 → 0 across two consecutive OFLC releases; first PERM filed FY2026 Q3; case numbers attached'), a dated diff over a public record rather than any prediction about sponsorship willingness.

finding_triage.finding: The signal is anti-correlated with the decision: newest record is 51 days to ~4.5 months old, and top historical filers (TCS, Walmart ~2,400 holders, Cognizant) publicly froze sponsorship while a filings index ranks them highest.
finding_triage.why: A product-truth constraint on the *lookup* framing — and simultaneously the strongest argument for the reposition, since volatility is precisely what makes 'this employer's filing behavior just changed' the valuable artifact rather than 'this employer filed N times'; the lag remains a genuine residual risk, not a disqualifier.

finding_triage.finding: Macro contraction: FY2027 registrations ~211,600 vs 336,153 (−37%), wage-weighted selection rule effective 2026-02-27 explicitly framed against IT staffing, RIA projects −10,099 Level I workers, $100k fee in First Circuit litigation.
finding_triage.why: Small-and-shrinking TAM is a constraint, not a kill — and the shrinkage is overstated against this corpus: the −37% applies to cap *registrations*, while the LCA file still carries 437,496 real records and 401,412 certifications in nine months, covering extensions, transfers, cap-exempt, E-3 and H-1B1 that the lottery never touches.

finding_triage.finding: Metered comparables show near-zero paid demand: Apify actors at $50/1,000 and $18.75/1,000 records report 26 total/2 monthly users and 5 total/0 monthly users respectively.
finding_triage.why: Weak negative evidence about commodity scrape-metering on a marketplace almost no job seeker or recruiter has heard of — a poor proxy for subscription demand, and it says nothing about the alert product that nobody in the category has ever offered.

finding_triage.finding: Build lift is understated 2–4× : 40 → 51 → 98 → 137 columns across three era-specific layouts, systematic renames, a June-2023 PERM 9089 form break, FY2009 shipping two incompatible systems, 40% of LCA rows needing a second workbook joined, and 58–88% blank-row padding to detect and discard.
finding_triage.why: Explicitly a Class B one-time setup cost with no per-customer human work — and it is the only durable moat left, since the free tier's uniform failure to join the 45MB worksites workbook is a direct consequence of nobody wanting to do this work.

finding_triage.finding: Employer-name entity resolution across 59,649 distinct raw LCA strings and 30,948 PERM strings is the one genuinely hard and valuable piece, and the card defers it to the user as 'plausible matches with a confidence indicator'.
finding_triage.why: An unbuilt product component, not a disqualifying fact — it is deterministic code rather than human judgment, and A3 requires exactly the ranked-candidates degradation the card describes; the reposition simply has to actually build it instead of shipping around it.

finding_triage.finding: A4/A5 autonomy hazard: uscis.gov and e-verify.gov return Akamai HTTP 403 to every headless method tried — plain curl, browser UAs, cookies, HTTP/1.1, Referer, WebFetch — so approval/denial and E-Verify data are not cron-fetchable.
finding_triage.why: It disqualifies a *dependency*, not the company: the corpus the product actually needs is dol.gov, which returns 200 to bare curl on a standing quarterly cadence with the FY2008 archive live, so the constraint is 'never build on USCIS' plus an in-product statement that we carry DOL certifications, not USCIS approvals.

finding_triage.finding: MyVisaJobs' actual paid differentiator after 22 years is HR contact names, titles, phones, emails and CSV export — not filing history, which its free tier already carries.
finding_triage.why: Informative about where value concentrated for the incumbent, and a deliberate flank we decline on A4 sourcing and privacy grounds rather than a fact that disqualifies a filing-history change monitor.

reposition.one_liner: A standing watch over DOL's LCA *and* PERM disclosure record that emails you the moment a specific employer's filing behavior changes — first PERM filed, filings stopped, a new worksite city, a new occupation — with the dated diff and the case numbers attached; the record publishes only snapshots, and nobody publishes the changelog.
reposition.price: $99/yr (or $12/mo) for a 25-employer personal watchlist; $49/mo for 250 employers plus CSV export and API. Anchors, all observed in the validation report: the browser lookup floor is $0 (h1bdata.info, h1bdatahub — /pricing returns 404, no paid tier exists — h1binfo, h1bsalaries.fyi, levels.fyi/h1b), so the lookup is conceded and given away free. The only verified paid clearing prices for this exact corpus are h1bapi.com's Free $0 / Dev $9 / Pro $29 / Business $79 per month, so $99/yr sits at the bottom of the observed paid band and the $588/yr top tier deliberately undercuts h1bapi's $948/yr ceiling while carrying PERM, which h1bapi does not sell at any price. Annual-first billing is chosen to match DOL's own cadence: FY2026 Q3 posted 2026-08-07 for a 2026-06-30 close, so there are roughly four release events a year and a monthly subscription is structurally hard to hold. The $49–$149/seat recruiter hypothesis and the $199 Gumroad anchor are both abandoned — the Gumroad citation was a job-board ad slot and the recruiter seat has no observed instance anywhere in the category.
reposition.wedge: vs h1bapi.com ($9/$29/$79, the exact API incumbent): it is a *salary* API — its own copy says '9,172,091 H-1B visa salary records', 19 LCA fields, no PERM, no worksites join, no change events; and its advertised MCP package h1b-salary-mcp returns 404 from the npm registry, so its integration story is partly vapour. Flank = PERM as a first-class dataset plus the quarter-over-quarter diff as the product object rather than a row dump. vs the free browser swarm (h1bdata.info's 28,035 scriptable rows/employer, h1bdatahub 3.29M filings, h1binfo 3.57M certified LCAs, h1bsalaries.fyi, levels.fyi 1.3M): every one is a search box you must remember to revisit, and every one silently drops the 40.3% of LCA rows declaring TOTAL_WORKSITE_LOCATIONS > 1 because the extra worksites live in a separate 45,032,522-byte workbook nobody joins. Flank = alerting, plus geography that is actually complete. vs h1btrack.com ('Free Always', 2.2M filings, USCIS approvals/denials, E-Verify, cap-exempt, updated 2026-08-19): the hardest competitor, broader at zero — flank is narrow and honest: no PERM longitudinal view, no standing watch, and its USCIS join rests on a source that Akamai-403s every headless method, so its freshness depends on a channel we deliberately refuse. vs MyVisaJobs (paid since 2004): its premium gates HR contact names, phones, emails and CSV export, while filing history is free there — we decline the contact-data flank on A4 sourcing and privacy grounds and compete only on time-series and PERM. vs the free Chrome extensions (H1BGrader v2.0.0 updated 2026-08-17, Interstride, FrogHire, Ultimate): they answer 'does this employer sponsor at all' on the posting in front of you; we answer 'what changed since you last looked', a different question at a different moment. vs USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub (free, first-party): annual, aggregate, employers keyed by last-four-of-tax-ID, no job title, no wage, no worksite, no PERM, no alerting — we state plainly in-product that we carry DOL certifications and never USCIS approvals, which is both honest and the reason we are not exposed to its 403 wall. vs Bullhorn/Ceipal/Elevate bundles: all scoped to the firm's own filings, PAF compliance, or candidate/sub-vendor verification — none does third-party employer filing-behavior change detection. vs Ellis (free 180k-company DB as lead-gen for $3,000–$15,000 legal services): they will keep the lookup free forever and we agree — ours is free too, and it is the funnel, not the product.
reposition.distribution: 1) Concede every head term — 'h1b sponsors {employer}', 'does {employer} sponsor h1b' — where the SERP test returned 18/18 page-1 slots held by incumbents with authority back to 2004. Instead generate the surface that structurally cannot exist for a lookup competitor: change-event and worksite-joined pages. Query patterns: '{employer} PERM filing history' (PERM-specific, not the LCA-salary terms the incumbents farm), 'employers that filed their first PERM in FY2026 Q3', 'employers that stopped filing H-1B after FY2024', 'new H-1B worksites in {city} {FY}', and '{employer} × {SOC_TITLE} × {worksite city}' built from the worksites workbook the free tier never opens. Public entity lists that seed it, all already parsed in validation: 59,649 distinct EMPLOYER_NAME strings and 30,948 distinct EMP_BUSINESS_NAME strings in nine months of FY2026 alone, plus the FY2008–FY2025 archive (H-1B_Case_Data_FY2008.xlsx and every intervening file verified HTTP 200). 2) The free quarterly changelog, published within 48 hours of each OFLC drop: 'what changed in this release' — N employers filed a first PERM, N stopped filing, N new worksite cities, N SOC shifts — as a page plus an email capture. This is the one artifact nobody in a 12-competitor category produces, it lands on a calendar four times a year, and it is inherently linkable from the forums already ranking on page 1 (Blind, Quora, r/h1b) without any human doing outreach. 3) Free-tool wedge: the per-employer LCA+PERM timeline page, complete with worksites, given away permanently — the lookup is the funnel; the watch is gated. 4) Agent/LLM surface: llms.txt plus an MCP server that actually publishes to npm, since the incumbent's advertised one 404s; SponsorStats already ships an 'Add to Claude' connector, so this channel is contested but not owned. Every one of these is cron-driven page generation and templated email — no calls, no partnerships, no institutional quotes (GoinGlobal/Interstride's university licensing motion is explicitly excluded as an A1 violation).
reposition.why_winnable: The mechanical case is strong and I believe it. dol.gov returns HTTP 200 to bare curl on a standing quarterly cadence with FY2008 forward live; the whole product is deterministic ETL, a snapshot diff, and a templated email; engine-never-arbiter is cleanly satisfied because a change event is a mechanism claim over a dated public record, never a prediction about willingness to sponsor; and the 4–8 weeks of unglamorous schema work (40 → 51 → 98 → 137 columns, the June-2023 PERM 9089 break, FY2009's two incompatible systems, 58–88% blank padding, the 45MB worksites join) is the only remaining moat precisely because it is the work the free tier declined to do. The honest doubt, stated plainly rather than buried: there is no observed instance anywhere in this report of anyone paying for a change alert on this data, at any price, to any buyer — the category's entire visible revenue is candidate-side lookup subscriptions, university licenses, and legal lead-gen. This reposition is a bet that the unserved artifact finds the buyer the lookup already has, and that bet is unvalidated. Compounding it: DOL's cadence caps the alert stream at roughly four events a year on a 51-day-to-4.5-month lag, so press coverage will surface a sponsorship freeze before our data can. This is the thinnest pass I would give on the ballot — fund it small, launch the free changelog against the next OFLC drop, and kill it if one quarterly cycle does not build a list.

residual_risks: No observed instance of anyone paying for a change alert on this corpus, at any price, to any buyer — the reposition's core bet is unvalidated and the report contains zero direct evidence for it.

DOL's publication cadence caps the alert stream at roughly four events per year with a 51-day-to-4.5-month lag; Newsweek and Blind surfaced the TCS/Walmart/Cognizant sponsorship freezes months before DOL data could, so the product is structurally slower than free press on the highest-salience events.

h1btrack.com is free, broader (USCIS approvals/denials, E-Verify, cap-exempt), and was updated the day before validation; lens 02 notes it already exposes a 'watchlist' surface — if it ships alerting, the primary flank closes overnight.

The PERM-neglect flank is inferred from what competitors advertise (h1bapi self-describes as a salary API), not from an exhaustive audit; h1btrends.com and myvisajobs.com do carry per-company PERM pages, so the flank may be narrower than modeled.

At $99–$588/yr against 12+ free competitors holding 18/18 page-1 slots, CAC must be effectively zero; if the free quarterly changelog does not build an email list within one OFLC cycle, there is no identified second channel.

Programmatic SEO on change events is unproven demand — nobody searches 'employers that stopped filing H-1B' today because the artifact has never existed, so the query volume may simply be zero and the channel unmeasurable until built.

Entity resolution across 59,649 raw LCA and 30,948 raw PERM employer strings is the product's entire credibility; a wrong merge emits a wrong change event, and A3 forces ranked candidates rather than an assertion — which materially weakens an alert whose whole value is a clean signal.

Ellis-class immigration firms and Elevate-class staffing platforms have a structural incentive to keep this data free forever and can outspend indefinitely on content, so any pricing above $0 for anything resembling a lookup will be eroded.

USCIS and E-Verify Akamai-403 every headless method tried, so approval/denial and E-Verify status — the fields that would most strengthen the product and that a free competitor already ships — are permanently off-limits to an unattended company.

The FY2027 −37% registration figure and the current collection status of the $100,000 fee are secondary-sourced only (USCIS unfetchable); if the fee is reinstated on First Circuit appeal, filing volume could contract faster than modeled.

Build is realistically 4–8 weeks before any differentiation begins — three era-specific layouts, the June-2023 PERM 9089 form break, FY2009's dual systems, 58–88% blank-row padding, and a 45MB worksites workbook to join — against a $99/yr entry price.

dol.gov's edge inverts the usual bot rule (403 to Chrome/Safari UAs, 200 to bare curl), an undocumented behavior that could flip without notice and silently break the only ingest path the product has.

Consumer-side ARPU with a job search lifespan of roughly one quarter implies severe churn; annual billing mitigates but does not solve it, and the segment overlaps heavily with users already served free inside LinkedIn by four Chrome extensions.

survivors.name: PortfolioWatch UK (Companies House portfolio monitor)
survivors.candidate: B8 — PortfolioWatch UK (Companies House portfolio monitor)

finding_triage.finding: Companies House gives away free email reminders for accounts and confirmation-statement due dates, up to 4 recipients including an agent, with bulk enrolment of 15+ companies via BulkERems@companieshouse.gov.uk
finding_triage.why: It is a free first-party tool but not equal-or-better UX for the portfolio job — it emits one email per company with no roll-up, no dashboard, no export and no history, and registration requires the company authentication code, which structurally excludes every third-party (credit, supplier, KYB) company a buyer does not act for; it kills the naive 'deadline reminder' headline, not the aggregation-and-record job.

finding_triage.finding: The free 'Follow' service is live, push-based, instant on filing acceptance, and has no documented cap on companies followed
finding_triage.why: Free substitute with worse UX for the portfolio job — Follow is per-company, per-event email with no portfolio view, no dedupe, no export, and it structurally cannot detect the absence of a filing (the overdue case); it is a latency constraint that forces building on the free Streaming API instead of a nightly cron, not a kill.

finding_triage.finding: CHWatch is a near-exact live competitor 'built for accountants' at Free(3)/£12(20)/£30(100)/£70(1,000) per month
finding_triage.why: Under the corrected standard a live incumbent selling the same job at a real published price is proof the market pays and sets the clearing price — it refutes the $49–199/mo hypothesis, not the market.

finding_triage.finding: The niche is crowded, not empty: CHWatch, ComplyTrack, CompanyChangeAlerts, CompanyMinder and Companies On The Go all live with published self-serve Stripe pricing
finding_triage.why: Five vendors selling self-serve with no sales motion is the strongest available evidence that this is a real, autonomy-compatible market; it is a differentiation constraint requiring a named flank against each, not a disqualifying fact.

finding_triage.finding: Price floor collapse — Companies On The Go sells 250 monitored companies for £7.50/mo incl VAT and unlimited for £15.00/mo
finding_triage.why: A price floor is explicitly a Class B competitive constraint; it means alerts must be given away or priced at commodity and the revenue must come from something the £7.50 product does not deliver, which is a repositioning requirement, not a kill.
