finding_triage.finding: The £200/mo Red Flag Alert anchor is a Capterra aggregator artifact with no billing period, no vendor attribution, and is for a credit-scoring product in the wrong category
finding_triage.why: This is a genuine misread, but the Class A test is whether NO real market signal survives its removal — remove it and five priced competitors (£7.50–£100/mo), Inform Direct (£43.81–£147.81/mo), Endole (from £25/mo) and BrightManager (£34–42/user/mo) remain, so the signal is not merely intact but better sourced; only the pricing hypothesis dies.

finding_triage.finding: Inform Direct dominates on price and scope — £43.81/mo at 50 companies and £147.81/mo at 250 including actual filing, and its FREE tier already lists 'Email reminders of key deadlines'
finding_triage.why: Classic bundling constraint: it sets a hard price ceiling for a monitoring-only tool and proves the deadline-reminder feature is an acquisition hook worth £0, which is a positioning fact to price around rather than a disqualifier.

finding_triage.finding: Practice-management suites already bundle Companies House deadline sync — BrightManager £34–42/user/mo ('filing deadlines are kept up to date within BrightManager'), IRIS Elements £13/user/mo, PracticeFlow £29/mo for 250 clients, Capium £140–£420/mo
finding_triage.why: Bundling kills only if near-universal in the segment AND genuinely adequate; the report's own Unproven list concedes it could not establish that these suites alert on officer/PSC/status CHANGES at all ('inferred from silence'), and no penetration figure exists — and the bundle is entirely absent for the non-accountant credit/KYB buyer.

finding_triage.finding: The pain is thinner than the penalty headline implies — CH reports 98.5% accounts and 97.1% confirmation-statement compliance, so the failure mode addresses 1.5–2.9% of the register
finding_triage.why: Small-but-real TAM is explicitly a constraint, not a kill, and the absolute number is not small — 317,985 late-filing penalties in a single year with a doubling rule, criminal liability and £5,000 strike-off exposure is maximal enforcement, so the Class A 'zero enforcement AND zero intrinsic pain' test fails decisively.

finding_triage.finding: Engine-never-arbiter strain: the claimed moat ('usually 3 days late, this time it's 90'), the 'early distress signal' framing, and competitors' £-denominated 'Penalty Exposure' and 'Filing Risk Score'
finding_triage.why: The Class A test is whether the CORE value only sells by asserting an outcome code cannot own — here the core is a deterministic roll-up and field-level diff of CH-published values, which sells on its own; the score is a bolted-on moat the report itself supplies the fix for (render observed dates and deltas, cite the published penalty band by lookup, never a score or label), so it is fixable by mechanism-framing.

finding_triage.finding: 'Never miss a deadline' is an outcome promise an unattended product cannot warrant (rule 2)
finding_triage.why: A promise-framing defect with a stated remedy in the report itself — the mechanism form ('we re-read each watched record and report every field that changed, with the date Companies House stamped it') is signable and is what the reposition must sell.

finding_triage.finding: No technical moat — the free Streaming API supplies a server-side fields_changed diff across nine streams, free bulk snapshots supply the register, and an Apify actor detects changes at $0.40/company
finding_triage.why: Absence of a technical moat is a competitive constraint, and the free real-time stream plus free daily/monthly bulk data is actually the enabling condition for a zero-marginal-cost unattended company — it lowers the cost floor for us as much as for anyone.

finding_triage.finding: The 'lateness baseline that compounds' is cosmetic — /filing-history returns dated historical filings and the full register ships as a free monthly CSV, so any competitor backfills ten years before launch
finding_triage.why: It removes the card's claimed moat (which also happened to be the engine-never-arbiter violation) but removing a false moat is a repositioning requirement, not a disqualifying fact about the market.

finding_triage.finding: PenaltyProof, a prior entrant at £29/mo for 50 companies with 30/14/7-day CH deadline alerts, is dead (HTTP 404 'Application not found')
finding_triage.why: One dead entrant is evidence that the undifferentiated pure-alert product at that exact price does not sustain — a sharp warning that dictates which flank to take, not proof the market is unservable while five others remain live.

finding_triage.finding: Total single-source, single-jurisdiction dependency on a landlord that reserves the right to 'ban without notice' rate-limit abusers, and whose 2026-27 business plan hints at deeper register search and digital customer channels
finding_triage.why: The Class A corpus test is dead/nonexistent/legally unobtainable — this corpus is live, free, self-serve-keyed, real-time-streamed, bulk-downloadable and refreshed daily (today's 2.2GB PSC snapshot was fetched), and the ban clause applies to exceeding limits, not to compliant commercial use, which five live vendors already conduct openly.

finding_triage.finding: Commercial resale terms for CH API-derived alerts are unverified — developer.company-information.service.gov.uk/terms-of-service returns 404 and the developer guidelines contain no redistribution clause
finding_triage.why: Absence of a prohibition plus five live commercial resellers carrying CH's own 'Official API' badge is practical evidence of obtainability; unverified is not 'legally unobtainable', so this is a residual risk to re-check, not a Class A corpus kill.

finding_triage.finding: The ECCTA tailwind the card would ride (software-only iXBRL, abridged accounts abolished, mandatory small/micro P&L) is dated 1 April 2028, not 2026
finding_triage.why: A timing error in the card's narrative, not a false premise about the mandate — the nearer ECCTA event (identity verification, legally required since 18 Nov 2025, 12-month transition, confirmed by primary GOV.UK release) is real and now exposed per-officer in the API as identity_verification_details.appointment_verification_statement_due_on.

finding_triage.finding: The card builds against accounts.next_due, which the live spec marks 'Deprecated. Please use accounts.next_accounts.due_on'
finding_triage.why: A one-line implementation correction from the live schema; it indicates a shallow read of the spec but is not a fact about the market.

finding_triage.finding: Economics only clear above ~250 monitored companies, exactly the segment demanding references and a security review — breaking the A1 self-serve autonomy case
finding_triage.why: This is an artifact of the card's inflated price, not of the market: every named competitor sells self-serve with Stripe at 10–250 company tiers with free trials and no onboarding call, proving A1 holds at market-clearing prices.

finding_triage.finding: Buyer pool is shrinking and unquantified — registered audit firms fell 25% to 3,760, and the ONS SIC 6920 file and ICAEW report yielded no practice count
finding_triage.why: Small-but-real TAM is a constraint, and the audit-firm count is a floor for the wrong denominator anyway (audit registration is not required to hold a client book, and the credit/KYB buyer is not an accountancy practice at all); it survives as an honest sizing risk.

reposition.one_liner: A dated, portable Companies House evidence record for people who must show what they knew and when about companies they do NOT act for: every night we re-read each watched company's register entry from the free Companies House stream, and every month we issue a timestamped pack of every CH-published due date, actual filing date, days-late delta, officer/PSC roster change and identity-verification statement date — each value printed exactly as Companies House published it, with the date Companies House stamped it and the timestamp we read it, and with no score, rating, opinion or prediction anywhere in the document.
reposition.price: £29/mo for 100 monitored companies, £79/mo for 500, £149/mo for 2,000 (adds webhooks and weekly packs); £6 for a one-off single-company dated pack, self-serve Stripe, no call, free tier of 25 companies with watermarked packs. Anchors, all from the validation report: the pure-alert commodity floor is Companies On The Go at £7.50/mo for 250 companies and £15/mo unlimited, plus ComplyTrack at £12/£35/£99 and CompanyChangeAlerts at £15/£35/£100 — so alerts are given away, never sold as the product. The hard ceiling is Inform Direct at £43.81/mo for 50 companies INCLUDING actual filing and PracticeFlow at £29/mo for a full practice suite covering 250 clients, which is why entry must sit at or below £29 and the top tier below £150, where CompanyChangeAlerts' £100/100 and Endole's 'from £25/mo' already sit. The £6 one-off flanks the Apify actor's $0.40 raw JSON report on format and citability rather than on price. The card's $49–199/mo hypothesis and its £200/mo Red Flag Alert anchor are both abandoned as unsupported.
reposition.wedge: Against free CH email reminders (the strongest substitute): they require the company authentication code, so they are structurally unavailable for any company the buyer does not act for — the entire credit, supplier, procurement and KYB use case is excluded from the free tool by design, not by UX; and even where available they emit one email per company with no roll-up, no export and no history. Against free CH Follow: it fires only on accepted filings, so it is blind to the single event that matters most — a filing that did not happen — and it produces email, never a document; we match its latency by consuming the same free Streaming API (fields_changed) rather than the card's nightly cron. Against CHWatch (£12–£70) and Companies On The Go (£7.50–£15): they sell a dashboard and alerts; we concede that entire surface at or below their price and sell the dated artifact they do not produce — a pack you attach to a credit file, an audit working paper, a lender pack or an onboarding record. Against ComplyTrack (£12–£99, ships 'Risk scoring' and a live '£4,870 penalty exposure' figure) and CompanyChangeAlerts (£15–£100, 'ECCTA-aligned monitoring'): our flank is precisely that we refuse to score — for a buyer who has to justify a decision to an auditor or a court, a scored inference is a liability and a citable record of published facts is the asset; we publish the CH penalty band table as a lookup with the band cited, never a computed exposure figure. Against Inform Direct and the practice-management bundles (BrightManager £34–42/user/mo, IRIS £13/user/mo, PracticeFlow £29/250 clients): we do not fight for the accountant's own client book, which is triple-covered by free auth-coded reminders, the suite bundle and five point tools — we sell to the buyer who has no suite and no auth codes. Against the Apify $0.40/company actor: it returns JSON to a developer; we return a dated, formatted, reference-numbered document to a non-developer. Against PenaltyProof's death at £29/50: it sold pure alerts, which is exactly the product we are not selling. Guarantee is a mechanism guarantee, never an outcome one: if we ever print a value Companies House did not publish, that month is free — we never promise that a deadline will be met.
reposition.distribution: 1) Programmatic SEO over a bounded, event-fresh public entity list, not the whole 5.48m register (which would read as doorway spam): the free Accounts Data Product (daily Tue–Sat) and the free Streaming API identify companies that newly went overdue, changed status to liquidation or dissolution, or had a PSC/officer change — a naturally bounded, continuously refreshed set of hundreds of thousands per year. Query patterns, one page per event-touched company: '{company name} {number} accounts overdue', 'when are {company}'s accounts due', 'is {company} still active companies house', '{company} director changes {year}', '{company} PSC change', plus weekly evergreen roll-ups ('UK companies that went overdue this week', 'UK companies entering liquidation this week') that are the acquisition surface for the credit buyer. Every page is a rendered fact table with the CH stamp date, zero generated prose. 2) Free-tool wedge that free CH cannot copy: paste or upload a CSV of company numbers and get an instant one-page dated roll-up of due dates, overdue flags and last filing dates across the whole list — this is the exact job the free per-company reminder cannot do, and it captures the buyer at the moment of pain (I have a list, I don't know its state). Free to 25 companies, watermarked pack; paid for recurring packs and the change log. 3) Marketplace listings, all self-serve, no humans: an Apify store actor (the $0.40 competitor's own shelf), a Zapier and Make integration published as a 'Companies House change' trigger, and Slack/Teams app-directory listings — competitors already ship Slack webhooks, so the directory is a proven surface. 4) Enforcement-event triggers: the ECCTA identity-verification transition (legally required since 18 Nov 2025, ~6–7m individuals, confirmation-statement-linked) gives a dated per-officer field in the API and a search surface ('{company} director identity verification status') for as long as the transition runs; London/Edinburgh/Belfast Gazette first notices of compulsory strike-off are a public, dated, fixed-window enforcement event that maps one-to-one onto a supplier-watch alert page — this channel is not verified in the validation report and must be confirmed before it is relied on. Deliberately excluded: partnerships, sales calls, security reviews, bespoke integrations, and any tier that requires them.
reposition.why_winnable: Winnable because the cost structure and the support surface both go to zero for an unattended operator: the corpus is free, self-serve-keyed, real-time-streamed and bulk-downloadable daily; the deliverable is a template render of published fields with no generative model in the paid path; and five live competitors selling self-serve with Stripe free trials at 10–1,000 company tiers prove no sales motion is required in this category. The buyer's job is under maximal enforcement — 317,985 penalties in one year, a doubling rule, criminal liability, £5,000 confirmation-statement fines and strike-off — so the pain is not manufactured. And the flank is a genuine structural gap rather than a UX preference: the free government reminder is gated on the authentication code, which the credit, supplier and KYB buyer will never hold, and no free service produces a document at all. The honest doubt, stated plainly: nothing in the validation report evidences willingness to pay a premium for a dated evidence artifact over a £7.50 dashboard — that is the reposition's single load-bearing untested assumption, and PenaltyProof's death at £29/mo is a warning that the adjacent version of this bet already failed once. The category clears at £7.50–£35/mo, so this is a low-ARPU, volume-dependent business whose buyer population the report could not quantify at all (ONS and ICAEW sources both failed). I would fund this as a cheap, fast, artifact-first test with a hard kill trigger — not as a portfolio monitor, which is dead at every price.

residual_risks: Artifact willingness-to-pay is entirely unevidenced. No source in the validation report shows anyone paying a premium for a dated, citable evidence document over a live dashboard. This is the reposition's single load-bearing assumption and the first thing the free-CSV-upload tool must test — conversion from free roll-up to paid pack is the kill metric.

identity_verification_details population is unproven. The officerList schema documents appointment_verification_statement_due_on, but no lens had an API key and the public officers web view for company 00000006 contained no 'verified' or 'Identity' string. If the field is sparse or unpopulated mid-transition, the entire ECCTA surface disappears. This is a 30-minute check with a free key on day one, before any build.

Companies House could extend Follow into a followed-companies dashboard. Its 2026-27 business plan commits to 'enabling users to search the register in more depth' and 'expanding the use of digital channels to keep in touch with customers'. That would zero the monitoring half outright, leaving only the artifact — which is precisely why the artifact, not the monitoring, is the product.

Commercial resale terms are unverified. developer.company-information.service.gov.uk/terms-of-service returns 404 and the developer guidelines contain no redistribution or commercial-use clause. Five live vendors resell CH-derived alerts openly, but the contractual position rests on absence of prohibition rather than on an affirmative permission.

The price ceiling is hard and set by products that do strictly more. Inform Direct is £43.81/mo for 50 companies including actual filing; PracticeFlow is £29/mo for a whole practice suite covering 250 clients. Any tier that drifts above ~£79/mo is competing with software that files, which we do not.

Buyer population is genuinely unknown. The ONS SIC 6920 enterprise file 404s, the ICAEW monitoring PDF yielded no extractable count, and FRC's 3,760 registered audit firms is a floor for the wrong denominator. The credit/KYB segment this reposition targets has no size estimate anywhere in the report. Plausible TAM is low single-digit millions of pounds.

Programmatic SEO over a register of 5.48m entities carries real doorway/thin-content risk with search engines. Bounding pages to event-touched companies mitigates but does not eliminate it, and a single algorithmic action would remove the primary distribution channel of a zero-human company.

The accountant segment is structurally hostile and must be conceded, not fought. Free CH reminders with bulk enrolment via BulkERems@, plus suite bundling, plus five point tools, leave no room. The reposition's viability therefore depends entirely on a buyer segment (credit, AR, procurement, KYB) whose size and willingness to pay are the least-verified things in the whole report.

The ECCTA identity-verification window is time-boxed and its end date is unproven. Two lenses could not confirm the mid-November 2026 transition end from a page they fetched; one cited a primary GOV.UK release stating 6-7 million individuals by mid-November 2026. Treat IDV as a launch traffic surface with a ~3-month horizon, never as a durable moat.

Single landlord with eviction rights and a hard HA ceiling. Companies House reserves the right to 'ban without notice' applications that exceed rate limits, and the Streaming API permits only two concurrent connections per account, which constrains high-availability design for a firehose that must be consumed whole and filtered locally.
The Gazette strike-off notice channel named in the distribution plan was not fetched or verified by any lens. It must be confirmed live before any distribution plan depends on it.

Engine-never-arbiter must be enforced architecturally, not by intention. Competitors have normalised the violation (ComplyTrack's 'Risk scoring' and live '£4,870 penalty exposure', CHWatch's 'Filing Risk Score'), which creates constant commercial pressure to match them. The rule: penalty bands appear only as a reproduced published table alongside a CH-stamped overdue date, never as a computed figure attributed to a named company, and no lateness statistic is ever labelled, ranked or characterised.

survivors.name: Starcheck (CMS PBJ XML + Five-Star)

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 1: CMS ships a free, schema-validating Excel-to-XML template (v4.10.0, HTTP 200, embedded XSD) — the premise 'the agency publishes the spec but not a generator' is factually false.
finding_triage.why: The template is a schema-shaped container the customer must hand-populate — it performs no payroll mapping, no job-title-code assignment, no employee-ID reconciliation and no agency-hours merge, so it is not equal-or-better UX for the actual job (this is the WH-347-free-PDF shape Ratepin shipped against); it caps what pure XML-emission can be priced at, which is a pricing constraint, not a kill.

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 1: XML is optional entirely — the PBJ Policy Manual and CMS FAQ confirm free manual data entry in iQIES updates the same database.
finding_triage.why: Hand-keying a quarter of daily shift rows for every employee is strictly worse UX than any automated path, which is why a paid vendor field exists at all; it constrains the low end, it does not remove the job.

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 1: CMS gives every facility free Five-Star Preview Reports plus seven free iQIES PBJ reports and an On-Demand Final File Validation Report with the 60-day wait removed.
finding_triage.why: All of these are retrospective — they score a file already built and mostly a quarter already closed — so they constrain the price of post-hoc scoring while leaving the in-quarter and pre-submission window unserved; note lens 03 could not even confirm the preview report survives the iQIES migration (the word 'preview' is absent from the July 2026 TUG).

finding_triage.finding: Free third-party substitute: Nursa's no-signup browser-local CSV/XLSX-to-PBJ-XML converter.
finding_triage.why: A shape-only converter published as lead-gen by a staffing marketplace, with no validation, no reconciliation and no risk analysis — a free substitute with worse UX, which is the textbook Class B constraint.

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 2 (called FATAL): PBJ360° Submit ships the identical feature list — submission, validation and Five Star forecasting — at $99/facility/month ($1,089/yr) against the $299 hypothesis.
finding_triage.why: Under the corrected standard a live incumbent selling this exact job at a published price is proof the market pays; it kills the $299 price point, not the market, and it sets the clearing price the reposition must undercut or flank.

finding_triage.finding: The stated differentiator (forward-looking Five-Star simulation with what-if testing) is already shipped by SimplePBJ/ezPBJ since ~2019 and is a line item in a $99 plan.
finding_triage.why: Loss of a claimed moat is a positioning fact, not a disqualifying one — the product must be repositioned onto a different axis (source-document ingestion and deterministic hard-trigger detection), which is exactly what a reposition is for.

finding_triage.finding: The proposed acquisition wedge — a free public projected-star calculator — is already the incumbent's free tier (PBJ360 Triple Check free forever up to 5 facilities; SimplePBJ Essentials free for all facilities).
finding_triage.why: A competitor's free tier is a conversion funnel, not a first-party substitute, and Triple Check materially presupposes the hard part is solved — the report states it ingests a PBJ XML you already have, so it scrubs rather than assembles.

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 3: PBJ generation and a Five-Star predictor are bundled into workforce/payroll suites the buyer already pays for (SmartLinx, OnShift, UKG, Inovalon, SBV, APS/Prime Care, Netchex, Fingercheck, ProCern).
finding_triage.why: The corrected standard requires the bundle be near-universal AND adequate, and the report proves neither — it lists vendor penetration among the 4,202 unaffiliated facilities as explicitly Unproven, and the existence of three live standalone scrubbers selling on top of suite-generated files is direct evidence the bundled output is not adequate.

finding_triage.finding: Autonomy break: QSO-26-12-NH requires a vendor to obtain iQIES access approved per-CCN by each facility's Provider Security Official, with 60-day inactivity deprovisioning — A6's zero human minutes per customer cannot survive it.
finding_triage.why: This binds only if the product submits on the customer's behalf; the report itself concedes it is 'avoidable if it only hands back a file,' so it is a scope constraint that removes one feature — and it is asymmetric in Starcheck's favour on cost, since the $99 incumbent is paying human minutes per facility for the handshake that Starcheck simply declines to make.

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 7 / engine-never-arbiter: 'never a one-star surprise' is an outcome claim resting on an MDS-lagged case-mix proxy and a current-quarter national average case-mix CMS has not yet published.
finding_triage.why: Class A requires the core value to be unfixable by mechanism-framing, and the report supplies the fix itself — the two hard one-star triggers (no submission by deadline; four or more days with zero RN hours while residents are present) are exact arithmetic on the customer's own file against a published TUG table with zero case-mix dependency, so the highest-value claim is fully signable as mechanism; the projection layer must simply be demoted and disclosed, never asserted.

finding_triage.finding: Input friction: agency/contract hours with unique employee IDs auditable to invoices live in accounts payable and agency portals, not in the payroll export the product ingests.
finding_triage.why: This is evidence of unpriced pain, not absence of it — it is the one input the $99 tier makes the customer solve by hand ('CSV & manual data entry'), the tier that automates it is enterprise-quoted, and PDF-invoice-to-shift-row extraction is precisely the mechanism an unattended pipeline can own; it is the wedge, misread as the kill.

finding_triage.finding: Market ceiling: only 4,202 truly unaffiliated buildings of 14,693; at a $99 clearing price roughly a $5M ceiling, collapsing the $2.2M ARR arithmetic ~3x.
finding_triage.why: Small-but-real TAM is explicitly a constraint, not a kill, and the ceiling is understated — 7,760 facilities sit outside 16+ chains, and the corrected count is a reason to size the company honestly rather than to abandon the market.

finding_triage.finding: Competitive timing collapse: PBJ360 Submit launches into the same Aug 17 iQIES migration with a free trial through Sept 30, capturing the re-evaluation moment.
finding_triage.why: A one-quarter head start on a transition is not a moat when the mandate produces four fixed statutory deadlines every year in perpetuity; the real launch window is Nov 14, 2026 — the first full quarter submitted through iQIES, when the most files break.

finding_triage.finding: Evidence problem: the '801 facilities dropped to one-star / >5% penalised' figure is vendor-blog-only with no primary CMS source, and SimplePBJ's $119 price could not be fetched (captcha wall).
finding_triage.why: Class A requires that no real market signal survive removal of the bad evidence, and abundant signal survives — the report independently establishes 790 of 14,693 facilities (5.4%) carrying a staffing-rating footnote in the first-party July 2026 file, plus a first-party-verified $99 published price; the unverified figures are simply struck from all marketing.

finding_triage.finding: Premise citation error: the entry cites 42 CFR 483.70(q); current eCFR renders the mandate at (p), undermining the fail-closed spec-watching story.
finding_triage.why: The mandate exists verbatim as required — only the paragraph letter is stale, and CMS's own July 2026 memos carry the same staleness, which is an argument for a product that hashes the text rather than the citation, not a false-premise disqualification.

finding_triage.finding: No data moat: the 'full-census panel' knowledge-base asset is a free quarterly CSV any competitor downloads in one curl.
finding_triage.why: Absence of proprietary data is a defensibility constraint shared by every entrant in this market including the incumbents; the differentiator has to be the pipeline and the distribution surface built on the free corpus, which is buildable.

reposition.one_liner: Starcheck turns the pile a nursing home actually has — payroll exports, timekeeping dumps, agency invoices, per-diem app CSVs — into a spec-conformant PBJ 4.10.0 XML plus a deterministic hard-trigger report that cites the exact published rule for every flag, and hands both back to the facility to upload itself; it never submits, never asserts a rating, and never touches iQIES.
reposition.price: $39/facility/month, or $390/facility/year (annual = ten months), with a $299/month cap for accounts of 10+ buildings. Anchor: the only first-party-verified paid price in the market is PBJ360° Submit at $99/facility/month / $1,089/facility/year (pbjcentral.com/pricing, fetched 2026-08-20); SimplePBJ Pro's ~$119 is captcha-blocked and is NOT used as an anchor. $39 is 60% under the verified clearing price and is honest about what is missing: PBJ360's $99 includes CMS submission, which costs them a per-CCN PSO handshake per facility; Starcheck declines that work and prices the gap. Free forever: one facility, one quarter, full ingestion and full hard-trigger scan, no card — deliberately narrower in building count than Triple Check's free-≤5 but wider in what it does, since it assembles the file rather than scrubbing one you already made. The $299/mo hypothesis is dead and is not defended.
reposition.wedge: vs PBJ360° Submit ($99, verified, launching this week): flank on the assemble step and on price. Its Submit tier's stated intake is 'CSV & manual data entry' — the customer maps by hand; the tier that connects to source systems (360Pro) is enterprise-quoted. Starcheck's paid tier is the invoice-and-export ingestion pipeline at 40% of the price, with submission removed. vs PBJ360° Triple Check (free, ≤5 facilities, no expiry): per the report it ingests a PBJ XML you already have — it presupposes the expensive step. Starcheck's free tier starts one step earlier, at the raw documents, and stays free at one building forever. vs SimplePBJ Pro/Essentials (~$119 unverified, free benchmarking tier): they win on projection accuracy because they hold live MDS; concede that publicly and never compete on it — Starcheck's flags are the two case-mix-free hard triggers (non-submission by deadline; ≥4 days with zero RN hours while residents present, TUG July 2026 Scoring Exceptions), which are exact and which MDS access does not improve. vs SmartLinx / OnShift / UKG / Inovalon / SBV / APS-Prime Care bundles: they emit a file from the system they control, which is why every one of the standalone scrubbers exists; Starcheck's flank is the hours those systems never see — agency and contract staff, whose IDs must stay stable across quarters and reconcile to invoices, and cross-quarter employee-ID drift diffing that a single-shot bundled export structurally cannot do. vs the free CMS Excel-to-XML template: it is an empty schema-shaped workbook requiring the Developer toolbar; it does no job-code mapping, no dedup, no ID continuity, no risk check — position against it as the thing that fills it, and cite it by name rather than pretending it doesn't exist. vs CMS manual entry: hand-keying a quarter of daily rows. vs Nursa's free converter: shape-only, no validation, no edit-code explanation, no memory of last quarter. vs CMS's free iQIES reports and preview reports: all retrospective — they grade a file already submitted; Starcheck's whole window is before the upload.
reposition.distribution: 1) Programmatic SEO on the free quarterly public census — Provider Information (4pq5-n9py, 14,693 rows, refreshed quarterly), the PBJ Daily Nurse Staffing PUF, and State US Averages (xcdc-v8bm) — all free, machine-readable, no license. Build 14,693 per-facility pages keyed to CCN (reported vs case-mix vs adjusted HPRD by staff type, weekend HPRD, RN and total turnover, staffing rating, distance in hours to the next published TUG band), ~50 state pages, ~600 chain pages (chain name is a column in the file), and 790 footnote-explainer pages for the currently footnoted facilities. Query patterns: '<facility name> staffing rating', '<facility name> nurse staffing hours', 'nursing home staffing ratings <state>', 'nurse HPRD benchmark <state>', 'what does staffing rating footnote <code> mean'. Regenerated wholly by cron each quarter; zero human minutes. 2) Two free-tool wedges on distinct unclaimed query clusters: (a) a browser-side PBJ XML validator and edit-code explainer built on the free nhpbj_4_10_0 XSD and the machine-readable data specs (itm_mstr.csv / itm_val.csv, the 40-value jobTitleCode table) — Nursa holds the 'converter' query, the 'why did CMS reject my PBJ file / edit code' query is adjacent and open; (b) a public Five-Star staffing band calculator built strictly on TUG Table 3, Table A1 and Table A2, prefilled by CCN from the public file, stating the published band as arithmetic and never a rating. Both link every facility page. 3) Deadline-event cadence, forever: Feb 14 / May 15 / Aug 14 / Nov 14 are fixed statutory dates. A free per-CCN countdown page and opt-in reminder with last-quarter's public risk scan is a legitimate recurring cold-open. Launch against Nov 14, 2026 — the first full quarter submitted through iQIES, when the most files break — not against the August migration the incumbent already owns. 4) Enforcement-event trigger: diff each quarterly Provider Information refresh and compute the set of facilities that lost a staffing star or gained a footnote. That is a few hundred freshly-motivated buildings per quarter, each with a public address and an already-published page on the site — a machine-built outreach list from a free CSV. 5) One-time directory listings: the QTSO PBJ vendor portal (a formal CMS-facing vendor registration channel per the report) and PBJ Central's own free PBJ Vendor Directory, which they publish as content marketing and therefore accept listings into. No partnerships, no demos, no sales calls, no per-customer human minutes at any point.
reposition.why_winnable: The mandate is statutory and permanent, enforcement is confirmed and harsh in primary text (one star for non-submission; one star for ≥4 zero-RN days; one star for three months on a failed audit; forced lowest turnover points per QSO-25-01-NH), the entire rule set is published and deterministic, the corpus is free, unauthenticated, machine-readable and refreshed quarterly, and a live incumbent publishes a $99 price — every ingredient of a payable job. The specific fight is winnable because Starcheck's structural disadvantage (no iQIES vendor access, no MDS) maps exactly onto the two things it should refuse to sell — submission and rating projection — leaving a coherent product at a price no human-touching competitor can profitably match, aimed at the one input the cheap tiers push back onto the customer. The honest doubt is real and I would say it out loud to a partner: PBJ360 can add a $39 tier in a week, its free tier already covers the target segment's building count at $0, the serviceable base outside 16+ chains is ~7,760 buildings so at $39 and 5% penetration this is roughly $180K ARR — a small, permanently contested business, not a large one. It clears the bar as a zero-human company because gross margin is 100% and the SEO surface compounds quarterly off a free file; it does not clear the bar as anything bigger, and it should be funded on that understanding or not at all.

residual_risks: Price flank is not defensible on its own — PBJ360 can publish a $39 tier in a week; the compounding assets have to be the ingestion pipeline and the 14,693-page SEO surface, and if those are not live before the Nov 14 2026 deadline the reposition is just a cheaper clone.

Competitors holding live MDS (SimplePBJ/SimpleLTC, suite vendors) will always compute a more accurate projected rating; the product must publicly concede projection accuracy and compete only on ingestion and deterministic hard triggers, which is a narrower and less emotionally compelling pitch.
Deliberately not submitting is a real feature loss against every paid competitor — some share of buyers will pay $99 precisely for the one thing Starcheck refuses to do, and that share is unmeasured.

Two free tiers (PBJ360 Triple Check free forever ≤5 facilities; SimplePBJ Essentials free for all facilities) cover the entire target segment at $0 for the scrub-and-benchmark layer; the whole conversion thesis rests on agency-invoice and payroll-export ingestion being worth $39/month, which is untested.

Serviceable base is ~4,202 fully unaffiliated plus ~3,558 in 2-15-building chains; realistic ceiling is single-digit millions and a realistic outcome is low-hundreds-of-thousands ARR. Real, small, permanently contested.

Vendor penetration among unaffiliated facilities is explicitly Unproven in the report — if most of the 4,202 already receive a usable XML from timekeeping, the addressable base is materially smaller than 7,760.

Agency-invoice-to-shift-row extraction is the core mechanism and it is an accuracy-critical LLM job feeding a federal submission; every extracted row must ship as a reviewable draft with a citation back to the source line, and the product must never present extraction output as an authoritative record.

Three unresolved platform questions each shift the product's value and none is answered in the report: whether iQIES retains manual data entry post-migration, whether the CY2026Q2 and Q4 PBJ PUFs publish on schedule now that submission moved, and whether free Five-Star preview reports survive the iQIES migration (the word 'preview' is absent from the July 2026 TUG).

The in-quarter band estimate carries two acknowledged unknowns — the facility's live PDPM case-mix distribution and the unpublished current-quarter national average case-mix — and the disclosure must appear on the number itself, not in a footer, or the mechanism claim quietly becomes an outcome claim.

The '801 facilities / >5% penalised' figure is vendor-blog-only and must be struck from every page; only the first-party 790-of-14,693 footnote count is usable. Similarly the ~$119 SimplePBJ price stays uncited until a first-party fetch succeeds.

The mandate's paragraph letter moved from (q) to (p) while CMS's own memos stayed stale — the fail-closed spec-watch cron must hash the mandate text and the TUG tables, not citation strings, or it will fail open on exactly this class of change.

Distribution depends on search traffic to per-facility pages that also serve families, attorneys and journalists; if operator-intent queries are thinner than assumed, the SEO surface generates volume without buyers and there is no human-driven fallback channel.

survivors.name: ChargeFile (hospital MRF v3.0 generator)
survivors.candidate: C1 — ChargeFile (CMS hospital MRF v3.0 generator), run-3 cycle-2 ballot. Validation report: /home/user/Octopus/run-3/phase-1-ideation/research/C1-validation.md; ballot card: /home/user/Octopus/run-3/phase-1-ideation/shortlist-cycle2.json

finding_triage.finding: FATAL (kill lens): Craneware Trisus Pricing Transparency is 'Available at no cost to all US healthcare providers' and demonstrably generates AND hosts a live v3.0.0 MRF for a Critical Access Hospital (CCN 161343, Regional Medical Center, Manchester IA) with 9,142 populated median/p10/p90 cells — the $3,900/yr tier is priced against $0.
finding_triage.why: This is a commercial vendor's loss-leader, not a first-party government tool, and it fails the standard's own three-part free-substitute test on the third prong — the same report proves large residual pain the free tool does not touch (Bucktail, a fined CAH, points its locator at a kinsta.cloud staging domain; Fulton County serves its MRF through show_image.php; Benson was warned while on Health Catalyst; not one vendor-hosting domain tested serves the root cms-hpt.txt that six of Pinnacle's seven itemized violations concerned), so it kills the pitched $3,900/yr generator and sets the price ceiling without killing the market.

finding_triage.finding: FATAL: the hardest field is commoditised — Turquoise's public docs (updated 2026-01-16) compute 10th/50th/90th 'directly from 835 remittance files'; SlicedHealth advertises the same from 'actual ERA/835 remittance data going back 12–15 months' to hospitals with 'lean compliance and IT teams'.
finding_triage.why: Live incumbents selling the same job is proof the market pays, and the correct response is to stop competing on the 835 percentile pipeline — which the same report shows is optional anyway — rather than to declare the market closed.

finding_triage.finding: Kill patterns 2 and 3 both land: Health Catalyst's Hospital Price Index generates and hosts MRFs at 20 min–1 hr per facility including the 2026 percentiles, proven deployed at Benson Hospital, a warned Arizona CAH, by reading that hospital's own cms-hpt.txt.
finding_triage.why: An incumbent proven live at the exact buyer is a validation and a flank target — and the flanking fact is in the same finding: Benson was warned by CMS on 2026-07-23 *while* on HPI, and sthpiprd.blob.core.windows.net/cms-hpt.txt returns HTTP 400.

finding_triage.finding: Three further unseen incumbents serving CAHs today (PARA/HFRI on apps.para-hcfs.com, cdmpricing.com, HPI on Azure blob) plus GoRev and SlicedHealth; the card's claim that 'the artifact is not currently bundled' is refuted.
finding_triage.why: Bundling kills only if the bundle is near-universal in the segment and genuinely adequate, and here it is neither — five different vendors split the segment and three of their hosting domains return 404/400/soft-404 on the root .txt CMS actually fines for.

finding_triage.finding: Turquoise Health sells a product literally named 'MRF Generation'; the card's kill-check 2 claim that Turquoise has no MRF-creation offering is factually false.
finding_triage.why: A false competitive claim in the card is a correction, not a disqualifier, and the mitigant is recorded in the same finding — it is gated behind Contract Intelligence which is gated behind Market Intelligence, i.e. structurally unavailable to a 25-bed hospital at any self-serve price.

finding_triage.finding: ClaraPrice owns the buyer and the channel: a rural/CAH product line, 'hundreds of hospitals nationwide', compliance in 'as little as 3 weeks', and the single vendor named in NRHA's own January 2026 rural guidance.
finding_triage.why: An association-endorsed managed-service incumbent is a distribution constraint that forces a different channel (programmatic SEO and enforcement-event triggers on free public lists), not a proof that no other channel exists.

finding_triage.finding: The channel advises against the product: Stroudwater tells rural hospitals to work through EMR vendors and clearinghouses as 'pivotal allies'; NRHA says 'work with a compliance expert or agency' and that 'relying on manual file building will be risky'.
finding_triage.why: Consultants and trade bodies routing to managed service is a positioning constraint — and it argues for a product that is a *check on* the managed service rather than a replacement for it, which is a position neither Stroudwater nor NRHA is steering away from.

finding_triage.finding: Hospital Pricing Specialists offers 'a written guarantee to assume financial responsibility for CMS price-transparency penalties'; SlicedHealth promises 'enforcement won't put your organization at financial risk' — an outcome guarantee the product structurally cannot match.
finding_triage.why: Refusing to sell an outcome is engine-never-arbiter working correctly, and the honest counter-position (an independent mechanism report priced at 1–2% of an indemnity fee, which tells you whether you need one) is available.

finding_triage.finding: THE PRICING HYPOTHESIS IS DEAD AS STATED: Health Catalyst's own marketing puts manual MRF production at ~8 hours per facility, contradicting the card's '0.2–0.4 FTE' anchor by an order of magnitude; $3,900/yr is not defensible.
finding_triage.why: A price floor established by the incumbent's own published burden figure is exactly the kind of constraint that gets repriced — it caps annual value at roughly $400–600 per facility and the reposition prices under it.

finding_triage.finding: No incumbent price is obtainable anywhere — Craneware, Turquoise, ClaraPrice, SlicedHealth, Health Catalyst, PARA, Stroudwater, GoRev, Hospital Pricing Specialists, Rivet, Panacea, PMMC and Payerset are all $0 or quote-gated; the $3,900/yr hypothesis has zero market anchor.
finding_triage.why: Universal quote-gating is a pricing-information gap, and it is also an exploitable flank — publishing a real price in a category literally about price transparency is a differentiator no competitor currently offers.

finding_triage.finding: THE $51,615 CMP IS CITED FOR THE WRONG SECTION: the June 3 2026 Pinnacle notice itemizes exactly one material violation, under 45 CFR 180.60 (consumer-friendly shoppable services), which ChargeFile does not produce.
finding_triage.why: The card misused this citation, but removing it leaves the market signal *stronger*, not absent — the February 4 2026 notice shows six of seven violations were the cms-hpt.txt and footer link, which is a more precise and more addressable target than the one the card aimed at.

finding_triage.finding: CMP BASE RATE IS ~1%: CMS's primary enforcement dataset shows 2,973 hospitals ever warned against 28–29 ever penalized, with only 2 CMP notices in all of 2026 (both to Pinnacle); dominant outcomes are 'Met Requirements' (3,620) and 'Closure Notice' (3,869).
finding_triage.why: This is not zero enforcement — 953 Warning Notices and 426 CAP Requests in 2026 alone are 1,379 named, dated, publicly-listed forcing events per year — it is a demand that must be priced at hundreds, not thousands, of dollars, which the reposition does.

finding_triage.finding: Enforcement cadence thinner than 'live' suggests: 25–29 CMP rows total since 2022-06-07, one hospital in all of 2026, a gap from 2025-05-13 to 2026-02-04.
finding_triage.why: Same constraint as above, stated twice by two lenses; the intrinsic pain (a public warning notice with a 90-day clock, plus the CFO's own signature on an attestation under 180.50(a)(3)(iii)) is independently non-zero, so the Class A 'zero enforcement AND zero intrinsic pain' bar is not met.

finding_triage.finding: THE 519 FIGURE DOES NOT RECONCILE: it is a mixed count of Warning Notices (322) plus CAP Requests, appears on no CMS primary page, and the card's '90-day then 45-day clock' gloss conflates two pipeline stages.
finding_triage.why: The misread number is fully replaceable by the primary CMS enforcement CSV (13,355 rows, modified 2026-08-14) that the mandate lens found, so removing the bad figure leaves a stronger, better-sourced signal rather than none.

finding_triage.finding: SEVERE — the demand signal points at a different buyer: the 519-letter wave went to 'acute-care, behavioral health, surgical hospitals and inpatient rehabilitation facilities' per Advisory Board; CAHs and REHs are not named, and only ~4 of the CMP-penalized hospitals are CAH/REH.
finding_triage.why: This finding is contradicted by primary data in the same report — the mandate lens cross-matched CMS's own enforcement CSV to hospital type and found 146 CAHs and 3 REHs among 953 hospitals warned in 2026, with 159 distinct CAH/REH warned or CAP'd since 2026-04-01 — so a secondary press enumeration loses to the primary file, and in any case it is a targeting instruction (serve all ~5,196 in-scope hospitals), not a kill.

finding_triage.finding: THE 835 ENGINE — the card's hardest differentiator and moat layer 2/3 — IS OPTIONAL: the schema's count=='0' escape hatch requires only additional_payer_notes, CMS slide 22 blesses it, and CMS's FAQ permits 'revenue cycle systems, EHRs, payer portals, clearinghouses, or third-party data aggregators' instead of 835s.
finding_triage.why: This deletes a claimed moat, not the premise — the mandate itself re-verified verbatim, and the reposition drops the 835 path entirely rather than defending a moat the regulation waives.

finding_triage.finding: PERCENTILES ARE CONDITIONAL, NOT UNIVERSAL, AND CMS TELLS HOSPITALS TO AVOID THEM: 180.50(b)(2)(ii)(C) fires only 'If the standard charge is based on a percentage or algorithm', and CMS slide 21 requires dollarisation where the hospital can 'do the math'.
finding_triage.why: The mandate is real and re-verified verbatim at every cite the card gave; this narrows the addressable pain within the mandate rather than showing the mandate does not exist, so it fails the Class A 'premise false against primary text' test.

finding_triage.finding: 'ALTERNATIVE, EQUIVALENT SOURCE OF REMITTANCE DATA' DISSOLVES THE X12/WASM MOAT — a posted-payments CSV qualifies, making the in-browser X12 parser the highest-friction input in the funnel defending a moat the regulation itself waives.
finding_triage.why: A dissolved moat layer is a product-design correction; the reposition removes remittance ingestion from the product entirely, so the moat that dissolves is one the company no longer needs.

finding_triage.finding: ENGINE-NEVER-ARBITER BREACH RISK AT THE ALLOWED-AMOUNT DERIVATION: CMS never defines which 835 values constitute an 'allowed amount', CLP is claim-level while MRF rows are per code, so choosing CLP04+CLP05 vs SVC-line reconstruction is a methodological judgement the hospital's CEO then attests to.
finding_triage.why: Class A requires the breach to be in the CORE value and unfixable by mechanism-framing; here it sits in an optional subsystem that the reposition removes outright, leaving a core of fetch + CMS's own CC0 validator + literal spec diff, which asserts no legal outcome at all.

finding_triage.finding: THE MOAT IS INVERTED: 'we never sign a BAA' is only an advantage if the BAA is the blocker, incumbents already sign them and ingest 835s, and the card's transmitted 'service date bucket' finer than year defeats 45 CFR 164.514(b)(2)(C) safe harbor outright.
finding_triage.why: Both halves are cured by the same reposition — a product that touches only files the regulation requires to be public, free and login-free (180.50(d)(3)-(4)) never encounters PHI, so there is no safe-harbor question and no BAA to be a moat or a liability.

finding_triage.finding: MODERATE — the real customer labor is input #2, not input #3: mapping every payer+plan to dollar/percentage/algorithm is contract modeling (Turquoise sells it as 'Clear Contracts'), which the card mislabels as 'a routine report out of any patient-accounting system'.
finding_triage.why: This is a decisive argument against the self-serve *generator*, and the reposition concedes it fully by never asking the buyer for a chargemaster or a contract-terms table.

finding_triage.finding: MOAT LAYER 2 IS AIMED AT THE WRONG PAYMENT MODEL: in a live CAH file, methodology is dominated by 'Percent of Total Billed Charges' (38,585) and 'Other' (28,479), with algorithm text reading 'Reimbursement is based on the facility specific Medicare Interim Rate letter' — CAHs are cost-reimbursed, and the interim rate is not derivable from any public file.
finding_triage.why: A wrong moat is dropped, not appealed; the RVU/GPCI/OPPS translation table leaves the product, and the report's own measurement (median/p10/p90 filled in 8.4% of 94,980 payer cells at a live CAH) becomes evidence of a gap to *report on* rather than a gap to compute.

finding_triage.finding: THE HOSTING TIER CARRIES THE EXACT LIABILITY CMS PENALIZES: because 180.50(d)(6)(i) binds the root cms-hpt.txt to the domain hosting the MRF, a vendor that hosts inherits the duty, and the 180.50(d)(6)(ii) footer link on the hospital's own site can never be delivered by the vendor.
finding_triage.why: This is a priced, bounded operational duty — serving one static text file correctly at a per-tenant subdomain — and the same finding proves not one incumbent hosting domain does it, which makes it the sharpest available flank rather than a disqualifier.

finding_triage.finding: BUYER UNIVERSE OVERCOUNTED: 45 CFR 180.30(b) deems Federal and State hospitals compliant, so 132 VA + 32 DoD + 42 Government-Federal + 17 Tribal = 223 rows are out of scope; addressable base is ~5,180–5,200, not 5,419.
finding_triage.why: A 4% correction to a small-but-real TAM is explicitly a constraint, not a kill, and the corrected figure is carried into the reposition.

finding_triage.finding: MINOR PREMISE-CITE ERROR: the card cites 45 CFR 180.50(b)(3) for the annual update requirement; the actual cite is 180.50(e), 'Frequency of updates'.
finding_triage.why: A wrong subsection pointer to a requirement that was independently re-verified verbatim at 180.50(e) is a typo, not a false premise.

finding_triage.finding: AMA CPT descriptor licensing exposure was not tested and remains an unresolved pre-code legal question.
finding_triage.why: This is a one-time design constraint obtainable without per-customer human work — publish conformance metadata (HTTP status, field presence, validator error codes and line numbers) and never redistribute descriptor text — not a licensing cost that scales with customers.

finding_triage.finding: A fabricated price ($2,500 audit / $12,500 remediation / $500-month, phone 888-555-1234 at hospital-pricetransparency.com) was surfaced by the summariser and correctly discarded as a bot-interstitial artefact.
finding_triage.why: The fabrication was caught and removed by the validator itself before it entered the record, and its removal leaves the real market signal — 953 warnings, 426 CAPs, a live measured 8.4% percentile fill rate, and four hosting-domain defects — entirely intact, so the Class A 'no real signal remains' bar is not met.

reposition.one_liner: Not a generator — an independent, public-data conformance monitor: it fetches a hospital's live cms-hpt.txt and posted standard-charges file, runs CMS's own CC0 validator (@cmsgov/hpt-validator 2.6.0) against schema V3.0.0, diffs the locator file field-by-field against the literal text of 45 CFR 180.50(d)(5) and (d)(6)(i), and returns a dated, reproducible evidence record of exactly what was public at that URL on that date — never a compliance verdict, never a penalty prediction, and it never asks for a chargemaster, a contract table, or an 835.
reposition.price: Ceiling and floor are both observed in the validation report and both are low, so the ladder sits deliberately underneath them. ANCHOR 1 (floor, $0): Craneware Trisus Pricing Transparency is 'available at no cost to all US healthcare providers' and was proven generating and hosting a live v3.0.0 MRF for CCN 161343, a Critical Access Hospital — so anything competing with MRF *generation* is worth $0 and is not sold. ANCHOR 2 (ceiling, ~$400-600/facility/yr): Health Catalyst's own marketing puts manual MRF production at 'roughly 8 hours per facility', the only quantified burden figure obtainable anywhere in the category; at a loaded small-hospital analyst rate that is the entire annual labour value of the job. ANCHOR 3 (urgency, $342/day): the CY2026 CPI-adjusted CMP at <=30 beds, verbatim from the Pinnacle notice — roughly $10,260 for one month of an undetected 404'd locator file, against a ~1% base rate that must not be oversold. ANCHOR 4 (information gap): no competitor in the category publishes any price at all. LADDER: (a) Free — a public observation record for each of the ~5,196 in-scope hospitals, regenerated weekly, showing observed HTTP status, filename against the CMS convention, validator error count and locator-field presence; (b) $149 one-time Conformance Dossier — the full validator error list with line numbers and field paths, the locator diff against 180.50(d)(6)(i)(A)-(D), the footer-link check, delivered as a dated PDF plus machine-readable JSON; (c) $349/yr Monitor — weekly re-run, alert when the posted file 404s, when the filename or content-type drifts, when the validator or schema version moves (six validator releases in 2026 alone, 2.6.0 on 2026-08-18), plus a content-hashed dated ledger of what was public on each date; (d) $588/yr ($49/mo) Locator Hosting — a per-tenant subdomain that actually serves a correct root cms-hpt.txt, legal under 180.50(d)(1) with the TXT FAQ's root-of-domain rule satisfied. Max ACV $937, blended target ~$400 — under Health Catalyst's own stated labour cost, and the price is published on the page, which nobody in a price-transparency category currently does.
reposition.wedge: vs CRANEWARE TRISUS (free, generates + hosts, proven at a CAH): it cannot audit itself. The buyer's residual exposure is not the file's existence but its plumbing — six of the seven violations in Pinnacle's February 2026 notice were the cms-hpt.txt and the footer link, and 180.50(d)(6)(ii) puts the footer link on the hospital's own site where no host can ever deliver it. We check the vendor's output, including Craneware's, and check the half of the duty no vendor can discharge. vs HEALTH CATALYST HOSPITAL PRICE INDEX: proven live at Benson Hospital — which CMS warned on 2026-07-23 while it was on HPI — and sthpiprd.blob.core.windows.net/cms-hpt.txt returns HTTP 400. Being on the incumbent did not prevent the letter; the flank is the observed defect, stated as an HTTP status, not an opinion. vs PARA/HFRI: apps.para-hcfs.com/cms-hpt.txt returns 404 while hosting North Valley Health Center's MRF. Same flank, same evidence form. vs CDMPRICING.COM: HTTP 200 serving an Angular SPA shell (soft-404) while serving North Valley Hospital, warned 2026-07-29, whose posted MRF is a legacy pre-July-2024 wide CSV with no payer_name/plan_name/attestation/NPI columns. Same flank. vs TURQUOISE 'MRF GENERATION': gated behind Contract Intelligence, itself gated behind Market Intelligence, all quote-gated — structurally unreachable at a card-swipe price, so we do not fight it on generation; we are the outside check its customers can buy for $149. vs CLARAPRICE (NRHA-named, 'hundreds of hospitals', 3 weeks, demo-gated): flank on latency and price disclosure — a free observation record today with no sales call, and a published price against a demo gate. vs SLICEDHEALTH: it sells the outcome ('enforcement won't put your organization at financial risk'); we sell the mechanism and print the evidence, and we are complementary — the buyer can hold both. vs HOSPITAL PRICING SPECIALISTS (written penalty indemnity): we will not match it and say so plainly; the counter is that a $149 dossier costs 1-2% of an indemnity engagement and tells the buyer whether they need one. vs CMS'S OWN FREE TOOLS (the real first-party substitute — validator, filename wizard, TXT generator, all CC0): we do not compete with them, we embed the same CC0 library. The residual pain they leave is precise and provable: they require the hospital to already have the file and upload it by hand, one at a time; they do not tell you your locator returns 404, do not check the footer link, do not notice when the schema or validator version moves, do not keep a dated record of what was public, and never run unprompted. vs DO NOTHING (the honest hardest competitor, ~1% CMP base rate): we do not oversell it — the pitch is that at $149-$349 the decision costs less than the arithmetic of arguing about it.
reposition.distribution: 1. PROGRAMMATIC SEO over a complete public entity list. Hospital_General_Information.csv gives 5,419 rows (~5,196 in scope after 180.30(b) removes 223 federal/tribal), each with name, CCN, address, city, state and type. One page per hospital, content = that week's actual observed check result, so every page is genuinely unique and regenerated weekly rather than thin. Query patterns targeted: '<hospital name> price transparency', '<hospital name> machine readable file', '<hospital name> standard charges file', '<hospital name> cms-hpt.txt', 'cms-hpt.txt 404', 'hpt validator error <error code>', '<ein>_<hospital-name>_standardcharges naming convention', 'hospital price transparency <state>'. Plus 50 state roll-ups and one page per hospital type. 2. ENFORCEMENT-EVENT TRIGGER, the strongest channel and entirely free. CMS's Hospital_Price_Transparency_Enforcement_Activities_and_Outcomes CSV (13,355 rows through 2026-07-31, dataset modified 2026-08-14, refreshed monthly) publishes every Warning Notice and CAP Request with hospital name, address, city, state, action and date — 953 warnings and 426 CAP requests in 2026 alone, 159 distinct CAH/REH since 2026-04-01. Each new row is a named hospital on a public clock. On the day a row appears: auto-run the dossier, publish the free observation page, and send exactly one plain-text email to the price-transparency contact that 45 CFR 180.50(d)(6)(i) itself requires that hospital to publish in its own cms-hpt.txt — a contact channel the regulation creates and the hospital publishes voluntarily. No calls, no CRM, no SDR. 3. FREE-TOOL WEDGE: a public 'check any hospital' box (paste a domain, get the locator diff and validator run in seconds) as the top-of-funnel, and a free CC0 national dataset of the full weekly crawl plus an llms.txt and a read-only JSON endpoint, so the crawl gets cited, linked and answered-from. 4. EARNED MEDIA WITHOUT A HUMAN: the vendor-defect table — which hosting domains do and do not serve a valid root cms-hpt.txt — is a novel dataset nobody has published, aimed at exactly the outlets (Becker's, Fierce Healthcare, Forvis Mazars) that already carried the 519-letter story. Publish it as observed facts on a fixed cadence and let it be picked up. 5. NOT DOING: partnerships, association endorsement, demos, or any managed-service motion — the channel ClaraPrice and Stroudwater own is conceded outright. IMPORTANT GUARDRAIL on the public pages: publish observed facts only (HTTP status, field presence, filename, content-type, validator error count and codes) with no compliance verdict, no ranking language and no penalty prediction, and never republish CPT descriptor text.
reposition.why_winnable: The whole product is public-data in, public-data out, which is why it can run with nobody in the loop: every check is an HTTP fetch, a run of CMS's own CC0-1.0 validator, and a literal diff against a 44KB CFR text and a 13KB JSON schema — one federal rule, one schema, one validator, no state layer, no prose extraction, no scraper fleet. It never touches PHI, so there is no BAA, no security review, no de-identification question and no per-customer legal work; it never asks for a chargemaster or a contract-terms table, so it does not inherit the contract-modelling engagement that makes the generator business human-shaped; and it needs no customer to start, because the crawl of 5,196 hospitals runs whether anyone has paid or not, which is simultaneously the product, the SEO surface and the lead list. The dated content-hashed ledger of what each hospital actually had public on each date is the one asset that genuinely cannot be backfilled by a later entrant — hospitals overwrite their file in place — and unlike the card's version of that moat, it accrues from observation rather than from customers, so it compounds from day one at near-zero cost. THE HONEST DOUBT, stated plainly: the price ceiling is brutal — bounded above by roughly $400-600/yr of the incumbent's own admitted labour and below by $0 from Craneware — the CMP base rate is ~1% so urgency is thin and must not be oversold, hospital procurement may defeat a card swipe at any price (NRHA is actively steering the other way and this remains untested), and the product has little lock-in beyond the ledger. On a base of ~5,196 hospitals with a blended ACV near $400, a 3-5% attach is a $60-100k/yr business, not a large one. I would fund it because the marginal cost of running it rounds to hosting and the crawl asset compounds unattended, but I would underwrite it as a small, durable, cash-positive utility — not as a venture outcome — and I would kill it fast if the first 40 enforcement-triggered emails convert at zero.

residual_risks: Price ceiling is hard and low: bounded above by Health Catalyst's own ~8-hours-per-facility burden figure (~$400-600/yr of labour) and below by Craneware's $0. Blended ACV near $400 against ~5,196 in-scope hospitals makes this a small business even at good attach rates.

Card-swipe conversion at a hospital remains completely untested and NRHA guidance ('work with a compliance expert or agency') points the other way. The $149 dossier is the cheap experiment; if the first 40 enforcement-triggered sends convert at zero, the thesis is dead and should be killed fast.

CMP base rate is ~1% (2,973 hospitals ever warned, 28-29 ever penalized; 2 CMP notices in all of 2026, both to one hospital). The urgency must be sold as the named public warning letter and the CEO's own attestation signature, never as penalty avoidance — and that is a materially weaker sales story.

Any incumbent can close the locator flank in an afternoon. Serving a correct root cms-hpt.txt is a single static text file; Health Catalyst, PARA and cdmpricing could each fix theirs at trivial cost, which would erase the sharpest wedge. The defensible residue is then independence (a vendor cannot audit itself) and the dated ledger, both weaker.

Publishing per-hospital observation records creates reputational and defamation exposure. Mitigation is absolute discipline: observed facts only (HTTP status, field presence, filename, content-type, validator error codes and line numbers), no compliance verdict, no ranking or grading language, no penalty prediction, a visible correction path, and same-day re-check on request.

AMA CPT descriptor licensing is untested and unresolved. Public pages and dossiers must carry conformance metadata only and must never republish descriptor text from a hospital's MRF; this constrains how rich the free pages can be.

Crawl legitimacy and hygiene: the files are ones 45 CFR 180.50(d)(3)-(4) requires to be public, free, login-free and directly downloadable, which is about as clean an obtainability story as exists — but 5,196 weekly fetches of multi-megabyte files needs robots.txt respect, rate limiting, conditional requests and a published crawler identity, or the company becomes the abuse complaint.

Validator parity is unproven: @cmsgov/hpt-validator 2.6.0 (CC0) is embeddable, but the report could not confirm the hosted CMS Online Validator runs the same version or ruleset. Every output must state 'validator vN against schema vM on date D' precisely, and a divergence from CMS's hosted tool would be a credibility event.

Spec churn is a live treadmill in both directions: six validator releases in 2026. A missed version bump silently degrades every customer's monitor, so staleness detection must fail loud and mark records stale rather than continuing to imply currency.
Regulatory reversal risk: AHA is lobbying to sunset parts of the framework. A repeal or a material narrowing of 180.50(d)(6) would remove the locator duty that the entire wedge is built on.

The pivot away from generation means abandoning every claimed moat in the original card (835/WASM parser, RVU translation table, no-BAA posture, generation ledger). What remains is a thin, fast, cheap product whose only durable asset is the observation ledger — if that ledger turns out not to be something buyers will pay for, there is no second line of defence.

survivors.name: Outfall (NPDES DMR generator)

finding_triage.finding: The price anchor is a phantom — effluentlabs.com is a six-month-old domain (RDAP 2026-02-16) with a generated team page, so '$1,500/mo proves money changes hands' is unsupported.
finding_triage.why: The anchor is correctly destroyed, but removing it does not leave zero market signal: AllMax Operator10 at $14,165 + $1,970/yr with 'over 2,000 customers' and Hach WIMS at $27,140 + $4,885.20/yr are both re-verified from primary municipal procurement PDFs, and Mapistry publishes $298/$498/$998 per year for this buyer class — so this is a forced re-anchoring, not evidence-collapse.

finding_triage.finding: The card's own named exemplar buyers have nothing to compute — IA0078484 has one parameter (pH), IA0075451 has two.
finding_triage.why: The miner picked the wrong two facilities off his own roster; the same live corpus shows AL0081558 with 8 outfalls / 14 parameters / 1,972 rows and small STPs clustering at 6–25 cells per period, so this is a segmentation error to fix, not a market that does not exist.

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 5 fires — the calculation conventions (BDL at QL, geometric-mean zero substitution, MAL substitution, flow weighting, <4-sample fallback, '>' over '<') live in state prose, not the CFR.
finding_triage.why: The corpus is bounded to ~47 permitting authorities with published guidance documents (TCEQ, PA DEP, Oregon DEQ QA guidance all fetched today) — a one-time setup cost, not per-customer human work — and the convention stays a customer-set, worksheet-printed setting so the engine never asserts which rule governs.

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 1 fires at state level — PA DEP ships a free Excel 'Daily Effluent Monitoring' calculator (up to 90 params/3 outfalls), MPCA e-services computes limit types, TCEQ ships a free geometric-mean calculator, NC ships a free Excel-to-CSV template, Oregon YDO auto-generates a pre-populated template.
finding_triage.why: This is the textbook Class B free-substitute-with-worse-UX case: each is a per-state, per-permittee manual artifact, none reads EPA's received-data file to tell you a required row is missing past its due date, none retains a cross-year ledger, and MPCA's own page concedes the operator must 'review and confirm the calculated values' — the same shape our product takes.

finding_triage.finding: Kill pattern 1 fires hardest in Ohio — 'eDMR only transfers your raw data to our system, not the statistics. Our internal system calculates the needed statistics on our end.'
finding_triage.why: This is the one place the free tool genuinely is equal-or-better for the exact job, and the correct response is to gate Ohio (4,307 of ~100,352 permits) out of the paid file product entirely while keeping it in the submission-channel-agnostic watch product — a coverage constraint costing ~4% of permits.

finding_triage.finding: Market shrinks ~34.7% before the first sale — 34,793 of 100,352 permits sit in states running their own eDMR (PA 12,061, WV 5,156, MO 4,350, OH 4,307, …), plus FL EzDMR and PA has no bulk import at all.
finding_triage.why: Small-but-real TAM is explicitly a constraint, and it applies only to the file emitter — the received-vs-required completeness watch runs off ICIS regardless of which portal the permittee submits through, so the haircut hits one module rather than the company.

finding_triage.finding: The corpus is incomplete for the artifact and the 'one public API call, zero configuration' moat is factually false — get_effluent_chart returns no frequency-of-analysis, no sample-type, no limit-set designator.
finding_triage.why: All three fields were proven present at 99.8–100% population in the free weekly npdes_limits.zip, which the corpus lens actually range-fetched and inflated today — so the corpus is alive and legally obtainable and the finding costs a one-time 526 MB ETL, not the business.

finding_triage.finding: The pain EPA measures is submission and timeliness, not calculation — and Outfall explicitly refuses to submit.
finding_triage.why: This is the single most useful finding in the report and it is a repositioning instruction rather than a kill: DMRDueDate and the received-vs-required row grid are both in the public corpus, so the product can address exactly the failure mode EPA names as over half of national SNC without ever transmitting or signing anything.

finding_triage.finding: Penalty urgency does not reach the buyer — $75.7M total penalties across 92,846 minors is ~$815 lifetime average, only 4.8% ever carry a formal enforcement action, Iowa minors total $134,484.
finding_triage.why: This is weak enforcement expectation, not zero enforcement: the $68,445/day statute is verified, EPA attests DMR reporting is the single largest source of SNC nationwide, and SNC status is publicly posted on ECHO — so it caps the price hard rather than removing the motive.

finding_triage.finding: EPA itself is a standing free-substitute risk — a calculator bolted onto NetDMR, or more states copying Ohio's raw-data-in model, would end the business.
finding_triage.why: A speculative future substitute is not a present disqualifying fact (the identical argument would have killed Ratepin against the free WH-347), and it reaches only the file emitter, not the watch layer.

finding_triage.finding: Moat layer 1 is already free — Georgia EPD: 'the information in NetDMR that describes your permit, effluent limits, etc., is pre-programmed into NetDMR by EPA.'
finding_triage.why: This refutes a moat claim, not the premise: the honest moat moves to the weekly received-vs-required diff and the retained calculation ledger, neither of which the free mandated channel performs.

finding_triage.finding: Buyer count miscited — the card's 92,846 is the minors-only subset; the unfiltered query today errors at 100,352.
finding_triage.why: The evidence was misread but in the direction that makes the market larger, and the state-slice method reproduces exactly (IA 1,835), so real signal survives the correction intact.

finding_triage.finding: The arithmetic-mean premise is thinner than stated — the card's own proof permit returns GEO MEAN and 7 DA AVG, and 7-day moving averages are not derivable from a statistical base code alone.
finding_triage.why: Not a false premise against the primary text: 40 CFR 122.41(l)(4)(i)–(iii) was re-verified verbatim by all four lenses, StatisticalBaseCode is supplied per limit row by the corpus, and moving averages are computable from dated sample rows — it narrows what the CFR alone supplies rather than voiding the mandate.

finding_triage.finding: Locus Technologies is a closer competitor than admitted — automates DMR assembly, calculation and formatting, adds new state formats regularly, claims users saved $2,000,000.
finding_triage.why: A live incumbent selling the same job is proof the market pays; Locus is demo-gated with no published price and sells to mid-to-large customers, which names the flank rather than closing it.

finding_triage.finding: Price floor risk — Mapistry publishes $298/$498/$998 per year for industrial facilities with air and water permits, well under the hypothesised $1,068/yr.
finding_triage.why: A published price floor is the canonical Class B constraint; it is also the most useful datum in the report because it is the only self-serve published price for this exact buyer class, and it becomes the anchor for the reposition.

finding_triage.finding: Value wedge narrows to lab-EDD mapping + the import file + the ICIS cross-check + the audit worksheet — thin against a free agency spreadsheet.
finding_triage.why: A narrower wedge is still a wedge, and the reposition widens it back with the received-vs-required watch, which is the one function no free first-party tool performs in any state examined.

finding_triage.finding: THE MEASURED TASK IS TOO SMALL TO SELL — median 10 DMR value-cells per monitoring period across 19 live permits, with 188 of 475 average/maximum pairs identical (one sample, zero arithmetic); a 20–40 minute monthly job.
finding_triage.why: This is the most damaging surviving finding and it destroys the $89/mo arithmetic pitch outright, but small-but-real pain is a constraint under the standard, not a kill — it forces both a lower price and a value source that is not proportional to cell count, which is precisely what the reposition does.

finding_triage.finding: The card's keystone kill-pattern-1 source is stale — Oregon migrated to Your DEQ Online and its current 81-page guide contains zero occurrences of 'NetDMR'.
finding_triage.why: A sourcing error in the card, not a refutation of the substance: the same lens confirmed Oregon's current 2026-07-20 guide still states permittees must perform calculations on raw data.

finding_triage.finding: TAM haircut — 12 of 52 resolvable sampled Iowa permits (23%) return zero outfalls, zero parameters and zero DMR rows; they have no DMR product to buy.
finding_triage.why: It shrinks the denominator, but the qualifying set is machine-identifiable from the same free corpus before a dollar of acquisition spend, which converts a TAM problem into a targeting advantage.

finding_triage.finding: Engine-never-arbiter survives only by shrinking the product to a worksheet — 40 CFR 122.22(d) makes the signer certify to 'a system designed to assure that qualified personnel properly gather and evaluate the information submitted', and 122.41(k)(2) carries $10,000 and 6 months per violation.
finding_triage.why: Worksheet-plus-permittee-signature is the compliant shape and the same shape MPCA's own free tool mandates; the core value is order statistics on the customer's own numbers plus a diff of a public federal file — mechanism, never a legal conclusion — so the gate is not breached by the core value, and BDL/NODI stay customer-set and worksheet-printed.

finding_triage.finding: The buyer already owns the job — contract operations firms 'complete and file the monthly DMR with the State' inside their service fee.
finding_triage.why: This identifies the economic buyer rather than removing one: a firm carrying dozens of permits is the portfolio tier, its alternative is its own repeated labour and multiplied deadline exposure across every site, and NC's public contract-operator registry makes those firms machine-addressable.

reposition.one_liner: Outfall diffs EPA's own weekly ICIS-NPDES files against your permit's published limit set and shows you which required DMR rows EPA has recorded no value for past their published due date — and, in states whose portal accepts the 31-column import, computes the period's summary statistics from your lab rows and emits the import file plus a line-by-line worksheet you review, upload and sign yourself.
reposition.price: $39/month per single-outfall permit ($390 annual prepay), $129/month for permits with 3+ outfalls or 15+ parameters, $349/month for a portfolio of up to 10 permits; the due-date and received-row watch on one permit is free forever. Anchors: Mapistry's published $298/$498/$998 per year (Capterra, fetched 2026-08-20) is the self-serve floor for this exact buyer class and sets the ceiling on what a card-swipe tier can ask; AllMax Operator10's re-verified $14,165 one-time + $1,970/yr with 'over 2,000 customers' (primary municipal procurement PDF) is the only transacted anchor in the report — $468/yr sits below its annual support line alone. Hach WIMS at $27,140 + $4,885.20/yr is the upper bound of the bundle. Effluent Labs' $1,500/$3,500/$5,500 is DISCARDED as an anchor: a published ask on a domain registered 2026-02-16 with no independent trace is not a clearing price, and the original $89 tier that leaned on it dies with it.
reposition.wedge: Ecesis, Klir, Locus and Hach WIMS: all four re-fetched 2026-08-20 with zero published price — Ecesis Pricing.aspx contains no dollar amount and reads 'Contact Us' in all three tiers; entry is demo, quote or phone only. Flank = a published price and card-swipe signup with no demo, at roughly 2% of the WIMS bundle. AllMax Operator10 ($14,165 + $1,970/yr, and the procurement reviewer notes it is 'very limited in it options' and still needs a separate LIMS purchase): flank = no install, no seat licence, no LIMS, and annual cost under its support line. Mapistry ($298–$998/yr, DMR generation unconfirmed at any tier): flank = artifact specificity — we emit the exact 31-column NetDMR/CIWQS import and the received-vs-required grid, not general air-and-water compliance.
