Effluent Labs ($1,500/mo, dedicated analyst, no self-serve): flank = unattended at 2.6% of its entry tier; and because its 15-page site already owns the generic DMR keywords, we do not fight it there — we fight on the 100,352-permit-ID long tail it has no pages for. Free state first-party tools (PA DEP Excel to 90 params, MPCA worksheets, TCEQ geo-mean XLSX, NC Excel-to-CSV template, Oregon YDO pre-populated DMRSummaryUploadTemplate.csv): flank = not one of them reads EPA's received-data file, so not one can tell a permittee that a required row is missing past its DMRDueDate; none retains a cross-year ledger; none scales to an AL0081558-shaped permit (8 outfalls, 14 parameters, 1,972 rows). Ohio is the honest exception — the regulator computes the statistics server-side and the permit limits are not even in eDMR — so Ohio is gated out of the paid file product entirely and sold only the watch. NetDMR itself (free, mandated, limits pre-programmed by EPA): flank = it validates and transmits and does not compute, per current state guidance, and it cannot surface a monitoring period the permittee never opened.
reposition.distribution: (1) Programmatic SEO over a public entity list that is already the product's onboarding: ~100,352 effective NPDES individual permits enumerated from ECHO cwa_rest_services.get_facilities per state (per-state slices reproduce exactly — IA 1,835, PA 12,061, OH 4,307), joined weekly to npdes_limits.zip (526 MB) and npdes_dmrs_fy2026.zip (455 MB). One page per permit plus one per county. Query patterns: '{PERMIT ID} discharge monitoring report', '{FACILITY NAME} NPDES DMR due date', 'NPDES permits in {COUNTY} {STATE}', '{PARAMETER} effluent limit {PERMIT ID}', 'NPDES minor permits {STATE} significant noncompliance', 'what is NODI code {CODE}', '{STATE} DMR due dates {YEAR}'. Every page is public record, dated to the file, and mechanism-framed. (2) Free-tool wedge: type a permit number, get that permit's due-date calendar and its received-vs-required row grid free forever, with a weekly email on each ICIS refresh; paid unlocks the import file, the worksheet, multi-permit and the retained ledger. (3) Enforcement-event trigger, fully automated: weekly diff of npdes_dmrs_fy2026.zip for newly appearing violation codes D80 and D90 (proven live at 1,057 and 2,952 occurrences in a 40 MB sample) and for CWPCurrentSNCStatus changes; the affected permittee gets one factual, opt-out, public-record-only email naming the file date and the code — never a legal characterization, never 'you are in violation'. (4) Public registries of multi-permit firms: state contract-operator registries (NC requires contract operator firms to register) yield a machine-readable list of firms each carrying dozens of permits — the $349 portfolio tier, reached by the same programmatic path. No partnerships, no demos, no calls anywhere in the funnel.
reposition.why_winnable: Every functional competitor re-verified in the last 48 hours — Ecesis, Klir, Locus, Hach WIMS, AllMax — is demo- or quote-gated with no published price and no self-serve path, which leaves the entire sub-$100/month card-swipe band structurally empty in a market of ~100,352 permits. The corpus that powers both the product and its whole SEO surface is free, national, weekly-refreshed and proven live to the byte (newest received value six days old). And the one function no free state tool performs anywhere examined — diffing what EPA has actually received against what the permit requires, by due date — is precisely the failure mode EPA itself attests is 'the single largest source of SNC nationwide' and 'over half of the facilities in SNC status.' The honest doubt, stated plainly: the arithmetic is genuinely small — median 10 value-cells a month, 40% of average/maximum pairs identical — and the enforcement expectation for a minor permittee is about $815 over a lifetime with only 4.8% ever facing formal action. The whole thesis therefore rests on one untested proposition: that a small permittee or a contract operator will pay ~$470/yr for a deadline-and-completeness watch on a public federal file. Nothing in four validation lenses closes that question, and it should be tested by free-tier-to-paid conversion before meaningful spend, not assumed.

residual_risks: No verified transacted price exists for this artifact at ANY price point — the $39/$129/$349 ladder is derived from adjacent anchors (Mapistry's published $298/yr floor, AllMax's $1,970/yr support line), not from an observed sale of a DMR generator. Willingness to pay is the single biggest open question and must be tested by free-tier conversion first.

The measured task is tiny (median 10 cells per period; 40% of concentration average/maximum pairs identical, i.e. one sample and zero arithmetic). If the received-vs-required watch does not carry the price on its own, the calculator cannot, and the company has no price at all.

Free first-party substitutes are moving in the direction that kills the file product: Ohio computes statistics server-side and does not even hold permit limits in eDMR, and Oregon's Your DEQ Online auto-generates a permit-specific pre-populated CSV. If NetDMR adds a calculator or more states adopt Ohio's raw-data-in model, the emitter dies; only the watch layer survives.

NetDMR end-to-end acceptance is still untested — no lens submitted a generated import file, and it is unknown whether the format requires NetDMR-internal identifiers only visible inside the permittee's own account. This must be closed with a real CDX/Login.gov account before any paid claim about the file is made.

Per-authority calculation prose (MAL substitution, BDL reported at the QL, geometric-mean zero-substitution, flow-weighted averaging, the fewer-than-four-samples fallback, calendar-week weekly averages) is a real ~47-jurisdiction build. Shipping into an authority whose convention is not published risks producing a number the permittee certifies under 40 CFR 122.22 — the exposure is symmetric, since an over-computed value self-reports a strict-liability CWA 309 violation and an under-computed one is a false report.

Effective TAM is materially below 100,352 and unquantified: 23% of sampled permits returned zero outfalls, parameters and DMR rows; ~34.7% sit in state-eDMR jurisdictions for the file product; and the monthly-vs-annual monitoring split remains unknown after four lenses tried to resolve it.

Contract operators cut both ways and it is unresolved which dominates: the same firms that would buy the portfolio tier already fold DMR preparation into their service fee, so their alternative is their own labour rather than a purchase.

The D80/D90 enforcement-event email is legally clean (public record, opt-out, factual) but reputationally delicate; a single mis-framed subject line implying a violation would breach engine-never-arbiter in the marketing layer even while the product itself stays clean. Copy must be template-locked and reviewed as a mechanism claim.

The 526 MB weekly ETL is a hard operational dependency with known silent-failure modes: a terminated permit returns HTTP 200 with an empty PermFeatures array (AL0074373), and 13% of one permit's rows carry a null LimitValueNmbr. Undetected, these emit blank or wrong artifacts.

Effluent Labs, whatever it is, already occupies this positioning and its search surface; if it is funded rather than pre-revenue, the generic-keyword lane is closed and the strategy depends entirely on the permit-ID long tail ranking.

survivors.name: Filing Period (UK payment practices report)
survivors.candidate: C4 — Filing Period (UK payment practices report generator, SI 2017/395 + SI 2024/444 + SI 2025/75 + SI 2025/1152)

finding_triage.finding: Zero prosecutions in nine years; ministers on record that there has been 'not much enforcement' and 'no prosecution as yet'; ~40% report-level compliance with no consequence.
finding_triage.why: The Class A gate is zero enforcement AND zero intrinsic pain — both conjuncts fail here: DBT has written to 500+ firms with over half returning to compliance (Lord Leong, 15 Oct 2025), the Bill hands the SBC penalties up to 1% of UK turnover, and the regulator's own IA monetises the intrinsic job at £1,167–£1,585/yr per business that ~6,600 entities actually perform twice a year.

finding_triage.finding: Roughly 60% of legally required reports are never filed at all, so the criminal-liability urgency is theatre and may be evidence against willingness to pay.
finding_triage.why: It refutes the fear-based copy device, not the market: 11,178–13,000 reports a year are still genuinely filed at real cost by people who chose to do the job, and the product sells to filers, not to nine-year refusers.

finding_triage.finding: Commercial Payments Bill [HL] (introduced 19 May 2026, Lords Report stage 2026-08-14) is entirely absent from the card; new interest-paid/interest-owed reporting, board commentary duties and SBC enforcement will move the spec.
finding_triage.why: A live Bill that adds reporting duties and a funded regulator with 1%-of-turnover penalties is a tailwind for a maintained generator and a scheduled spec-revision event, not a disqualifying fact — and spec churn is the moat, not the risk.

finding_triage.finding: The construction retention block — one of only two differentiators over Sage X3 and D365 — is legislatively targeted for abolition (retention clauses void after a two-year transition).
finding_triage.why: It is a dated erosion of one narrow feature covering 13.6% of filings, arriving no earlier than 2028-29, against a regime extended to 6 April 2031 and simultaneously gaining new interest-reporting fields — a differentiator with a sunset, not a false premise.

finding_triage.finding: Premise misstatements vs primary text: retention block said to be 'mandatory from 1 Mar 2025' (SI 2025/75 reg 1(4): FYs beginning on or after 1 Apr 2025); 'DBT's 52-field published spec' does not exist (52 is the register export column count, 5 of them registry metadata); 'elements 4-6' vs SI 2025/1152 reg 1(4) applying the whole of Part 9; 'total number of payments' is Microsoft's framing, not a Schedule field.
finding_triage.why: The mandate itself verified verbatim on every load-bearing point (reg 2 filing period, reg 8 offence on company and every director, reg 9, SI 2024/444 sunset to 2031, SI 2025/75 Schedule 2, SI 2025/1152 in force) — these are commencement-scope and labelling errors in the copy that must be corrected, not a false artifact.

finding_triage.finding: 'One AP ledger CSV' is an incomplete input premise: SI 2025/75 Sch 2 para 10 defines sum B as retention withheld by the company's CLIENTS (receivables-side, ~13% of filers), SI 2024/444 para 14 makes a payment 'made' when received by the supplier not when the AP run clears, and the SI 2025/1152 directors' report block is group-consolidated and full-year.
finding_triage.why: This is a product-spec correction that changes the uploader and the disclosure copy — ask for a second extract where the law needs one, name the substitute date field on the face of the pack — and it is in fact the strongest evidence that the arithmetic is non-trivial enough to be worth paying for.

finding_triage.finding: Price ceiling published by the regulator sits below the product's price: DBT Final Stage IA central ongoing burden £1,195–£1,285/yr per non-construction business (£1,702 construction); the £99/month tier is ~99–102% of the entire annual cost of the obligation.
finding_triage.why: Explicitly a Class B price constraint — and it is the only observed anchor in the entire space, so it sets the number to price under rather than killing the company; only the £99/£349/£899 monthly ladder dies.

finding_triage.finding: Seasonality destroys the subscription shape: 73.1% of 2026 reports cover June/December period ends and 63.1% of all 2026 filings landed in January + July alone.
finding_triage.why: A packaging fact that mandates per-filing pricing (or an annual pass), which the corpus supports and which also fits under the IA's ~£350/report 'prepare' estimate — a shape correction, not a market fact.

finding_triage.finding: The group tier's evidence is a misread: of the 3,762 companies filing 2+ reports in 2026, 3,492 filed exactly two with distinct periods — the ordinary twice-yearly cadence of one entity, not multi-subsidiary groups; only ~270 filed 3+.
finding_triage.why: A misread that deletes the group-tier justification, but not the market signal — the unit the law uses (entity × period, ~13,000 filings/yr) survives intact once the tier is repriced off filings rather than fictional group structures.

finding_triage.finding: The card's data-quality pain signal is refuted by its own corpus: all 658 all-value-blank reports are nil returns, zero paying reports omitted the new value statistics, and only 1 of 819 retention reports has a blank ratio — the register shows a compliant, competent population.
finding_triage.why: It removes 'filers are visibly struggling' from the pitch and forces the honest thesis (time, cost and defensibility, not rescue), but real signals remain after removal — the IA's monetised burden, two ERP vendors funding recurring localisation, a top-10 firm's service line, and 30.2% of companies filing at least one report late.

finding_triage.finding: The register-driven GTM reaches the wrong half of the market — the acute non-compliers (~5,000–9,000 companies) never appear in the register at all.
finding_triage.why: A distribution constraint with a named free remedy the validator itself found: the Companies House Accounts Data Product (live, free, daily iXBRL) permits enumerating in-scope non-filers, and in any case the enumerable half is the half that pays.

finding_triage.finding: The enumerable buyer list is a minority of the obliged population and is shrinking: 7,538 distinct filers in 2019 → 6,340 in 2026 YTD, with only ~297–450 genuinely new filers a year and a threshold-uplift drop-out landing from 2027.
finding_triage.why: Small-but-real, flat-not-dead TAM is explicitly a constraint, not a kill — like-for-like Jan–Aug filers were 6,338 (2025) vs 6,340 (2026), and the base has held between 6,307 and 6,991 every year since 2018.

finding_triage.finding: TAM ceiling is roughly £3m/yr gross at 100% share (≈13,000 filings across ~6,600 entities), and lower after the April-2025 threshold uplift.
finding_triage.why: Small-but-real TAM is a Class B constraint; for a zero-marginal-cost unattended company a plausible 10–25% share is a low-six-figure annual business, which is a real outcome even if it is not a venture one.

finding_triage.finding: No price anchor of any kind: ten independent search angles across four lenses found no SaaS, no published consultant fee, no directory listing, no GitHub repo — willingness to pay is unproven in both directions.
finding_triage.why: Absence of an incumbent price is the classic contested-market ambiguity, not a disqualifying fact — and it is now partly resolved by the DBT IA (£700–£760/yr to prepare both reports) plus IA footnote 20's observed £3,000–£15,000/yr self-reported spend, thin as that evidence is.

finding_triage.finding: ERP bundling can close in one release and both vendors are shipping now (Sage X3 page dated 28 Jul 2026, D365 F&O ms.date 2026-05-12); D365 already exports per-vendor/per-payment detail and exposes the receipt-date parameter, pre-empting the workbook and lineage differentiators for its users.
finding_triage.why: Textbook Class B bundling: the bundled feature is documented as inadequate today (Sage X3 explicitly performs 'no amount-based calculations'; D365 ships no value sums, no retention, no directors' report block, and its own doc tells the user to go prepare the final report), and the exposure is confined to two ERPs out of the buyer's whole software landscape.

finding_triage.finding: Moat layer 3 is free — the public register as a pre-publication benchmark is a free first-party service, and Capitalise already surfaces payment performance in a free credit report.
finding_triage.why: A free substitute for one auxiliary feature; concede it entirely and demote benchmarking to a lead-generation surface rather than a priced layer — it never touched the core arithmetic.

finding_triage.finding: DBT now owns a modern, extensible service (rebuilt Jun–Dec 2024) and the Bill forces another change cycle; a CSV import would delete the keying friction the submission pack sells against.
finding_triage.why: A forward risk to one component of value, not a present fact — verified today: no upload route, no API, no calculator, no template, and DBT's own roadmap blog names none; and an import would still not classify invoices, apply reg 6 exclusions, compute value sums or retain lineage.

finding_triage.finding: Two outcome-claim landmines in the card's own copy: the PPN 018 sentence ('the number a company publishes gates its eligibility for £5m+ contracts') is an inference the PPN text does not support, and 27.2% is presented as a measured non-compliance rate when it is Filing date minus End date.
finding_triage.why: Engine-never-arbiter is violated by the marketing, not by the core value — the engine is pure arithmetic over the customer's own rows against published formulas behind a Companies House auth-code gate the product structurally cannot pass — so both sentences are struck and the mechanism framing survives.

reposition.one_liner: Filing Period turns a UK qualifying company's own AP ledger export — plus, where the law requires one, a client-retention extract — into the statutory payment practices report field-for-field in the order the GOV.UK publish service asks for it, with an invoice-level derivation workbook naming which date field, which exclusion rule and which speed band produced every figure; priced per filing, computed as arithmetic against DBT's published formulas, with the director reviewing, approving and publishing.
reposition.price: £149 per entity-report (standard) / £249 per entity-report where the SI 2025/75 construction retention block applies; £999/yr multi-entity pass covering up to 10 entities (20 filings) plus the SI 2025/1152 directors'-report payment block. THE ANCHOR IS THE REGULATOR'S OWN NUMBER: DBT's Final Stage Impact Assessment (Feb 2024, DBT024(F)-23-BG) puts 'prepare reports twice yearly' at £630/£700/£770 low/central/high per non-construction business — roughly £350 per report — with collate/approve/submit at £377 and a total ongoing burden of £1,195 central (£1,702 construction). £149 is ~43% of the government's own per-report preparation estimate; two filings a year is £298, ~25% of the total burden, leaving the director-approval and submission portion the product does not do clearly outside the price. Construction at £249 sits against a £1,051 prepare estimate. The £999 group pass prices at ~£50/filing against IA footnote 20's observed £3,000–£15,000/yr self-reported reporting spend (n<5, the only observed transaction range in the category). THE MONTHLY LADDER IS DEAD AND MUST BE DELETED: £99/month = £1,188/yr is 99.4% of the entire annual burden, and 63.1% of 2026 filings landed in January and July alone, so a subscription bills ten months a year for zero use. Per-filing is the only shape the corpus supports.
reposition.wedge: DBT PUBLISH SERVICE (free first-party): concede the entire eligibility-and-deadline half — /decide/ and /deadlines are free, good, and in the buyer's path, and a reminder product is why the prior ballot died. Flank on the half DBT publishes a spec for and prepares nothing of: its own words today are 'Once you've prepared all your report data, you must publish your report online.' No calculator, no template, no CSV upload, no API, verified 2026-08-20 (/api, /report/upload and /account/sign-in all 404). Residual pain to price: receipt-date convention (guidance: explicitly not the software posting date), reg 6 qualifying-contract tests, the four exclusions, value sums mandatory for FYs from 1 Jan 2025, the two retention ratios, and the derivation record. Design so keying convenience is never more than a third of the value, because a DBT CSV import would delete that third and nothing else. SAGE X3 (KUK, page dated 28 Jul 2026 — actively maintained): sharpest flank in the file. Its documented Excluded calculations list opens with 'Invoice, open item, or payment amounts' — value statistics are impossible in X3 by design, not by omission — and it ends 'you need to manually enter the data on the UK government website.' Every X3 filer must compute the mandatory value block somewhere else. DYNAMICS 365 F&O (ms.date 2026-05-12, ER v67.18): the weakest flank, so target it last. It already ships per-vendor/per-payment detail tabs and a receipt-date parameter, pre-empting the workbook and lineage story for its users. Position as the consumer of its export, not its replacement: ingest Payments_made/Payments_due and complete the value sums, the retention block, the directors'-report block and the assembled artifact — the three things its own doc declines, ending 'use the report data to prepare the final report about payment practices for publication.' BUSINESS CENTRAL (the mid-market ERP that actually serves this buyer, ms.date 2024-06-21): ships a generic global report producing average agreed payment period, average actual payment term and % within agreed period — the Swedish shape, not one field of the UK 0-30/31-60/61+ bands, and not updated for the 2024 or 2025 amendments. It produces zero usable UK output. XERO / QUICKBOOKS / SAGE 50/200 / NETSUITE (NetSuite UK Localization verified: payment formats and tax framework only, no payment-practices report): total absence of any helper. THIS IS THE BEACHHEAD — BC and the no-report packages first, X3 second, D365 last. FORVIS MAZARS + ACCESS GROUP 'bespoke reporting package': quote-only, unpriced, human-paced, and the Mazars page is stale enough to still cite 'BEIS' (abolished Feb 2023) and to call the duty 'annual' when it is twice-yearly. Flank on price transparency, same-day turnaround inside a 30-day window, and a machine-readable derivation record; and sell TO them as a self-serve multi-entity white-label back end rather than only against them. FREE REGISTER BENCHMARKING (gov.uk check service, Capitalise credit reports): concede outright. Benchmarking is a lead-generation surface and must never appear as a priced feature or a moat claim.
reposition.distribution: (1) PROGRAMMATIC SEO OFF THE OGL v3 REGISTER — the largest free surface, one nightly GET of check-payment-practices.service.gov.uk/export/csv/ (102MB, 52 cols, 114,624 reports, 10,235 named companies, live to yesterday). Page classes: one per company for all 10,235 ('<Company> payment practices report', '<Company> average time to pay', showing their own published history, days between period end and filing for each report, and sector percentile); ~700 SIC-sector distribution pages ('payment practices benchmark — <sector>'); period/deadline pages ('payment practices reporting deadline for period ending <date>'). Query patterns targeted: '<company> payment practices', '<company> average time to pay', 'payment practices report <sector> average', 'how to calculate payment practices value statistics', 'construction retention reporting SI 2025/75', 'directors report payment data SI 2025/1152'. (2) FREE-TOOL WEDGE — upload an AP CSV, get the count-based statistics (average days, the three bands, % not paid to terms) free, because that is precisely what D365 and Sage X3 already give away so it costs nothing competitively; pay for the value sums, the retention block, the directors'-report block, the assembled submission pack and the derivation workbook. Trial-by-doing with no human in the loop. (3) ENFORCEMENT-EVENT TRIGGER — the highest-intent list in the corpus, and the one that survives the 'you only reach people already doing the job' objection. DBT has written to 500+ firms and over half returned to compliance (Lord Leong, 15 Oct 2025); a company that returns to compliance publishes catch-up reports, and 992 of 2026's late filings are >90 days late with 860 reports >180 days late. A daily register diff names every late and catch-up filer, with company number, within 24 hours of publication — companies that have just been forced through the job manually and must repeat it in six months. (4) CALENDAR TRIGGER, PER ENTITY, FROM THE REGISTER — each company's period end + 30 days is computable from its own filing history, so outbound is dated, entity-specific and carries their own last-published figures; concentrated into the two real windows (January and July carry 63.1% of filings), not a year-round drip. (5) NON-FILER ENUMERATION VIA COMPANIES HOUSE ACCOUNTS DATA PRODUCT (free, live, daily ~100MB iXBRL zips) — tag turnover / balance sheet / employees, intersect against the register, produce the 'appears in scope, never filed' set that the register-driven plan is blind to. Ship it as a second-wave SEO surface ('does <company> have to report payment practices?'), not as the acquisition thesis, because that cohort has nine years of revealed preference for doing nothing. (6) SPEC-EVENT CONTENT — when the Commercial Payments Bill passes and its secondary legislation specifies interest-paid/interest-owed reporting and the persistent-late-payer board commentary, that is a new spec, a new field set and a fresh page class; a maintained generator is the natural landing page for every 'what do I have to report now' search. NO SALES CALLS, NO PARTNERSHIP MOTION, NO DEMOS ANYWHERE IN THIS PLAN.
reposition.why_winnable: The job is arithmetic over the customer's own rows against a formula the regulator publishes — one jurisdiction, one regulator, one HTTP GET, no scraper fleet, no per-customer human work, and the product literally cannot file or sign because the publish journey is gated behind a Companies House authentication code, so engine-never-arbiter is structural rather than promised. Nobody is in the market: ten independent search angles across four validation lenses found no SaaS, no published price, no directory listing and a GitHub search returning zero. Two ERP vendors fund recurring UK localisation and both stop at the identical line — no value sums, no retention, no artifact — and a top-10 accountancy firm staffs a service line for it, which is what a real recurring job looks like. The spec churns constantly (thresholds Apr 2025, value stats Jan 2025, retention Apr 2025, directors' report Jan 2026, a Bill in Lords Report stage now), and churn is exactly what an unattended maintained generator monetises and an ERP release train does not. THE HONEST DOUBT, STATED PLAINLY: willingness to pay is unproven at any number and the register shows a competent population with near-100% field completion, so there is no visible distress to rescue — the sale is time, cost and a defensible derivation record, not fear. The pitch cannot lean on criminal liability, which is legally exact and commercially inert after nine unprosecuted years. The gross ceiling is roughly £1.9m/yr at £149 across ~13,000 filings at 100% share of a flat-to-shrinking base with a known threshold-uplift step from 2027, so a realistic 10–25% penetration is a £200–500k/yr business — real for a zero-marginal-cost company, not a venture outcome. And the first build must be the free calculator with a live checkout behind the paid half, because the one thing that must be tested before anything else is whether a finance manager will actually pay £149 in a filing window.

residual_risks: WILLINGNESS TO PAY IS THE WHOLE BET AND IS UNTESTED. Not one price, invoice, quote or listing exists for this artifact anywhere; the nearest evidence is IA footnote 20's n<5, 5x-wide £3,000–£15,000/yr range. The £149 figure is derived from the regulator's cost model, not from anyone's observed purchase. Gate: a live checkout on the free calculator must convert before any further build.

DBT SHIPS A CSV IMPORT. The service was rebuilt Jun–Dec 2024 specifically because the original was 'hard to maintain and update', the codebase is now extensible, and the Bill forces another change cycle. No upload route or API today (verified: /api, /report/upload, /account/sign-in all 404), but an import would delete the keying-convenience third of the value. Mitigation is to keep keying convenience under a third of the value; watch the DBT digital blog and the publish service weekly.

SAGE OR MICROSOFT CLOSES THE VALUE-SUMS GAP IN ONE LOCALISATION RELEASE. Both are actively maintaining (X3 page 28 Jul 2026, D365 12 May 2026). If either adds the sum totals per band and the sum not paid within terms, the residual product is pack assembly, lineage and the directors'-report block. D365 shops are already partly pre-empted (per-vendor/per-payment tabs, receipt-date parameter) and should be the last segment targeted, not the first.

THE RETENTION DIFFERENTIATOR HAS A LEGISLATED DEATH DATE. The Commercial Payments Bill voids new and pre-existing construction retention clauses after a two-year transition. The £249 construction tier and the SI 2025/75 block have a horizon around 2028–29; the offsetting new interest-paid/interest-owed fields are not yet specified in secondary legislation, so the replacement revenue is promised, not scheduled.

SPEC AMBIGUITY THE PRODUCT MUST RESOLVE AND DISCLOSE, NOT SILENTLY DECIDE. SI 2025/75 Sch 2 para 10(1) requires a percentage 'of the difference between' sums A and B while para 10(2) gives the formula sum A / sum B x 100 (same conflict in para 11); DBT guidance resolves to the ratio. Similarly, SI 2025/1152 reg 1(4) applies the whole of Sch 7 Part 9 from FYs beginning 1 Jan 2026 while DBT guidance phrases it as elements 4 and 5 only. Every such divergence must be shown on the face of the pack with both readings named — this is reg 9 territory and the exact place an unattended engine could accidentally arbitrate.

GARBAGE IN ON THE RECEIPT DATE. SI 2024/444 para 14 makes a payment 'made' when received by the supplier, not when the AP run clears, and guidance says invoice receipt is not the software posting date — yet D365 defaults Receive document date to invoice date. The average-days statistic is wrong no matter how good the arithmetic if the field is wrong. The substitute field used must be named on the pack and in the workbook every time, never quietly substituted.

THE INPUT IS NOT ALWAYS ONE CSV. Retention sum B is receivables-side (company vs its clients) and absent from any purchase ledger for the ~13% of filers with qualifying construction contracts; the SI 2025/1152 block is group-consolidated and full-year. The uploader and the marketing must both stop claiming one-CSV universality, which narrows the frictionless case to the plain-vanilla non-construction single entity.

SEASONAL CASH AND SEASONAL CHURN. With 63.1% of filings in January and July, revenue arrives in two bursts and there is no monthly relationship to retain a customer between them; the persisted settings and lineage archive are the only retention mechanism and they are unproven as such.

TAM IS SMALL, FLAT, AND STEPS DOWN. ~6,340 distinct filers in 2026 vs 7,538 in 2019, only ~297–450 genuinely new filers a year, and ~6,000 companies economy-wide reclassify as medium under the April 2025 uplift with drop-out landing from 2027 (two-balance-sheet test). Model the ceiling at ~£1.9m/yr gross before committing build time.

TWO CARD STATISTICS ARE DEAD AND MUST NOT SURVIVE INTO MARKETING. The '696 blank value fields' signal (all nil returns) and the '3,762 group structures' claim (3,492 filed exactly two, ordinary cadence) are refuted by the corpus itself. The 27.2% figure must be restated as 'filed more than 30 days after period end' (30.2% of companies filed at least one such report), never as a measured non-compliance rate, and the PPN 018 register-gating sentence must be struck entirely — the PPN text does not reference the register.

REGISTER COUNTS DO NOT RECONCILE WITH DBT'S OWN STATISTIC. Local parse gives 13,308 reports filed in 2025 against DBT's published 11,178 valid reports, and at least one exact duplicate row exists. Any register-derived number used in a public benchmark page must carry a stated derivation and definition, or the SEO surface itself becomes an accuracy liability.

THE PUBLISH JOURNEY MAY ALREADY PREFILL NARRATIVE ANSWERS. It sits behind a Companies House auth-code gate that could not be tested. If DBT prefills last period's tick-box and narrative answers, a meaningful slice of the 'persisted answers' value evaporates on day one and cannot be discovered without a real filer's credentials.

THE REGIME HAS A LEGISLATED HORIZON. SI 2024/444 moves the sunset to 6 April 2031 with a review at 6 April 2029 — comfortable, but finite, and the review is a real decision point that a company built entirely on this one mandate must watch.

votes.rationale: Judged only on whether a company with nobody in it can get discovered at the moment of pain. C1 wins outright: CMS's own enforcement CSV (13,355 rows, monthly refresh, 953 warnings + 426 CAP requests in 2026, each with name, address, action and date — the validation calls it "the go-to-market, and it is free and public") is a named dated buyer list, and 45 CFR 180.50(d)(6)(i) forces every hospital to publish a price-transparency contact block in its own cms-hpt.txt, so the regulation itself manufactures a legitimate zero-human outreach channel; on top of that sit 5,196 genuinely-unique weekly-regenerated pages, a paste-a-domain free checker, and a novel vendor-defect dataset (PARA 404, HPI 400, cdmpricing soft-404) that is free earned media. B2 is next because its free tier structurally beats the first-party substitute (25 names vs OIG's hard 5-at-a-time cap), its counterparty packet is a permalink the agency mails to its hospital client — self-propagating acquisition with zero outbound — and its monthly LEIE digest pages compound precisely because OIG deletes its own supplements after 12 months; the OIG CMP settlement listing is a real recurring trigger. C2 owns the largest genuinely unoccupied long tail (100,352 permit IDs, county and parameter pages) plus the highest-volume trigger on the ballot (D80/D90 codes at 1,057 and 2,952 in a single 40MB sample, weekly), discounted only because a rural STP operator is not a searcher. B4 has the best raw event volume anywhere (26,807 office actions and 18,958 NOAs per day, each an owner about to search) and perfect buyer enumerability, but the register SERP is held by Justia/Trademarkia/TrademarkElite and cold mail is rightly excluded, so it is single-channel into a contested surface. B1's GitHub Marketplace Action and a canonical free KEV→CRA feed nobody publishes are real self-serve channels with a hard 11 Sept date, but buyers are not enumerable anywhere and the trigger fires ~0.88 times a day globally. STAR and B5 both have flawless buyer enumeration (CCN roster with addresses; NPPES taxonomy 302F00000X) and fixed statutory purchase calendars, but STAR's 14,693 facility pages draw families, attorneys and journalists rather than administrators and both free tiers already occupy the wedge, while B5's document surface is only ~3,000 pages and CLV has already shipped the identical GTM including free SEO pages. B8 has multiple working self-serve shelves (Apify, Zapier, Make, Slack directories) and a free CSV roll-up the auth-code-gated government tool structurally cannot copy, but UK company-data SERPs are among the most saturated anywhere and the credit/KYB buyer is unenumerable. C4's surface is perfectly unowned (zero SaaS, zero listings, zero repos) with per-entity deadlines computable from the register, but the total searcher pool is ~6,600 people twice a year and there is no contact channel. B6 fights a free incumbent holding the same corpus, a deeper archive and its own MCP server, and CAISO's file carries no developer name at all. B3 has its primary surface foreclosed by usdotwatch's 4.49M free pages and is pushed into negligent-hiring queries — the single most aggressively contested SEO vertical in existence — with only the forwardable tender PDF as a genuine asset. B7 is last and not close: two live SERP tests returned 18/18 page-1 slots to twelve incumbents, one monetising since 2004, the MCP/LLM channel is already taken by SponsorStats, and the fallback is invented queries the report itself concedes may have zero volume, aimed at transient individuals who cannot be enumerated.

Judged purely on whether the arithmetic closes at prices someone has actually been observed charging. B1 leads because it has the highest observed floor on the ballot with a live self-serve seller proving it — CVD Portal Free/€99/€299/€1,499 fetched 2026-08-19, sbomify Business $159/mo — so a €149 entry needs only ~250-300 forced regulatory buyers to be a real company, and the 11 Sep 2026 obligation date supplies the conversion trigger; the doubt is demand-side, not price. B2 and B5 follow because both sell into buyers whose alternative is payroll: B2's band is proven by eight vendors with live pages ($30/$40 capped, $89 uncapped, $249+$10-12/head bundlers inverting to $2,249/mo at 200 workers), so $59-349 sits inside a demonstrated clearing range with thousands of agencies to draw from; B5 meters the CRA-of-billing — $5/client NPI floors at $99 but lands at $200-1,000/mo per billing company against CLV's observed $749 Practice and $2,995 Agency, which is the best revenue-per-conversion on the ballot even if measured value density threatens retention. B3 is next on ARPU-versus-population: $79-199 sits under a proven $99/$149/$515 band in a buyer pool of tens of thousands of brokers, but $19-29 per-tender entries and latent (sued-or-not) pain make the realized ARPU fragile. C2 clears mainly because every functional competitor is quote-gated at $14,165-$27,140, leaving the entire sub-$100 card-swipe band structurally empty across ~50k+ qualifying permits — offset by a job measured at 10 cells and 20-40 minutes a month, which is thin at $468/yr. STAR and C4 are honest small utilities: $468/facility/yr against a $99 incumbent whose free tiers already cover the target segment (~$180k realistic), and £298/yr per filer against a regulator-published £1,195 burden but with nine years of zero prosecutions and a flat-to-shrinking 6,340-filer base capped near £1.9M gross. Below that the price floors fail. B6 keeps a decent $149-399 ask but has no observed buyer anywhere at that band and only ~1,300-5,000 filers against a genuinely good $0 incumbent. B8 is the textbook failure of my lens: the category clears at £7.50-£15/mo unlimited, PenaltyProof already died at £29, so a £29-149 ask must be carried entirely by an unevidenced artifact premium in an unsized buyer pool. C1 is bounded above by the incumbent's own admitted ~8 hours of labour (~$400-600/yr) and below by Craneware at literal $0 across only ~5,196 hospitals — its own author scores it at $60-100k. B4 chooses $79/yr against a $890/yr proven incumbent and a free USPTO push, so it needs ~2,500 paying owners off pSEO contested by Justia and Trademarkia — a £15/mo-shaped problem with no volume engine. B7 is worst: $99/yr to consumers with a one-quarter job-search lifespan, twelve free substitutes including one broader and free-always, an $79/mo API ceiling already set by an incumbent, and 18/18 page-one SERP slots occupied — the price is too low, the churn too fast, and the only channel is closed.

Judged only on who bleeds least with nobody at the console. C1 is the cleanest machine on the ballot: public data in, public data out, no customer upload at all (it fetches the hospital's own mandated-public URL), no PHI, no BAA, no security review, and the validation confirms the narrowest corpus anywhere here — one federal rule, one 13KB JSON schema, one CC0 validator (@cmsgov/hpt-validator 2.6.0, CC0-1.0), zero state layer, zero prose extraction, zero scraper fleet; its output asserts nothing but HTTP status and validator error codes, so blast radius is bounded to defamation hygiene on public pages, and $149 one-offs refund trivially. Six validator releases in 2026 is real churn but it is versioned, dated and fail-loud. B8 is second on the same logic at slightly higher fragility: one landlord, one jurisdiction, a free stream that hands you `fields_changed` as a server-side diff, no PII, deterministic template render — offset by a landlord who reserves the right to "ban without notice", a two-concurrent-connection ceiling on a whole-UK firehose, and unverified resale terms (dev ToS 404s). C4 third: one nightly unauthenticated GET of a 102MB OGL register, one regulator, one country, per-filing pricing (clean refunds, no "I paid ten months for nothing"), and the product structurally cannot file or sign because the publish journey is auth-code gated — its penalties are AP-CSV mapping support and a Jan/July burst pattern that concentrates inbound into two unattended windows. B6 and B3 next, both zero-customer-data and low-consequence, and I put B6 ahead because its architectural invariant (never render a future date, only observed cells with file provenance) makes its failures visibly empty rather than confidently wrong, despite three of seven sources behind Cloudflare walls (MISO domain-wide 403, PJM 403, gridstatus.io 403) and four schemas never read; B3 slips because the card's entire named pipeline was measured dead-while-reporting-fresh (zero rows after 2026-05-15 against rowsUpdatedAt of today), current baseline status exists in no bulk file, coverage of the Motus successors is ~103k of 1.86M USDOTs with no published coverage statement, and fmcsa.dot.gov 403s so the agency's own pages cannot be monitored — a confidently-wrong artifact here surfaces two years later in litigation. B4 sixth: corpus is actually redundant (verified 53MB daily zip plus statusview, maintenanceview and a free key), but the ingest is an undocumented incidental interface with no manifest, and it pairs the ballot's most terminal blast radius (a missed §8 is cancellation with no revival) with a watch tier whose text-only false negatives read as clearance — the worst shape for a silent one-day feed gap, cushioned only by USPTO's own free reminders. B5 seventh (stable free ungated CMS zips and a technical, low-headcount billing-company buyer, but an unbudgeted binary AMA licensing gate and empty-digest refund pressure from measured zero-hit quarters) then B7 (a single ingest path with inverted, undocumented UA behaviour — 403 to browsers, 200 to bare curl — no fallback, a quarterly cadence that hides a break for months, and a consumer horde on annual billing with a one-quarter job lifespan). Bottom four all fail multiple lens categories at once. B1: the target system is not live, the only field spec is FAQ prose, the format act is discretionary, weekly diffing is mandatory, and silent-green matching failure was demonstrated live (Debian vs Debian:12, aliases:null) — a machine that goes stale confidently on a 24-hour fuse while charging EUR149-899/mo for 0-2 events a year. STAR puts an LLM on agency-invoice PDFs feeding a signed federal submission with a different payroll format per facility, plus three unresolved post-iQIES platform unknowns — the highest support-load-by-design here. C2 asks the customer to certify a number under 40 CFR 122.41(k)(2) (symmetric catastrophe: over-compute self-reports a violation, under-compute is a false report) off ~47 jurisdictions of unmonitorable convention prose, with documented silent-failure modes (HTTP 200 on empty PermFeatures, null limit values). B2 is last and not close: unresolved FCRA classification would inject a statutory duty to answer consumer disputes (the definitive unattended-killer), DOB ingestion makes it an HR-PII processor inviting negotiated BAAs, monthly false-positive hand-back volume is unmeasured against 9.24% exact-name collisions, 44 state lists showed five ingestion patterns with email-only states that can never be automated, SEO pages name excluded parties, and a false negative hands the customer a $25,595-per-item exposure.

Judged only on whether the mechanism-only one-liner still sells, the ballot splits into three shapes. Shape one — the artifact a third party already demands — survives honesty untouched: B2 wins because OIG's own guidance defines the sellable thing as "documentation of the name search performed" and the hospital client contractually collects it, so "we document what the files said on a date; we never say anyone is clear" costs the pitch nothing (the buyer never wanted our opinion, they wanted the paper); STAR and C4 are the same shape in generator form — "your payroll pile / your AP ledger, in, spec-conformant file plus a line-by-line worksheet, out" is a pure labour-arithmetic sale that has never needed an outcome claim, which is why STAR ranks above C4 only on urgency (four fixed statutory deadlines and two exact case-mix-free hard triggers versus nine years of unprosecuted UK filings). C1 ranks third because it converts by demonstration rather than assertion: showing a CFO that their own cms-hpt.txt returns HTTP 400 today creates the alarm without anyone characterising it, and the free 5,196-page crawl is simultaneously the proof and the funnel — its handicap is that "so what?" can only honestly be answered with a ~1% penalty base rate. B3 and B1 both sell evidence for a future interrogation, and both one-liners are legible and vivid ("what the record said on the day you tendered"; "the timer is yours"); B1 in particular turns the compliance gate into the pitch — "we never start your clock" is a genuine counter-position to CVD Portal for counsel who has read FAQ 5.1 — but both are discounted because the pain is latent and the honest copy must forgo the fine anchor. Below that, honesty starts costing real money: B4's mechanism differentiator ("USPTO mails once to a decade-old address; we mail at T-180/90/30/7 to the address you bill from") is legible but emotionally thin once "never miss a deadline" is struck; C2's "EPA has recorded no value for a row that was due" is a strong factual alarm attached to a 10-cell, $815-lifetime-exposure job; B8's refusal to score is coherent to an auditor but is a negative sell against competitors whose £4,870 exposure figures are exactly what buyers click, and the one-liner is bloated past reading. The bottom three are gutted: B5's honest brief routinely says "0 of 1,847 codes touched" once the $41k exposure number is deleted, and a signed-off negative is a hard first sale; B7 can state only that a stale DOL snapshot moved, never the one thing the buyer wants to know; and B6 is fatal — the reposition amputates the countdown and then markets the amputation ("it never renders a deadline"), leaving a diff feed advertising the absence of the feature that justified it, against a free incumbent.

I rank purely on how few days stand between writing the first line of code and a stranger's card clearing, and how little has to exist for that to happen. C1 wins outright: the v1 is an HTTP fetch, `npm i @cmsgov/hpt-validator` (CC0, 2.6.0, verified live) and a literal diff against one 13KB schema and one CFR paragraph — no state layer, no prose extraction, no PHI, no BAA, and crucially zero customer input, because the crawl of 5,196 hospitals runs before any buyer exists and is simultaneously the product, the SEO surface and the lead list; the demand event is CMS's own monthly enforcement CSV (953 warnings + 426 CAPs in 2026), each row a named hospital with a contact email the regulation itself forces them to publish, and the ask is a $149 one-time swipe. B8 is second because the checkout is already proven to clear in that exact category (CompanyChangeAlerts, Companies On The Go, CHWatch all Stripe-billing today), the corpus is a free self-serve stream key, the v1 is a CSV paste → dated roll-up, and the ECCTA window is live right now — I only demote it below C1 because pasting company numbers is friction C1 doesn't have and the ARPU is £6–£29. B4 is third on the smallest single build on the ballot — one unauthenticated GET to tsdr.uspto.gov/maintenanceview returns the computed §8 dates in 2,155 bytes, so the free tool is essentially one HTTP call, the input is a registration number, billing is a flat $79/yr, and ~27k office actions and ~19k NOAs mail every single day, which is a continuously refilling pool of freshly-motivated buyers (the 1GB daily XML is a v2 problem, not a v1 one). B3 follows: a single DOT number in, a hash-sealed PDF out, $19 one-off, per-tender recurring trigger — docked only because the baseline capture depends on a QCMobile key whose rate limits are untested. B2 has a small build and a proven $25–$89 self-serve band, but the roster+DOB upload is real friction and the unanswered FCRA question is a legal gate that sits *before* code. B5 has the nearest hard date (Q4 NCCI files ~Sept 1, eleven days) and a clean $249 one-time entry, but a billing company must assemble per-NPI code lists across a book and the AMA licence is an unpriced pre-build unknown. B1 has the loudest calendar (11 Sept) and the largest v1 behind it — per-release SBOM ingestion wired into CI, evidence packets, SRP skeletons against a portal that isn't even live — so the deadline arrives before the product can. C2 and STAR both bury the dollar behind heavy ingestion (a 526MB+455MB weekly ETL plus ~47 jurisdictions of calculation prose; payroll exports plus LLM extraction from agency invoice PDFs feeding a federal filing) — STAR's input friction is the worst on the ballot and two free tiers already cover its segment at $0. B6 needs 4–7 churning ISO schemas and hand-typed queue numbers with no dated event and a genuinely good free incumbent. C4 has a pleasingly small build but its next real demand window is January 2027 — five months of nothing — which is disqualifying under this lens. B7 is last: 4–8 weeks of schema archaeology across three era layouts, a PERM form break and a 45MB worksites join, all before differentiation begins, against a $99/yr price, a quarterly corpus that won't refresh until November, and 18/18 page-one slots already held.
